docs.title: About the CiviCRM User Guide
docs.text: This page explains what belongs in this guide, how it relates to the System Administrator Guide, and where you can find help with searching or editing the documentation.

docs.title: Browse by content category
docs.text:
To match your learning needs, browse the documentation by content category:

  • Tutorials Learn CiviCRM through guided, practical lessons. Start here when discovering a feature or workflow.
  • How-to Guides Complete a specific task in CiviCRM. Use these guides when you know your goal.
  • Explanation Understand CiviCRM concepts, relationships and design choices.
  • Reference Look up fields, settings, options and product behaviour.

docs.title: What this guide covers
docs.text:
The User Guide is for CiviCRM users. It covers functionality available through CiviCRM’s web-based interface.

The System Administrator Guide covers installation, upgrades and some more complicated setup tasks. The guides overlap on some setup and configuration topics. In general, the User Guide covers actions you can perform within CiviCRM’s interface; the System Administrator Guide covers work outside it, such as tasks requiring file-system or shell access.

docs.title: Searching the documentation
docs.text: The docbot-extension provides a CiviCRM Dashboard widget for quickly searching the CiviCRM documentation. To use it in the dashboard, see installing an extension.

docs.title: Editing this guide
docs.text: This guide is made with MkDocs and stored in a GitLab repository. For simple editing instructions, see contributing to this guide. For a more in-depth tutorial, see writing documentation in the Developer Guide.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: The CiviCRM community writes this guide collaboratively, with facilitation from the Documentation Working Group. See History of this book for more details.

docs.title: Why CiviCRM is Free Software
docs.text: You will learn what CiviCRM’s Free Software licence allows you to do and why access to its source code matters to your organisation.

docs.title: What Free Software means
docs.text:
CiviCRM is developed by a community and is available for you to use free of charge for whatever you want. Free and Open Source Software is also called FLOSS, FOSS, Software Libre or Open Source. Anyone can download, share and change it.

You may never need to change CiviCRM or employ someone who can read its source code—the instructions written by programmers. The ability to do so still gives your organisation options:

  • You can use and customise the software free of charge.
  • Nobody can suddenly take away features or change the terms under which you may use the software and its features.
  • If CiviCRM lacks a feature you need, you can hire someone to create it or submit a feature request to the CiviCRM team.
  • Anyone with the necessary skills can fix a bug—an error in the software. Access to the source code can also help clients find bugs.
  • Community members can read the code, make changes and have more input into CiviCRM’s development than is traditionally possible with closed-source commercial software. People can try different implementations of a feature, and the community can choose one to make official by vote or consensus.

Unlike non-free software that a company might abandon if it goes bankrupt or discontinues a product, CiviCRM does not depend on one company’s decision to keep developing it.

docs.title: Free software and open source
docs.text:
The terms describe largely the same software: nearly any software that qualifies as free software also qualifies as open source, and vice versa. Free software emphasises your freedom from the control of the original programmers. Open source emphasises the convenience and potential for innovation that come from access to the source code.

The free software definition describes software that people can use, study, modify, copy and redistribute, whether modified or unmodified. Restrictions, if any, are minimal and intended to preserve those freedoms for later recipients and to allow users to modify their consumer-facing hardware. Free software is available gratis—free of charge—in most cases.

The open source software definition describes software whose source code and certain rights normally reserved for copyright holders are made available under a licence that meets the Open Source Definition, or that is in the public domain. People can use, change, improve and redistribute it in modified or unmodified forms. It is often developed publicly and collaboratively.

When you install and use CiviCRM, there is no click-through software licence imposing a long list of restrictions. Free and open source software does have licences, but they are simpler than and different from proprietary software (“closed software”) licences. CiviCRM is available under the Affero General Public License version 3.0, a free software licence used by many other projects.

docs.title: Why this matters for non-profits
docs.text:
FOSS projects, including CiviCRM, prioritise involving users in designing and building the software. Over time, this helps the software meet users’ needs and lets organisations exchange knowledge and experience indirectly. Using CiviCRM lets your organisation benefit from the experience of other non-profit and advocacy practitioners.

Access to the source code gives your organisation a degree of independence. Proprietary software usually cannot be customised to meet your specific needs; with FOSS, you can hire a developer or consultant to build the functionality you need. If you contribute those improvements to the project community, other organisations may use, test and improve them.

If a company providing closed software goes out of business, an organisation that relies on it may have to replace the software—an expensive and resource-intensive process. FOSS is less likely to have that single point of failure: if the main organisation behind a project closes or changes focus, its community can take over, form a new organisation and continue development and support.

There is also an overlap between the values of many non-profits and those of FOSS communities. Working with users, giving feedback and contributing your changes to the project can strengthen the non-profit sector.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Use this page to look up CiviCRM terms and technical words you may encounter while working with the guide.

docs.title: Accidental techie
docs.text: Someone who has inherited responsibility for IT technical support, although their main job is something else. They may have little or no formal IT training.

docs.title: Accordion
docs.text: A JavaScript effect that reveals or hides content on a web page without taking you to another page. The content may be described as collapsed or uncollapsed.

docs.title: ACL (Access Control List)
docs.text: ACLs define permissions for a group of contacts to perform an operation, such as viewing, editing or deleting, on a set of data or type of record. For example, an “Administrators” group could view and edit all contact records, while a “Volunteers” group could view them but not edit them.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text: In CiviCRM, an activity records a scheduled or completed interaction with one or more contacts. Examples include meetings, phone calls, emails, event attendances and contributions. You can define additional activity types.

docs.title: Admin / administrator
docs.text: A person who maintains a server or web-based software such as CiviCRM. Administration can include maintenance, configuration, backup, security, and creating or deleting user accounts.

docs.title: AGM (Annual General Meeting)
docs.text: A meeting held every year to inform an organisation’s members about its previous and future activities. Certain types of organisations are required by law to hold an AGM.

docs.title: AGPL (Affero General Public License)
docs.text: A license for open source software. CiviCRM uses the AGPL version 3.0 license, which gives you the right to use the software and ensures that its source code remains available under terms that protect those rights.

docs.title: Alpha version
docs.text: A software version containing very new source code, functionality and bug fixes. It is released for testing and for people following its development, not for general use.

docs.title: Apache
docs.text: Popular web server software that is free and open source. See also FLOSS.

docs.title: API (Application Programming Interface)
docs.text: An interface that lets one software application interact with other software.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: A copy of your data, stored independently of the original files so you can restore the data if necessary. Making backups regularly helps protect your data.

docs.title: Bandwidth
docs.text: The speed at which information can be transferred through a network or internet connection. A connection that can transfer a lot of information is described as “high bandwidth” or “high speed”.

docs.title: Beta version
docs.text: A software version that is in good condition but still needs testing before general release. Testing beta versions is one way to participate in the CiviCRM community.

docs.title: Blog
docs.text: Short for web-log: a website regularly updated with news and views from one or more people.

docs.title: Bug
docs.text: An error that prevents software from behaving as a user expects.

docs.title: Bug reporting / bug fixing
docs.text: Reporting bugs to software developers, then fixing them so the software operates as intended.

docs.title: Bug tracker
docs.text: A repository for recording bugs. CiviCRM bug trackers are at https://lab.civicrm.org/; the main core tracker is at https://lab.civicrm.org/dev/core/issues.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
A recent copy of frequently used data that can be accessed quickly, especially when generating the original data takes time or effort. Cached data can become out of date. Even a five-minute cache may help: if a page is accessed 1,000 times in that period, the data needs to be generated only once.

A web cache keeps copies of recently visited page files. You may sometimes need to clear your web cache to see updated information on a page.

docs.title: Canvassing
docs.text: Systematically contacting a target group of people, commonly during political campaigns. A campaign team or candidate may visit homes in a geographic area to speak with voters. Contact by telephone is called telephone canvassing.

docs.title: Captcha
docs.text: A spam-prevention tool. See reCAPTCHA.

docs.title: CiviCase
docs.text: The case-management component of CiviCRM. It gives service organisations tools to structure, schedule and record case activities.

docs.title: CiviContribute
docs.text: An online fundraising and donor-management component for tracking and managing contributions to your organisation.

docs.title: CiviCRM
docs.text: Web-based, open source software for recording and managing information about your constituents, including volunteers, activists, donors, employees, clients and vendors.

docs.title: CiviDog
docs.text: See Scout.

docs.title: CiviEngage
docs.text: A Drupal module that enhanced CiviCRM’s core functions for non-profits focused on community organising and civic engagement. CiviEngage is deprecated.

docs.title: CiviEvent
docs.text: A CiviCRM component providing integrated online registration and management for paid and free events.

docs.title: CiviMail
docs.text: A mass-mailing component for engaging constituents through personalised email blasts and newsletters.

docs.title: CiviPledge
docs.text: A component for creating different types of fundraisers and allowing individuals to donate daily, weekly, monthly or yearly.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
A term sometimes used instead of constituent or contact, particularly in the context of a financial transaction.

In computing, a client is a computer or application that accesses a remote computer, such as a web server, to receive information. Examples include a personal computer connected to the internet and an email application that downloads email from a server.

docs.title: Closed software
docs.text: Software whose source code users cannot access, unlike open source software. See also proprietary software.

docs.title: CMS (Content Management System)
docs.text: An application for creating, editing, managing, searching and publishing digital content, such as text, images and videos. A web-based CMS helps an organisation manage website content without advanced technical skills. Every CiviCRM instance must be integrated with a CMS—WordPress, Drupal, Backdrop or Joomla!—which helps facilitate client interaction.

docs.title: Component
docs.text: A type of extension that provides a major part of CiviCRM’s core functionality. Examples include CiviEvent and CiviCase.

docs.title: Community Advisory Group
docs.text: A representative group from the CiviCRM community that works with the CiviCRM team on project development.

docs.title: Cookie
docs.text: A file stored on your computer that a website uses to identify you when you return. Some websites require you to allow cookies before you can access them.

docs.title: Constituent
docs.text: A constituency is a group of people connected by shared identity, goals or loyalty. In CiviCRM, “constituents” means an organisation’s current or potential supporters. See also contact and client.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: In CiviCRM, an individual, organisation or household whose information is stored in the database. See also constituent and client.

docs.title: Contact Summary Screen
docs.text: A page that displays, at a glance, the information stored in CiviCRM about an individual, organisation or household.

docs.title: Core code
docs.text: The official source code of CiviCRM. Also called core.

docs.title: Core data field
docs.text: A field included in a record structure “out of the box”. For example, First Name is a core field in a CiviCRM contact record.

docs.title: Core Team
docs.text: The people most closely involved in CiviCRM development.

docs.title: CRM
docs.text: An acronym for Contact, Constituent, Customer or Client Relationship Management. CRM, or eCRM, software was originally developed to help companies organise interactions with current and potential customers. CiviCRM focuses on non-profits, advocacy organisations and non-governmental organisations, so it uses “constituent” rather than “customer”. Outside the USA, CRM is often called Contact Relationship Management.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text: A time-based job scheduler in Unix-like operating systems. It runs commands or shell scripts periodically, often to automate maintenance or administration. In CiviCRM, cron triggers tasks such as sending membership renewal reminders and processing ongoing payments, or runs enabled jobs on the Scheduled Jobs page at their configured frequency.

docs.title: CRUD
docs.text: Create, Read, Update and Delete: four basic database functions.

docs.title: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)
docs.text: A way to control a website’s design and layout through a file linked to its pages. Changing an element, such as heading formatting or background colour, in the CSS file can change it across the site.

docs.title: CSV (Comma Separated Values)
docs.text: A simple spreadsheet format understood by many programs. A CSV file is a text file with commas separating cells and returns separating rows.

docs.title: Custom data field
docs.text: A field your organisation adds to the structure of a CiviCRM record to store additional information. Examples include a contact’s professional qualifications or an event participant’s food preferences.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: A user’s homepage when they log in to CiviCRM. It can be personalised with dashlets.

docs.title: Dashlet
docs.text: A report on data in the CiviCRM database that appears on a user’s dashboard. Examples include monthly figures shown as a graph or numbers, appointments for the day, and new memberships.

docs.title: Data centralisation
docs.text: Storing all your data in one place.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: A collection of information organised so it can be accessed, managed and updated. Databases can be classified by content, such as bibliographic, full-text, numeric or image data.

docs.title: Demo site
docs.text: A website where you can test and explore software. CiviCRM maintains three demo sites: one integrated with Drupal, one with Joomla! and one with WordPress.

docs.title: Dedupe
docs.text: Finding and merging multiple entries for one contact.

docs.title: Developer
docs.text: Someone who develops software.

docs.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
docs.text: A system that converts easy-to-remember domain names, such as example.com, into numeric IP addresses, such as 123.456.123.234. Each computer on the internet has a unique address, somewhat like an area code and telephone number.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text: See DNS.

docs.title: Donor
docs.text: Someone who voluntarily gives money to an organisation.

docs.title: Drupal
docs.text: An open source CMS that integrates with CiviCRM to provide a user interface and additional website functionality. See http://drupal.org.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: A way to disguise data while it moves between computers so that other computers it passes through cannot read it.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: The hardware and operating system on which your software runs.

docs.title: Event listing feed
docs.text: An RSS feed listing events defined in CiviEvent.

docs.title: Extension
docs.text: A package of CiviCRM functionality that can be installed, enabled, disabled or uninstalled on a site for particular uses.

docs.title: Firefox
docs.text: A free, open source web browser developed by the Mozilla Foundation. See http://www.mozilla.org.

docs.title: FLOSS (Free/Libre Open Source Software)
docs.text: Software licensed to protect users’ freedoms to access and reuse its source code. The term combines “free software” and “open source software”; “libre” emphasises that freedom concerns rights, not price.

docs.title: FOSS
docs.text: Free and Open Source Software. See FLOSS.

docs.title: Forum
docs.text: A web-based discussion tool. See http://forum.civicrm.org/.

docs.title: Free software
docs.text: Software licensed so you can use and distribute it without restriction. CiviCRM is free software. See also FLOSS.

docs.title: FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
docs.text: A protocol for transferring files between computers over the internet. It can be used for downloads and for uploading files to web servers. FileZilla is a free, open source FTP client for Windows; web-based FTP clients can also be used through a browser such as Firefox.

docs.title: Functionality
docs.text: The tasks a piece of software can perform.

docs.title: Geocoding
docs.text: Finding geographic coordinates, often latitude and longitude, from information such as a street address or postal code.

docs.title: GUI (Graphical User Interface)
docs.text: An interface with features such as windows, icons, mouse controls and multiple fonts. It is the usual way for non-programmers to interact with computers; an alternative is a text-only command line interface.

docs.title: Hook
docs.text: A way to extend CiviCRM functionality, add business logic or integrate CiviCRM with external systems.

docs.title: Household
docs.text: A family or group of people who share a physical location.

docs.title: Hosting service
docs.text: A service, usually commercial, that provides server space for a website. It may also provide physical space for your own server and connect it to the internet.

docs.title: ICT
docs.text: Information and Communication Technology.

docs.title: Internationalisation: i18n
docs.text: Preparing software for use in different countries and cultures without requiring technical changes for each one. A developer does this while writing the software. See also localisation.

docs.title: Internet Service Provider (ISP)
docs.text: A business providing services such as internet access, email and website hosting.

docs.title: Intranet
docs.text: A network of computers connected within a home or office that cannot be accessed from outside the local network.

docs.title: IT
docs.text: Information Technology.

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text: A scripting language used primarily to display dynamic content on web pages.

docs.title: Joomla!
docs.text: A CMS that can integrate with CiviCRM to provide a user interface and additional website functionality. See http://www.joomla.org.

docs.title: LAMP
docs.text: An acronym for a stack of free, open source software used to build a general-purpose web server. It originally referred to Linux, Apache HTTP Server, MySQL and Perl/PHP/Python.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text: An operating system, like Windows or Mac OS. Linux has long been popular for web servers and is also used on personal laptops and desktop computers. It is free software and open source.

docs.title: Local computer
docs.text: A computer running CiviCRM that is not publicly available over the internet, such as a home or office computer. In the context of receiving information from a server, it can also be called a client computer.

docs.title: Localisation: L10n
docs.text: Translating a product into other languages or adapting a language for a particular country or region. Translators can do this without making technical changes. See also internationalisation.

docs.title: Mail server
docs.text: A computer that transfers email from one computer to another.

docs.title: Mapping provider
docs.text: A service that lets CiviCRM display contact locations on maps. Examples include Google Maps and Yahoo Maps.

docs.title: Module
docs.text: Sometimes used to mean extension.

docs.title: MySQL
docs.text: A popular database engine that CiviCRM uses to store its data. MySQL is free software. See http://mysql.com.

docs.title: NGO (Non-Governmental Organisation)
docs.text: A legally constituted, non-business organisation without government participation or representation. In the United States, such an organisation is more often called a non-profit. Other terms include civil society organisation and not-for-profit.

docs.title: Non-profit
docs.text: See NGO.

docs.title: Online contribution page
docs.text: A CiviCRM function for creating a website page where visitors can make online donations by credit card.

docs.title: Open ID
docs.text: A free system for using one digital identity across the internet.

docs.title: Open source software
docs.text: Software whose source code is publicly available, unlike proprietary software. Its underlying idea is that sharing and collaborating on code leads to better software and wider benefits. See also FLOSS.

docs.title: Payment instrument
docs.text: The medium or method used for online payments.

docs.title: Payment processor
docs.text: A company, usually a third party, appointed by a merchant to handle credit card transactions for merchant banks. A payment processor is required for online transactions through a system such as CiviCRM.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Controls that limit different users’ access to different parts of a system.

docs.title: Personal Campaign Pages
docs.text: A CiviCRM feature that can be enabled to let constituents create their own fundraising pages.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text: The programming language in which most of CiviCRM is written.

docs.title: Ping
docs.text: Sending and receiving small amounts of data to and from a server, often to measure response time across a network.

docs.title: Point person
docs.text: Someone responsible for keeping an eye on a particular issue.

docs.title: PhoneBank List
docs.text: A list created with CiviReport to help volunteers call many constituents. Calls may invite people to vote, volunteer, take action or donate.

docs.title: Premium
docs.text: A gift offered to a contributor in exchange for a donation. CiviCRM allows premiums to be offered as part of fundraising.

docs.title: Price Sets
docs.text: A way to store and reuse complex event prices. For example, you can charge for different elements of an event.

docs.title: Primary location
docs.text: The contact information a constituent wants used as their main point of contact, such as for mailings.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: Sets of fields for collecting, modifying and sharing data. See Profiles for more information.

docs.title: Proprietary software
docs.text: Also called closed software or closed source software. Its license prevents you from accessing and modifying the source code without first reaching an agreement with its authors. See also open source software.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text: An agreed method of doing something. HTTP specifies how website data is transferred across the web; SMTP specifies how email is transferred.

docs.title: Radio button
docs.text: A web-interface element that lets you select one option from a predefined set. It is usually shown as a circle that can be filled by clicking it.

docs.title: reCAPTCHA
docs.text: A tool for testing whether a user is a person or a computer, used to prevent spam.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: The things you need a particular software application to do.

docs.title: Rich text editor
docs.text: A text editor that lets you format text, including making it bold, italic or underlined, rather than working only with plain text.

docs.title: Root domain
docs.text: The basic URL of a website, without www or another subdomain. For example, http://civicrm.org/ is a root domain, while http://www.civicrm.org/ is not.

docs.title: RSS (Really Simple Syndication) feed
docs.text: A way to publish frequently updated information for inclusion on a website or reading in an RSS reader.

docs.title: RSVP
docs.text: From the French “Répondez s’il vous plaît”, meaning “please respond”. It is commonly used to request confirmation or declining of attendance at an event.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: A short program that performs one task. Web pages often use scripts to manage interactions without requiring the server to send a new page after every change.

docs.title: Scout
docs.text: The CiviCRM Book Sprint’s official dog. Scout likes dog biscuits, rolling on the ground, eating snow and proofreading.

docs.title: Sendmail
docs.text: A popular mail transfer agent (MTA) for handling email on a server. Sendmail is free and open source software.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The term has two meanings:

  • Software that serves content to a client, such as Apache or a mail server.
  • A computer used primarily to serve content. Any computer can be set up this way, although the term traditionally refers to computers delivering web content. See also client computer.

docs.title: Shared hosting
docs.text: A website hosting service in which multiple websites reside on one server.

docs.title: Smart Group
docs.text: A CiviCRM group whose contacts are assigned automatically. You create one by running and saving a search. It is useful when membership may change frequently—for example, a group based on “donations over $1000 in the last month”.

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: a standard protocol that email software uses to send email.

docs.title: Soft Credit
docs.text: A way to credit a contact for a donation someone else made—for example, the person who inspired the donor to give. See Personal Campaign Pages.

docs.title: Software
docs.text: Applications, also called programs, that perform tasks on a computer. Categories include web browsers, word processors and email clients. Each category has different products: Firefox and Internet Explorer, for example, are web browsers.

docs.title: Software license
docs.text: The terms you must accept before using a piece of software.

docs.title: Source code
docs.text: The instructions written to create software. These instructions are also called code.

docs.title: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer)
docs.text: A way to make internet communication secure. The source describes a URL beginning with https, rather than http, as an indication that the connection uses SSL.

docs.title: SSL certificate
docs.text: A certificate a server provides to prove its identity, much as a person might use a passport or driving license. See also SSL.

docs.title: Stable version
docs.text: A software version that has been tested and is considered ready for general use.

docs.title: Token
docs.text: Tokens insert elements such as a contact’s name or a standard greeting into emails sent from CiviCRM. In an email sent to a group, {first.name} is replaced with each recipient’s name in the message they receive.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text: Replacing software with a newer version. An upgrade may fix bugs, improve security, keep the software working with upgraded operating systems, or add features and other improvements.

docs.title: URL
docs.text: Given here as an acronym for Unique Resource Locator and sometimes referred to as a Universal Resource Indicator, or URI. A URL identifies where a resource, such as a web page, is located on a network. For example, www.civicrm.org is the URL for CiviCRM.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text: A story or scenario describing someone completing a specific task with a software application. In software development, a use case generally focuses on real-world objects and events rather than technical or database terms such as “fields” or “record”, so people without technical knowledge can understand it.

docs.title: Version
docs.text: A release of software. Releases occur periodically and can have different levels of readiness: a stable version has been tested for general use, while an alpha version is very new and untested.

docs.title: VPN (Virtual Private Network)
docs.text: A way for members of an organisation to share information over encrypted connections.

docs.title: Walk List
docs.text: A list created with CiviReport to help volunteers go door-to-door, often for voter engagement.

docs.title: Web application
docs.text: Software that adds functionality to a website. CiviCRM is a web application.

docs.title: Webmail
docs.text: An email service used through a website. It sends and receives messages as other email services do, but lets you read and manage them through a web interface instead of a mail client such as Outlook Express or Thunderbird on your computer. One free example is https://mail.google.com/.

docs.title: Web-server
docs.text: A computer equipped with software and networking capabilities to deliver web pages over the internet or an intranet. Web servers use programs such as Apache or IIS to deliver pages over the HTTP protocol.

docs.title: Wiki
docs.text: Web-based software that lets people edit content through a browser. Wikipedia is a well-known example.

docs.title: Wildcard
docs.text: A character that matches any number of characters, normally written as *. In a search, ab* finds ab, abba and abracadabra, but not fabulous; *ab* finds fabulous.

docs.title: WordPress
docs.text: The source describes WordPress as the most popular CMS on the internet. CiviCRM has integrated with WordPress since CiviCRM version 4.1 and WordPress version 3.3.1. Before those versions, CiviCRM did not work directly with WordPress, although a Drupal/CiviCRM installation could run alongside WordPress on the same server.

docs.title: Work station
docs.text: A computer used for work, often in an office with other computers, which may include servers.

docs.title: WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get)
docs.text: A visual editor that shows how web content will look in a browser while you edit it, instead of requiring you to work in HTML code. See also rich text editor.

docs.title: History of this book
docs.text:
This page explains how contributors created and revised the CiviCRM manual. Much of its content was written during book sprints held in Tahoe, USA, in 2009 and

  1. Individuals also contributed between and after the sprints.

docs.title: Fifth edition
docs.text:
The fifth edition was written at the Woolman Sierra Friends Centre (woolman.org) in April

  1. Woolman uses and contributes to CiviCRM. We are grateful for their hospitality.

docs.title: Fourth edition
docs.text:
The fourth edition was written in Bourne, Lincolnshire, UK, in September

  1. We were too busy writing to say much about how it was put together.

docs.title: Third edition
docs.text:
The third edition includes minor updates reflecting changes in CiviCRM 3.3, which was released in December

  1. It was published on the eve of the second annual CiviCon conference. Thanks to the generous contributions of the CiviCon Sponsors listed in the front of the book, each conference participant received a copy.

docs.title: Second edition
docs.text:
The second edition was published after a four-day Book Sprint organised by CiviCRM and led by Adam Hyde of FLOSS Manuals. The sprint was sponsored by the Information Program initiative of the Open Society Institute. We are especially grateful to Janet Haven for pushing it forward.

This edition added sections on CiviReports, CiviCase, CiviEngage and Extending CiviCRM, as well as a section to help developers get into the code. Nearly every section was extensively rewritten. The material was reorganised into Introduction, Planning, Configuration and Everyday Tasks, with the last intended as an easy-to-follow manual for people working with CiviCRM daily. The book was also updated to match CiviCRM 3.2, which was a few weeks away from release at the time of writing.

We felt that the reorganisation made the book easier to read and helped people working with CiviCRM in different capacities find the chapters relevant to them.

The following photo shows the people who worked on the second edition.

In the back row, from left to right, are Dave Greenberg (San Francisco, USA), Kyle Jaster (NY, USA), Xavier Dutoit (Geneva, Switzerland and Brussels, Belgium), Kurund Jalmi (Mumbai, India), Michael McAndrew (London, UK), Wes Morgan (Washington DC, USA) and Josue Guillen (DC, USA). In the front row, from left to right, are Jack Aponte (NY, USA), Mari Tilos (San Francisco, USA), Sarah Gladstone (Chicago, USA) and Alice Aguilar (NY, USA).

docs.title: First edition
docs.text:
The first edition was written during a five-day book sprint organised by CiviCRM and led by FLOSS Manuals. The sprint was sponsored by the Information Program initiative of the Open Society Institute. We are especially grateful to Janet Haven for pushing it forward.

With sponsorship secured, the CiviCRM Core team invited people from around the world to gather for a week at Lake Tahoe in California. Our modest goal was to turn our varied experience of CiviCRM into a manual that would help people use the software. It was an interesting and, at times, difficult challenge.

The following photo shows the people who wrote the first edition.

In the back row are Michael McAndrew (London, UK), Tony Guzman (Salt Lake City, USA), Brian Shaughnessy (Albany, NY, USA), Dave Greenberg (San Francisco, USA), Yashodha Chaku (Mumbai, India) and Adam Hyde (Berlin, Germany). In the front row are Mari Tilos (San Francisco, USA), Cynthia Tarascio (Philadelphia, USA), Michal Mach (Warsaw, Poland) and Peter Davis (Wellington, New Zealand). At the very front is Eileen McNaughton (Wellington, New Zealand).

We came from different backgrounds, used CiviCRM in different ways and worked with very different organisations. Bringing those perspectives together was challenging, but we felt it made for a better book. We discussed whether to use a “z” or an “s” in organisation/organization, and a “q” in cheque/check, before agreeing to use both spellings in the spirit of internationalism. We also struggled with constituent: a core term in the American non-profit sector that was unfamiliar to contributors from elsewhere.

The five days were intense. Adam kept us realistic, on track and working hard, even bringing us back to work after dinner each evening. It was also fun and productive, and we appreciated his help in producing a book within a week. Thank you, Adam.

For many of us, the highlight was the food cooked by Jill Klein. We wish we could take you home with us, Jill. We are also grateful to Dave Greenberg, Bob Concannon and Mari Tilos for their hospitality, and to Scout, also known as “CiviDog”, for being there.

We had help from around the world before and during the sprint. Andy Oram helped with planning, then provided editing and feedback during the sprint. Others logged in to write and edit the manual: Robert Santiago, Xavier Dutoit, Joe Murray, Sarmeesha Reddy, Jay Maechtlen, Dream Gomez, Leila Johnson, Duncan Hutty and Kurund Jalmi.

Our office for the week was Dave and Bob’s house.

We eased the late-night work with some tasty beverages.

Occasionally, we got to go outside, too.

docs.title: Campaign dashboard and fields
docs.text: Use this reference to identify the controls for managing campaigns and the information you can record for each campaign.

docs.title: Campaign Dashboard
docs.text:
Go to Campaigns > Dashboard > Campaigns to view the Campaign Dashboard. From there, you can create campaigns and Edit, Disable or Delete existing ones. You can also manage surveys and petitions; see Surveys and Petitions for specific information.

If you have many campaigns, open the campaign search accordion and set filters to display the campaigns you want to see.

docs.title: Campaign fields
docs.text: Field Description Title Required. A unique name that describes the campaign. A naming convention can make campaigns appear in a useful alphabetical order in drop-down lists and easier to find when associating an activity with a campaign. Campaign Type Required. Select a type, such as Constituent Engagement. See setting up CiviCampaign to add options to the drop-down list. Description Text that describes the campaign. Include group(s) If appropriate, select the group containing the individuals you are targeting. See Tags and Groups for information about creating groups. Start Date & Time Required. The campaign’s start date and time. End Date & Time The campaign’s end date and time. If these fields are empty, the campaign is considered ongoing. Campaign Status Select a status, such as In Progress or Planned. See setting up CiviCampaign to add options to the drop-down list. Campaign Goals Text describing the campaign’s goals or objectives. You can also describe the activities you plan to carry out to meet them. Revenue Goals If applicable, a number indicating the amount you plan to raise during the campaign. External ID The campaign ID from another database, if you want to track the ID of a campaign that existed there. Is Active? Check the box for an active campaign; uncheck it for an inactive campaign.

docs.title: Coordinate campaign outreach and events
docs.text: Use a campaign when organising mailings, events and contributions, and record who participates in an event.

docs.title: Target a group
docs.text: To target specific individuals for campaign activities, create a group containing those individuals. See Tags and Groups for instructions on creating a group.

docs.title: Send a mass mailing
docs.text:
A mass mailing to your target audience can generate interest and participation or ask for donations.

  1. Create the email using CiviMail. See Email for information about configuring and using CiviMail.
  2. Select the appropriate campaign from the drop-down list when setting up the mailing.

docs.title: Promote an event
docs.text:
Events created using CiviEvent can be associated with a campaign.

  1. Create and configure the event.
  2. Select the appropriate campaign from the drop-down list when setting up a mailing for the event.
  3. Send a mass email using CiviMail to your target audience, using a group or groups, and ask people to register for the event.
  4. Select the campaign name on the mailing set-up.
  5. Search for individuals who have indicated that they want to register for the event.

docs.title: Record campaign contributions
docs.text: When recording an online or offline contribution, select the appropriate campaign from the drop-down menu to associate the contribution with it. See Contributions for information about configuring and using CiviContribute.

docs.title: Record event participation
docs.text:
During or after an event, you can collect sign-in sheets and enter participants manually, or record participation directly online. Ask participants to write their contact information on sign-in sheets when they arrive. If you have an internet connection at the venue, you may be able to enter participants directly into the database.

See Events for information about recording participant information.

docs.title: Create a campaign
docs.text:
Create a campaign by entering its required details and any other information your organisation needs.

  1. Go to Campaign > New Campaign.

  1. Enter a unique, descriptive Title.
  2. Select a Campaign Type.
  3. Enter the Start Date & Time.
  4. Complete any other fields that apply to your campaign, such as Description, End Date & Time, Campaign Status or Campaign Goals. If you leave End Date & Time empty, the campaign is considered ongoing.
  5. Click Save to save the campaign.

docs.title: Campaign searches and reports
docs.text: Use this page to look up where you can search by campaign and which reports can show campaign information.

docs.title: Campaign searches
docs.text: Searches for components that can be part of a campaign, such as events and contributions, include a campaign filter. The component tabs in advanced search also include a campaign filter, so you can find contacts based on their participation in campaigns.

docs.title: Campaign reports
docs.text:
There is no specific campaign report because a campaign can include many components. Once CiviCampaign has been enabled, you can add a column showing the associated campaign to contribution, pledge, event, mailing and membership reports. You can also filter these reports by campaign to restrict the records displayed.

The activity report can display both the campaign and the engagement index. You can filter it by either criterion or by both.

docs.title: Set up CiviCampaign
docs.text: Enable CiviCampaign, then configure the campaign types, statuses and engagement index your organisation needs to track related contributions, surveys, mailings and other activities.

docs.title: Enable CiviCampaign
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > System Settings > Components.
  2. Select CiviCampaign.
  3. Click Enable.
  4. Click Save.

The Campaigns menu item appears along the top of your CiviCRM screen.

docs.title: Add a campaign type
docs.text:
CiviCampaign provides three default campaign types: Direct Mail, Referral Program and Constituent Engagement. You can add types that suit your work and disable those you do not use.

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCampaign > Campaign Types. The page lists the existing campaign types.

  1. Click Add Campaign Type.
  2. Enter a label.
  3. Optionally, enter a description.
  4. Optionally, change the default weight. Smaller numbers place the type higher in drop-down menus.
  5. Click Save.

The new type is available to assign the next time you add a campaign.

docs.title: Add a campaign status
docs.text:
A campaign status helps you track a campaign’s stage internally. The default statuses are Planned, In Progress, Completed and Cancelled.

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCampaign > Campaign Status.
  2. Click Add Campaign Status.
  3. Enter a name.
  4. Optionally, enter a description.
  5. Optionally, change the weight to control where the status appears in drop-down menus.
  6. Click Save.

The new status is available to assign to campaigns.

docs.title: Configure the engagement index
docs.text:
The Engagement Index lets you record an individual’s level of interest or engagement in an activity. It can apply to general activities or actions such as Send an Email, Meeting, Phone Call and Interview, as well as additional custom activities or actions you create. It can supplement your outreach employees’ or organisers’ assessment of a member’s engagement or interest in your organisation. For information about recording an activity for an individual, see Contacts in the Organising Your Data section.

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCampaign > Engagement Index.
  2. Configure the index using numbers. For example, 1 can represent high engagement and 5 low engagement.

docs.title: What is CiviCampaign?
docs.text:
CiviCampaign brings related work together under one campaign so your organisation can track progress towards a programmatic goal and assess the effectiveness of its outreach and mobilization.

You can link events, mailings, activities and contributions to a campaign. Because CiviCampaign is integrated with other CiviCRM components, you can choose which activities belong to the overall campaign or goal. You can also use it to:

  • create surveys and petitions, and record responses to them;
  • track who has voted using Get Out The Vote (GOTV);
  • record individual members' levels of interest and engagement in a particular activity.

docs.title: Example: A year-long mobilization campaign
docs.text:
The Townsville Organisation For Tenants (TOFT) began a year-long effort to mobilize community members with a protest at the Capitol. Its lead organiser created a campaign called “Mobilize the Masses 2011” to connect communications about the event, participation, and financial contributions for transport and food.

The organisers used CiviCampaign to bring the work together:

  • They created a Campaign as an umbrella for related activities, including its duration and revenue goal.
  • They created a group of people to target for campaign activities.
  • They called their most active members to help organise other constituents in their neighborhoods. They recorded each phone call as an activity in the individual's record, with the campaign and the member's response.
  • They sent a mass fundraising mailing and indicated the campaign. The campaign was then recorded in the contribution information of individuals' records.
  • They created an event to track who would attend the mobilization and indicated the campaign in the event setup.

Throughout the year, the program lead periodically searched for activities related to the campaign and/or individuals with campaign-related activities. This helped them monitor outreach and fundraising effectiveness and adjust strategies if needed. Organisers could link later events, mailings and other activities to the same campaign, then review the information in the context of the whole campaign at its end.

docs.title: How CiviCampaign supports campaign planning
docs.text: CiviCampaign can work alongside your organisation's existing strategies and processes. Understanding what you want to achieve and what you need to record will help you decide how to use it.

docs.title: Goals and revenue
docs.text: Define your campaign's concrete goals and, if applicable, how much you hope to raise. Record these in the campaign information so you can use reports to analyse the campaign's effectiveness when it concludes.

docs.title: Activities and information
docs.text: As you plan your strategy and identify your target audience, consider which activities and information you can record in CiviCRM. Connect what you record to the campaign so you can track campaign efforts and individuals' activities. This gives you information for periodic reviews and an overall evaluation of your activities, strategies and outreach.

docs.title: Questions to consider
docs.text:
For your organisation or a specific campaign, consider:

  • Who is your target audience, and how will you reach them? The people involved in your campaign activities may differ from the people the campaign itself aims to reach. Knowing the difference can help you choose strategies and communication activities that support your goals.
  • Which activities and strategies, such as events and mailings, will be associated with the campaign?
  • How will you gather data, such as surveys, petitions and event registrations? Who will enter it into CiviCRM?
  • Which reports will help you monitor progress and evaluate the campaign when it concludes?

docs.title: Find a case
docs.text: Search by Case ID when you know it, or use the case search form to narrow down cases by client, type, or status.

docs.title: Search by Case ID
docs.text: Use full-text search at Search > Custom Search > Fulltext Search. You can also use the fulltext search block if it has been enabled.

docs.title: Filter cases
docs.text:
1. Open Search > Find Cases, or find Cases in the menu bar at the top of the CiviCRM screen.
  2. Choose one or more of these search criteria:
  3. Client name or email: Enter characters from the client’s name or email address in Client name or email.
  4. Case type: Check the case types you want.
  5. Case status: Select a status from the dropdown menu.
  6. All cases or your cases: If you do not select all cases, the search defaults to your cases.
  7. Deleted cases: Check Deleted cases to include them.

You can use a criterion on its own or combine criteria. When you use different sets of criteria, a result must meet at least one selection in each set: for example, it must match the client name and a selected case type. When you make several selections within one set, a result needs to match at least one of them: for example, either of two selected case types.

docs.title: Open a new case
docs.text: You can open a case for a contact already in CiviCRM or create the contact and case together.

docs.title: Open a case for an existing contact
docs.text:
Starting from a contact’s summary screen or Actions menu automatically links the case to that contact.

  1. Open the contact’s summary screen.
  2. Select Add Case from Actions, or click the Cases tab.
  3. Complete the required fields in the Add Case form.
  4. Click Save.

docs.title: Open a case for a new contact
docs.text:
When you open a case for a new contact, CiviCRM creates the contact record at the same time.

  1. Go to Cases > New Case or select Create New > Case. The Create New button is provided as a block in Drupal or on the left-hand side in Joomla!.
  2. To check whether the contact already exists, type their name or email address in Select Contact. Potential matches appear as you type.

  1. If you do not find the contact, select a contact type from create new contact. A pop-up window opens so you can enter the contact’s name and other information while opening the case. Its fields are controlled by the Add Individual profile, so those fields can be added or modified. For more about profiles, see the Profiles chapter.
  2. Complete the case fields that apply. The following details can help you choose what to enter:

  3. Medium and Location record where and how the case came to your attention. For example, you might select In Person for Medium and At the Annual Gala for Location. You can manage Encounter Mediums with the edit icon.

  4. Details holds information about the overall case, rather than a specific activity. For example: “Jane is concerned about some illegal land use that she has witnessed in her neighbourhood, and would like us to see what can be done about it. I told her that the best person to look into this was Tom, and she asked whether her husband could be included on any correspondence.”

  5. Subject appears beside the client’s name in search results and other case listings. A brief, unique description is more useful than repeating the client’s name.
  6. Case Type identifies the type of case. Many case types have specific activities and timelines, so choose the appropriate type when you create the case. You can change it later through Manage Case on the CiviCase Dashboard or the contact’s Case tab, then Change Case Type in New Activity. Changing an ongoing case may require you to update or re-enter some data.
  7. Case Status indicates the current status. You will generally use a status such as Ongoing or Urgent. If you are entering an already completed case for tracking, select Resolved.
  8. Case Start Date defaults to the current day. Adjust it for an already completed case or an upcoming case that has not started.
  9. Duration records, in minutes, the time spent collecting the information needed for the create case form—not the time spent filling in the form. For example, you might record the minutes spent on the phone while a constituent described the case.

Cancel discards the case data you have entered and returns you to the CiviCRM dashboard. Once you have completed the fields in the pop-up window, choose how to finish:

  • Click Save to save the case and open the Manage Case page. There you can modify activities, add attachments, and assign case roles.
  • Click Save and New to save the case and reset the form for another new case. This can be useful when entering several cases.

docs.title: Assign case roles
docs.text:
Assign roles to contacts who work on a case or need to stay informed about its activities. A contact with CiviCase access who has a case role will see the case in their My Cases view.

The Manage Case page brings case information together on one screen. You can view summary information; change case status or reassign a case; create or manage activities, timelines, and roles; identify or manage client relationships; and run case audits (reports).

The case displays the phone number and email address of each person with a role, making it easier to contact them.

docs.title: Fill an unassigned role
docs.text:
1. In the case, click Case Roles to open it.
  2. Find a role marked (not assigned) in the Name column.
  3. Click its edit icon.
  4. In Assign Case Role, type the contact’s last name until their name appears in the dropdown list.
  5. Select the contact.
  6. Click OK.

docs.title: Add another contact to a role
docs.text:
Use Add New Role when more than one contact needs the same role.

  1. Click Add New Role.
  2. In the pop-up window, select a role defined in your case configuration.
  3. Select a contact from your database.
  4. Complete the pop-up window. The new role relationship then appears in the Roles pane of the case management screen.

People who might be assigned to a case should generally already be in the database. If you cannot find someone, add them as a contact first at Contacts > New Individual.

docs.title: Contact or change a person with a role
docs.text: Assigned roles have mail, edit, and delete icons under Email and Actions. You can email a contact, change their relationship to the case with the edit icon, or remove a case role with the delete icon. Emails sent from here are automatically added to the case activities in sequence, providing an audit trail of case-related communications.

docs.title: Add contacts to a case in bulk
docs.text:
Use an action in contact search results when you need to assign several contacts to a case with a specific role.

  1. Search for contacts.
  2. Select the contacts to add from the search results.
  3. Choose Add to case as role.
  4. In the form shown, choose the case.
  5. Choose the role the contacts will have in that case.
  6. Click Submit to add them, or Cancel to return to the search results.

docs.title: Find activities within a case
docs.text:
Use Case Activities to find an activity you need to review or change.

  1. Scroll to Case Activities in the case.
  2. Click the section to open it. By default, scheduled activities appear first, sorted by date, followed by completed activities.
  3. To sort by another column, such as activity type, click its column header.

If the case has many activities, click Search Filters to narrow the list. The available filters are:

  • Reporter/Role
  • Activity Status
  • Activity Dates: Fill in both date fields for a range, or only the first for a specific date.
  • Activity Type: For example, select Follow up to find follow-up activities.
  • Deleted Activities: Available to people with permission to view deleted activities.

After selecting your criteria, click Search on the right. The table filters out activities that do not match.

docs.title: Add activities to a case
docs.text: You can add one activity or a set of activities to a case. While working on an activity, you can also send a copy, schedule a follow-up, or attach files.

docs.title: Add one activity
docs.text:
1. Open the case through Find Cases or the Cases Dashboard.
  2. In Case Summary, choose an activity type from New Activity.
  3. Click Go.
  4. Complete the activity form. Client is pre-populated with the case’s client data.
  5. Click Save to save the activity and return to the case page.

The activity dropdown is configurable. See the set-up chapter for more information. If you do not want to save your work, click Cancel to discard it.

docs.title: Add a timeline or sequence
docs.text:
The Standard Timeline is added when a case is created. You can add another set of activities when appropriate.

  1. Open the case through Find Cases or the Cases Dashboard.
  2. In Case Summary, choose a Timeline or Sequence from New Timeline.
  3. In the dialog box, click OK to confirm. The set of activities is added to the case.

docs.title: Include other activity details
docs.text:
While working on an activity form, use the areas that apply:

  • Send a Copy: Open this area and check the contacts or case roles you want to alert about the activity.
  • Schedule Follow-up: Open this area and select the follow-up activity type, the number of days until it should occur, and a subject—for example, “confirm that Jane’s problem is fixed”. Click Go, complete the follow-up form, and click Save.
  • Attachments: Open this area and click Choose file. Select a file in your file browser, then click Choose; its name appears beside Choose file. You can attach up to five files to an activity. An attachment is not saved in CiviCRM until you save the activity.

docs.title: Edit and update case activities
docs.text: Open an activity to change its details, or update its status directly from the Activities table.

docs.title: Edit an activity
docs.text:
1. Open the case from the Case Dashboard, Find Cases, or the contact’s Cases tab.
  2. Click Edit at the far right of the activities table at the bottom of the case form.
  3. Change the activity in the activity form. It works as it does when creating an activity, but many fields are already filled in.
  4. Click Save to return to the case page, or Cancel to discard your changes.

To assign a scheduled task while adding or editing a case, start typing the staff member’s name in Assigned to. Select the person from the suggestions and check that their full name appears in the field. You can assign multiple contacts to an activity. If you select the wrong person, click the X beside their name to remove them.

docs.title: Update an activity’s status
docs.text:
You do not need to open the activity edit form to change its status.

  1. Open the case from the Case Dashboard, Find Cases, or the contact’s Cases tab.
  2. In the Activities table, click the status text in the activity’s row, such as Scheduled.
  3. Select a new status in the pop-up form.
  4. Click Ok to save the update.

docs.title: Change the status of a case
docs.text:
A case status helps you see how the case is progressing. Example values include Ongoing, Resolved, Not Assigned, and Urgent.

  1. Open the case from the Case Dashboard, Find Cases, or the contact’s Cases tab.
  2. Click Manage Case.
  3. In the Case Summary table, click the Edit icon beside the current status column. This opens Change Case Status, an activity form with an additional Case Status field.
  4. Set Case Status to the new value.
  5. If linked cases appear in the form and you also need to change their status, check Update Linked Cases Status. When checked, this also records a status-change activity for a linked case whose status differs from the parent case’s new status.
  6. Complete the other fields as you would when editing a case activity. Status is required and is not set by default, so set it before saving.
  7. Click Save. You return to the case page with a message that the Change Case Status Activity has been created.

CiviCase records an activity when a case status changes so the case history can capture who changed it and why, as well as what changed. This behaviour is consistent throughout CiviCase.

docs.title: Review case work on the Case Dashboard
docs.text:
Use the Case Dashboard to see what is happening in your cases and open the work you need to do.

The dashboard shows a Summary of Case Involvement, your cases with activities scheduled in the next 14 days, and your cases with activities completed in the last 14 days. If you have permission to view cases other than those you work on, you can also see all cases with upcoming or recently completed activities.

To switch between Your Cases and All Cases, click the link at the top right of the content area.

docs.title: Open an activity or case
docs.text:
• To view a Next Sched. activity in a pop-up window, click its title. In the example shown, the activity is Medical evalution. To work on it, click the Edit pencil beside the title.
  • To see every activity in a case, click the triangular expand icon (►) beside the client’s name. You can view or edit any activity in the expanded list.
  • To work on several tasks in a case, click Manage Case. You can also use it to change the case status, print a case report, or view case roles.

To add a case from the dashboard, click Add Case at the top left of the content area.

docs.title: Print reports and documents for cases
docs.text: Use these options to print a case report, export a document for one case, or merge documents for multiple cases.

docs.title: Print a case report
docs.text:
To print a report listing all case and case activity data:

  1. Open the case from the Case Dashboard, the Find Cases search form, or the contact's Cases tab.
  2. Select Print Case Report in the Case Summary section.

docs.title: Create a document for one case
docs.text:
You can create a letter or document with case tokens on the case management screen. Beside Print Report, select Export Document to export it as a PDF, DOCx, ODT or HTML page.

When working with DOCx, turn off spelling and grammar check for best results.

docs.title: Merge documents for multiple cases
docs.text:
1. Select the cases through a Find Cases search.
  2. Select Print/merge Document.

This creates a document for each case and compiles them into a single PDF.

docs.title: Case reporting and search options
docs.text: Use this page to find ways to review casework, from dashboard totals to reports and searches.

docs.title: Case dashboard
docs.text:
The Case Dashboard shows your current cases. Each row represents a case type, and each column shows the current total for a status. Select a number to see the cases of that type and status; 0 is not linked.

The dashboard provides a quick overview. For more detailed or customised views for case workers and administrators, use CiviCRM searches or CiviReport.

docs.title: QA Audit / Redact
docs.text:
You can run QA Audit / Redact from a contact's case management screen to audit activities for a case. Like Print Report, it produces a report, but it includes only activities defined in a selected timeline. You can include activities with any status or exclude activities with Completed status.

If you select Redact (hide) Client and Service Provider Data, the report uses randomly assigned numbers instead of names. The same contact has the same number throughout the report.

Your installation may define additional audit or quality-assurance reports. If it does, they appear in the Run QA Audit/Redact dropdown menu.

docs.title: CiviCase report templates
docs.text:
Four report templates are specifically for cases:

  • Case Summary Report
  • Case Time Spent Report
  • Contact Demographics Report
  • Case Detail Report

Cases are made up of activities, so the Activity report template can also provide a dashlet for each person involved in casework to track activities assigned to them. Case activities appear alongside non-case activities. You may want a naming convention that includes a case reference in activity names.

docs.title: Searches
docs.text:
Find Cases lets you search by Case Type, Status, client name or email. It can help you identify a few cases needing attention when your Case Dashboard is large or cluttered.

Advanced search combines those case options with other search criteria. For example, you can find case types filtered by location or by custom fields applied to the contact.

Activity Search, under Search > Custom Searches > Activity Search, searches activities rather than contacts, unlike Advanced search.

If the Case Dashboard, CiviReport, and contact and activity searches do not provide the analysis you need, consider commissioning a new report or custom search. See reporting and searching for more information.

docs.title: Add custom fields for case information
docs.text: Choose whether information belongs on a case or on a particular activity, then create fields for the relevant case or activity types.

docs.title: Choose where the fields belong
docs.text:
Custom fields attached to a case are visible in the case management screen. Fields attached to an activity are visible only when a user views that activity’s details.

For example, an Employment Counselling case might use a Skills Assessment activity with checkboxes for client job skills. A generalised application case might instead use a case field for the type of application being tracked. If you are moving from a paper-based system, use your existing forms to identify information worth recording.

Review the section on configuring custom data fields before starting these steps.

docs.title: Create the fields
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Fields.
  2. Click Add a Set of Custom Fields.
  3. Under Used For, select Activities or Cases.
  4. Select one or more activity types or case types for the set.
  5. Enter any help information you want users to see.
  6. Click Save.
  7. Add one or more custom fields to the set.
  8. Repeat these steps for each activity type or case type that needs custom data.

If an activity type needs many fields, consider dividing them into logically related sets. This can make the form easier for users to work through.

docs.title: How emails are filed on cases
docs.text:
Case-related emails can become part of a case’s record. For example, a work disability case coordinator might want both an inquiry sent to a state agency representative and the reply recorded on the case.

You can send outbound emails from the Manage Case screen. You can also set up CiviCRM to integrate with your usual email client, so you can send and receive emails as usual and have them filed in CiviCRM.

The Email Processor, described in the CiviMail chapter, can bring inbound and outbound emails into CiviCRM as non-case activities. When CiviCase is enabled, an action becomes available to file a non-case activity onto a case. If the Email Processor is set up, replies to email activities sent from Manage Case are filed directly on the case automatically.

You can also record an email or other activity on a case by putting case, a space and the case’s #id in square brackets in the subject. For example, an email or activity with the subject [case #123] Any subject is recorded under case ID 123.

docs.title: CiviCase accounts and permissions
docs.text: Use this reference to check who needs a contact record and user account, and what each CiviCase-related permission allows.

docs.title: Contact records and accounts
docs.text:
Each staff member or service provider who enters or views case information needs a contact record and a Drupal, Joomla! or WordPress user account. On Joomla! and WordPress installations, these users need back-end (administrator) access because all CiviCase functions are performed in the Administrator interface.

Service providers assigned case roles but not using CiviCase should also have contact records. Staff can then use CiviCase to email them relevant case and client information and record case-related interactions they report.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Configure CiviCase-related permissions in your CMS for users who add or manage cases. You may want case management-specific user roles based on staff responsibilities. Permissions control access to CiviCase and the case data users can see.

Permission What it allows Access my cases and activities Create cases, add activities to cases the user created, and edit those activities. The user cannot see cases or activities created by others. Access all cases and activities Create cases, and view and add activities to any case, regardless of who created it. Delete in CiviCase Mark cases or case activities as deleted. This hides them; it does not physically delete them from the database. The user can also find and undelete them using Deleted Cases in Find Cases or Deleted Activities in the Case Activities Search Filter. Administer CiviCase Access Administer > CiviCase options, including creating and editing case types and case statuses, and setting rules to redact data that could identify a case client in reports shared with external reviewers.

To restrict a user to only case data and hide all other contact information, assign Access my cases and activities without edit and view contacts. This can be useful for someone outside your organisation who should not see contact details.

docs.title: Configure a CiviCase case type
docs.text: Use this guide after you have planned the cases, activities and case roles your organisation needs.

docs.title: Enable CiviCase
docs.text:
CiviCase is included in CiviCRM downloads but is not enabled by default.

  1. Go to Administer > System Settings > Components.
  2. Select CiviCase.
  3. Click Save.

Cases now appears in the navigation menu. Enabling CiviCase also installs sample case types, which you can use as examples of complete case types or as starting points for your own.

docs.title: Create a case type
docs.text:
You can create one or more case types.

  1. Go to Administer > CiviCase > Case Types.
  2. Click New Case Type.
  3. Enter a Title and, optionally, a Description.

The title is displayed to users. CiviCRM automatically fills in the Name, which it uses internally. The default name is usually suitable. An advanced user can unlock and change it, but the name should not be changed after the case type is created.

docs.title: Set activity assignment
docs.text: By default, any contact can be selected as the assignee for a case activity. If needed, restrict Activity Assignment to a group or to contacts with a user account on your website.

docs.title: Add case roles
docs.text:
Case Roles identifies the types of people involved in a case. The roles you list here are included automatically when a new case is opened. You can assign specific people to those roles after opening the case.

  1. Select the roles to include from the Add role drop-down below the list of roles.
  2. If you need a new role, type its name into the drop-down field. Existing matches appear alongside a blue bar containing your underlined entry. Click the blue bar to define the new role.
  3. For each role in the list, set Assign to Creator or Is Manager as needed.

A role marked Assign to Creator is automatically assigned to the person who creates the case. You can mark one role as the manager; the case manager’s name is displayed prominently in case listings and reports. You can define multiple new roles this way, and they are created when you save the case type.

New roles, or relationship types, created through the Case Type interface are individual-to-individual relationships. If you need an individual-to-organisation relationship, finish creating the case type, then change the relationship definition at Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Relationship Types. You can also review and edit other role or relationship details there.

docs.title: Choose available activities
docs.text:
The Add Activity menu in the case summary lets users quickly record an activity on the case. For example, a case manager can select Phone Call, record a call with a colleague and have it filed on the case.

The Activity Types tab controls which types are available for users to choose from that menu. Include types your users will find useful, such as Phone Call, Email, Meeting and Follow Up, along with any useful custom types. You do not need to add CiviCRM’s special types, such as Open Case, Change Case Status and Change Case Type, manually.

Include only activities a user might choose to add. Activities in a Standard Timeline, another timeline or a Sequence do not need to be in this list. If most of your custom activity types are in a timeline or sequence, leaving them out of Add Activity can give you tighter control over the workflow. Including some or all of them gives users more flexibility.

  1. Select activity types from the Add activity type drop-down below the list.
  2. If you need a new custom type, enter its name in the drop-down search field. Existing matches appear alongside a blue bar containing your underlined entry. Click the blue bar to define the new type.
  3. If needed, use Max Instances to limit how many times a listed activity type can be used in a case.

You can define multiple new activity types this way. They are created when you save the case type. Afterward, you can review or amend them at Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Activity Types. Their default settings should suit most situations, but you can change the label or description. To make a new type available outside CiviCase, you can change its Component setting from Cases only to Contacts AND Cases.

docs.title: Define timelines and a sequence
docs.text:
Every case type must have a Standard Timeline. It contains essential elements for the case type to work correctly, starts with a predefined Open Case activity, and adds its activities automatically when the case opens.

A timeline groups activities into a workflow. Its Reference and Offset fields schedule each activity relative to the date the case opens or to another activity. All activities in a timeline are created and shown in the case summary when that timeline is added to the case. You can create multiple timelines for a case type. Additional timelines start empty, so you choose their first activity when defining them; that activity may be a key reference for the timeline.

A Sequence sets the order of activities without setting time intervals. Each next activity is created only when the preceding activity is marked completed. You can add only one sequence to a case type.

Do not put an activity type in both a timeline and a sequence.

Use the (Add) menu to add an additional timeline or a sequence.

To add activities to a timeline:

  1. Select the timeline’s tab.
  2. Select or create an activity from the drop-down list.
  3. Select its status. The default is Scheduled.
  4. Enter a Reference Activity. The default, Open Case, is often appropriate. In the Standard Timeline, you can reference any other activity in that timeline. In an additional timeline, you can reference any activity in the case type, but that activity must already exist in the case when the additional timeline is activated.
  5. Enter an Offset in days. It can be positive, negative or zero.
  6. If the reference activity type can occur more than once, use Select to choose whether to reference its oldest or most recent instance.

You can also use a case’s “end date” — its final defined activity — as a reference and use negative offsets to schedule earlier activities. In this example, a quote is due 21 days before an event, a site visit 14 days before it and accreditation 7 days before it.

To add activity types to a sequence, select or create them using the Add Activity drop-down menu. You can reorder activity types in a timeline or sequence using the drag-and-drop handles to the left of each type. You can rename additional timelines or a sequence in the Advanced section below the main Activities section.

Save the new case type when its roles, available activity types, timelines and any sequence are ready.

docs.title: What is CiviCase?
docs.text:
CiviCase helps your organisation track sequences of interactions with contacts in CiviCRM. You can use it for work with clients or constituents, as well as for internal organisational interactions.

A case brings together activities in a complex process. It can help staff follow a workflow involving several people, see what others have done to avoid duplicating work, and remember and schedule follow-up activities. CiviCase relies heavily on Activities, so understanding activities will help you understand cases.

docs.title: Coordinating constituent enquiries
docs.text:
A legislator’s office may handle hundreds of interactions with constituents and communities each day. Staff can check the activities in a case before responding to an enquiry. For example, if someone calls about an issue, the staff member can see whether a colleague is already working on it and tell the caller. A list of upcoming case activities also shows staff what needs their attention.

The office used cases for several kinds of work:

  • When a constituent reported illegal dumping near their home, a staff member created a case with the details and location. They assigned a colleague to follow up with the Health Department. That colleague saw the assigned task when they logged in to CiviCRM, contacted the Health Department on the constituent’s behalf, and confirmed with the constituent that the department had been informed.
  • When a constituent called requesting support from an agency, a staff member logged the call in CiviCase and scheduled a follow-up call for the next week to check that action had been taken on the agency’s behalf.
  • Staff recorded event invitations that the legislator’s scheduler needed to respond to.

docs.title: Managing a grant application process
docs.text:
An organisation administering a health department programme worth several million dollars used CiviCase to manage grant applications. An initial application automatically created a case containing activities assigned to staff involved in the review.

People from three organisations assessed each application in turn. The first organisation checked basic criteria; an external organisation then carried out a more technical assessment. Activities were offset from the case start by the number of days in which they were expected to be completed. As applications arrived, a coordinator from each organisation assigned activities to staff according to their capacity.

The case status changed at various stages. The main options in this process were:

  • passed basic checks
  • failed basic checks
  • technically feasible
  • technically infeasible
  • suppliers approved
  • suppliers disallowed
  • deferred to next round
  • accepted

There were thousands of applications and tens of thousands of parts of the review process. Coordinators from the first two organisations assigned activities so that each staff member’s case dashboard showed only their assigned work. For the final assessment, the two organisations hired an external organisation to process the remaining applications.
