  3. To override built-in CiviCRM error handling for your site, enter the path and class of a custom PHP error-handling function in Fatal Error Handler.
  4. Click Save to save your changes, or Cancel to cancel them.

If your changes are saved, you will see “Your changes have been saved.”

Debugging options are covered in the developer documentation.

docs.title: Review the initial configuration checklist
docs.text:
After CiviCRM is installed, use the Configuration Checklist to review general settings for your organisation. Configuration specific to a component is covered in that component's section.

  1. Log in to your CiviCRM site.
  2. Go to Administer > Administration Console > Configuration Checklist.
  3. Review and complete the configuration tasks for your site. After you save a setting, CiviCRM returns you to the checklist.

Settings you have not reviewed appear in red. A link turns green after you visit its page, but you may still need to return to complete or update the setting.

docs.title: Review address layouts
docs.text:
At Localization > Address Settings, you can change the fields used to edit contact and event addresses, the address layout shown on screen, and the mailing-label layout. Check the defaults before changing them:

  1. Add a contact record and note the address fields on the form.
  2. Save the record and note the field order on the Contact Summary screen.
  3. If you plan to produce mailing labels, search using Find Contacts, then select Mailing Labels from the -actions- drop-down to review the label layout.
  4. Return to Address Settings and make any needed changes.

If you change the mailing-label format, test it with the label type and printer you plan to use to check the spacing.

docs.title: Test outbound email
docs.text:
If you use CiviCRM to email contacts, enter settings that allow it to connect to your mail server. This includes email for contribution receipts, event registration confirmations and CiviMail bulk mailings. If you are unsure which settings to use, check with your system administrator, ISP or hosting provider. The Email System Configuration section of the System Administrator Guide has more detail.

After entering or changing the settings, click Save and Send Test Email. CiviCRM sends the test to the email address associated with your user login account; its From address is the default From address you configured. If CiviCRM cannot send it, an on-screen message gives the specific error and suggestions for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Review system workflow templates
docs.text:
CiviCRM includes system-generated emails, such as contribution receipts and event registration confirmations. These system workflow templates will be sent with your organisation's name. Review them and, if needed, customise their style and wording.

Workflow messages contain necessary program logic as well as text. Take care not to change that logic when editing a template. After a change, test the workflow and review the email it sends. If the change causes problems, errors or missing information, you can Revert to the system default for that workflow.

The remaining checklist tasks involve how you record and use contact data. They are best left until you have read more about those uses.

docs.title: Initial configuration settings
docs.text: Use this reference to check what the general configuration settings control, including their defaults, options and important limitations.

docs.title: Language and region
docs.text:
Localization changes the language displayed in CiviCRM and region-specific formats for dates and money, including currency. CiviCRM is localized for the United States by default. Review these settings if you use CiviCRM in another country or language, or need to store contact addresses in countries other than the United States.

Translations for a number of languages are available when you download CiviCRM. Community members contribute them; if your language is unavailable, you may wish to translate it. A translation guide is available on the wiki.

A site can support multiple languages. Users can then choose from available languages after logging in, and you can store language-specific text such as custom field labels, online contribution pages, campaign information and event descriptions.

Setting Behaviour Default Language If additional language files are installed, selects a default other than US English for all CiviCRM users. Inherit CMS Language By default, CiviCRM's language is independent of the CMS language. Set this to Yes to use the language in use in the CMS. Available Languages Appears when Inherit CMS Language is No and makes additional languages available to users. Selecting more than one shows a language switcher block for choosing the interface language. In multi-lingual mode, the available languages are those configured in the database. Default Language for contacts Sets the default preferred language for a new contact. Preferred Language is used for some communications on multi-lingual sites. Multiple Languages Support Multi-lingual mode modifies database tables to store translations of certain fields. For example, with English and French configured, it creates an English and a French field for information such as an event title. This can help organisations operating in multiple languages.

The localization page also has thousands separator and decimal delimiter settings for displaying numbers: for example, 1,000.00 in the US and 1.000,00 in Denmark. From CiviCRM 5.43, these settings are ignored if you add the following line to civicrm.settings.php; the system then decides based on the locale. Letting the system decide is likely to work better if you communicate in more than one language.

define('IGNORE_SEPARATOR_CONFIG', TRUE);

docs.title: Organization Address and Contact Info
docs.text:
This screen identifies the organisation or entity that owns the installation. Its name and address identify your organisation in CiviMail mailings when you include the {domain.name} and {domain.address} tokens.

Enter a valid email address belonging to your organisation. It is used as the From field in system-generated, automated emails.

docs.title: Enable components
docs.text:
A new installation has CiviContribute, CiviEvent, CiviMail, CiviMember and CiviReport enabled. You can disable components you do not need, enable CiviCampaign, CiviCase, CiviGrant or CiviPledge, and return to this page later.

Disabling a component you have used retains its information; it will be there if you re-enable the component. Disabling a used component would be unusual. If your goal is to simplify the administration menu or advanced search page, consider permissions instead.

docs.title: Display Preferences
docs.text: Setting Behaviour Viewing Contacts Controls tabs on a contact record. For example, deselect Relationships if you do not track them. Contributions, Pledges, Memberships, Events, Grants and Cases tabs are also hidden when their corresponding components are disabled. Viewing Smart Groups Controls the display of smart groups to which a contact belongs. Editing Contacts Controls sections of the add and edit contact forms. For example, deselect Demographics if you do not record Gender and Birth Date for individuals. Contact Search Controls sections in Advanced Search. For example, deselect Relationships if you do not track or search them. Check for Similar Contacts Controls how new contacts are checked for similarity to existing contacts. Notify Activity Assignees When enabled, emails assignees of new activities a copy of the activity. You can suppress emails for specific Activity Types by entering them in Do not notify assignees for. Contact Dashboard Controls which sections constituents can see, including subscribed groups, contribution history and event registration information. For example, deselect contribution history if constituents should not see their own. WYSIWYG Editor Select CKEditor for an editor that helps users enter text in fields allowing HTML formatting, such as the introduction to an online contribution page. You can configure CKEditor to change its functions and toolbar order through Configure CKEditor. Select Textarea if you do not want a WYSIWYG editor. Enable Popup Forms On by default. Uncheck it to open forms by refreshing the page instead. Individual Display Name Sets the display-name format for individual contacts. Individual Sort Name Sets the sort-name format for individual contacts. Menubar position Places the CiviCRM menu above, below or in place of the CMS menu, or hides it. Menubar color Sets the menu's background colour. For accessibility, choose one that contrasts with the menu font colour; use a free online contrast ratio checker if unsure. Backend Theme Selects a theme installed through the Extension Manager, or turns off CSS theming with None (Unstyled). Automatic uses CiviCRM's default theme, Greenwich. Frontend Theme Selects a theme or removes theming for front-end pages.

docs.title: Address Settings
docs.text: At Localization > Address Settings, you can change address-editing fields and the layout of addresses displayed on screen or printed on mailing labels. CiviCRM uses tokens, such as {contact.street_address}, to refer to database fields.

docs.title: Mailing Labels
docs.text:
Mailing Labels controls label formatting. The default is:

{contact.addressee}
{contact.street_address}
{contact.supplemental_address_1}
{contact.supplemental_address_2}
{contact.city}{, }{contact.state_province}{ }{contact.postal_code}
{contact.country}

Keep {contact.addressee} in the format if you want the addressee's name on the label. When generating labels from a contact list, users can choose from label types corresponding to label manufacturer codes.

docs.title: Address Display
docs.text:
Address Display controls the layout of contact and event location addresses shown on CiviCRM screens. The default is:

{contact.address_name}
{contact.street_address}
{contact.supplemental_address_1}
{contact.supplemental_address_2}
{contact.city}{, }{contact.state_province}{ }{contact.postal_code}
{contact.country}

The format also applies to event locations, despite using contact tokens. {contact.address_name} is useful when an event location has a name such as “Smithson Hall”.

docs.title: Address Editing Fields
docs.text:
Address Editing Fields lets you hide unused fields to simplify forms. For example, you can deselect latitude and longitude if you do not record them for contacts.

  • Street Address Parsing uses the US Postal Service's (USPS) Postal Addressing Standards to separate an address into Street Number, Street Name and Apt/Unit/Suite. Addresses that follow these standards help keep data consistent and make best use of parsing. When parsing is on, Edit Address Elements lets you view or edit the parsed address while editing an address.

  • Address Standardization is an optional interface to the USPS Address Standardization web service. You must register for the USPS service. If approved, you receive a User ID and service URL. The URL supplied by USPS does not begin with http://; add that prefix when entering it in the CiviCRM settings field.

docs.title: Mapping and Geocoding
docs.text:
CiviCRM supports Google and OpenStreetMap mapping services to show contact addresses and event locations on a map. Enabling mapping requires a provider selection and a key for your site from that provider.

You can select a Geocoding Provider that is the same as or different from the mapping provider. Once enabled, geocoding calculates or retrieves latitude and longitude and inserts them into contact and event records as you add or edit address data. Extensions can add other mapping and geocoding services.

docs.title: Search Settings
docs.text:
These settings control search behaviour, including wildcards and the data included in quick search results. Changes can improve performance with large datasets.

A wildcard substitutes for other characters in a search: % matches zero or more characters, while _ matches one character. For example, Volunteer% as an Activity Subject matches subjects beginning with “Volunteer”, such as “Volunteer for Open House” or “Volunteering Opportunities”.

Setting Behaviour Automatic Wildcards By default, Name searches act as though the text has % on both sides: ada can match “Adams, Janet” and “Nadal, Jorge”. Disabling this can speed searches significantly in large databases, but users must enter % or _ for partial-name searches. Include Email By default, Name searches also search email addresses. Disabling this can speed searches significantly in large databases, but users must use Email fields in Advanced Search, Search Builder or Profiles to find contacts by email address. Include Nickname Nicknames are not included in Name searches by default. Set this to Yes to include them. Include Alphabetical Pager Disabling it hides the alphabetical pager on search screens and improves response time for large datasets. Include Order By Clause Disabling it leaves search results unordered and significantly improves response time for large datasets. Default Contact Search Profile Selects a Profile to override the default columns in Find Contacts results. Smart group cache timeout Sets how many minutes to keep a smart group's cached contact list before refreshing it. Smart groups are saved searches; caching avoids rerunning the search on every access. The default, 0, empties the cache as soon as a contact is edited or added. A value such as 5 minutes or longer may reduce server load when contact data changes frequently, but users may see old results for a few minutes. Autocomplete Contact Search When enabled, selected fields appear in autocomplete lists and the navigation menu's Quick Search box. Contact name is always included. Contact Reference Options Selects fields shown in autocomplete results for Contact Reference custom fields. Contact Name is always included. Autocomplete Results Sets the maximum contacts shown at one time while typing in an autocomplete field. The default is 10. InnoDB Full Text Search Enables InnoDB full-text search optimizations when using MySQL 5.6 or later.

Public Contact Reference fields: To use custom contact reference fields in profiles on public pages, assign the access contact reference fields permission to the anonymous role. In most situations, use Limit List to Group when configuring a contact reference field for a public form so that you do not expose your entire contact list.

docs.title: Miscellaneous Settings
docs.text: Setting Behaviour Dashboard Cache Timeout Sets how many minutes to cache dashboard dashlet content. Checksum Lifespan Sets how many days a personalized, hashed link remains valid. Contact Trash and Undelete When enabled, moves deleted contacts to the trash instead of destroying them. Users with the proper permission can find and restore them, or delete them permanently. Logging See Logging Settings in the System Administrator Guide. Attach PDF copy to receipts When enabled, attaches a PDF receipt during event sign-up or online contribution. Path to wkhtmltopdf executable Specifies the executable path for an alternative PDF-generation utility that may perform better for large numbers of PDF letters or receipts. A system administrator must download and install it. Warning: wkhtmltopdf is no longer under active development. Its latest tagged release, 0.12.6 from June 2020, is insecure and should not be used. New Version Alerts When enabled, displays on-screen alerts about new CiviCRM versions to users with Administer CiviCRM permission. Requires Version Check & Statistics Reporting to be enabled. Version Checking and Statistics Reporting Checks for a newer stable CiviCRM version and displays alerts on the main CiviCRM Administration page. It also anonymously reports CiviCRM, PHP, MySQL and framework (Drupal/Joomla!/WordPress) versions, the default language, and record counts—but no actual record data—to the CiviCRM team to help prioritize development. Set it to No if you do not want this information reported. Display "empowered by CiviCRM" When enabled, shows “empowered by CiviCRM” at the bottom of public forms to increase awareness of CiviCRM. Maximum Attachments Sets the maximum number of files, such as documents or images, attachable to emails, activities and grant records. The default is 3. Maximum File Size (in MB) Sets the largest file attachable to emails or activities. The PHP configuration file, php.ini, must support a file size at least as large. Allow second-degree relationship permissions When enabled, a contact who can edit a related contact inherits that contact's permission to edit other related contacts. For example, this could let a class teacher edit student records when both teacher and students are linked by relationships to the class, set up as an organisation sub-type.

docs.title: Contact Types
docs.text: You can rename the built-in Contact Types—Individual, Household and Organizations—and create or change contact subtypes for more specific uses, such as Student, Parent or Team.

docs.title: Outbound email
docs.text:
CiviCRM supports three ways to connect to a mail server: mail (PHP's built-in mail function), SMTP (Simple Mail Transport Protocol) and Sendmail. Each requires its own settings. See Email System Configuration in the System Administrator Guide for more detail.

  • Disable Outbound Email sends no mail. Warning: If you use Online Contribution pages or online Event Registration, turn off their automated receipts and registration confirmations, which are enabled by default, before disabling outbound email. Otherwise, constituents will see errors after completing a contribution or registration.
  • Redirect to Database records all emails as archived mailings instead of sending them.

docs.title: From Email Addresses
docs.text:
CiviCRM uses the default From address defined here for automated emails. If you entered an address on the Domain Information screen, it appears here.

For an email sent by a user, that user's primary email address is the default From address. They can instead select a general address defined under From Email Address Options. To restrict users to those options rather than their own Primary address, use the Outbound Mail settings at Administer › System Settings › Outbound Email(SMTP/Sendmail).

docs.title: Payment Processors
docs.text:
Payment processors handle credit card transactions and transfer funds to your organisation's bank account. You need one configured if you plan to accept online contributions, online membership sign-up or renewal, or online event registration.

CiviCRM supports several processors, and third-party developers can add others. Pricing and features differ, so review the factors for selecting a processor. Configuration and testing steps differ by processor; see installing payment processors in the System Administrator Guide.

docs.title: Permissions and system status
docs.text:
See Permissions and access control for information on setting permissions.

The system status screen at Administer > Administration Console > System Status, or /civicrm/a/#/status, reports potential problems with your installation, configuration or server environment. See System Status in the System Administrator Guide for help interpreting its results and responding to reported problems.

docs.title: Plan for a CiviCRM installation
docs.text:
This page explains the decisions and ongoing responsibilities to discuss with the people who will install and maintain CiviCRM for your organisation.

This material is for technicians and may be difficult to use if you have little or no experience setting up web applications. You may wish to seek help or share it with your organisation's technical staff.

docs.title: Installation requirements and choices
docs.text:
CiviCRM must be installed on a computer with a web server, such as Apache or nginx, PHP and MySQL. Some people try CiviCRM on a local computer before installing it on a dedicated web server. If that computer does not have the required software, packages available online include WAMP and XAMPP for Windows, MAMPP for Macintosh, and LAMP for Linux.

Discuss hosting with your System Administrator and review the Hosting information in the System Administrator Guide. Before installation, decide whether to use Standalone CiviCRM or integrate CiviCRM with a content management system (CMS) for building and managing websites: Drupal, WordPress or Joomla!. Full installation instructions are in the System Administrator Guide.

docs.title: Internet or internal access
docs.text: Most organisations access CiviCRM over the internet. An organisation that wants access limited to internal staff may instead install it on an internal network. If the installation is not publicly available, contacts cannot use CiviCRM to update their own data.

docs.title: Security and upgrades
docs.text:
Once CiviCRM is installed, secure the server and website. The System Administrator Guide describes important security measures.

New versions of CiviCRM are released every month. Although extensions are typically how you add major features, you need to upgrade CiviCRM core periodically for security fixes and, if you want them, smaller features and improvements. Apply upgrades containing security fixes in a timely manner.

Plan for the people and time needed to upgrade. Read release notes to understand how an upgrade may change your site, and test the upgrade on a copy of your live site. Back up both your site and database before upgrading the live site, even if testing went smoothly. Because upgrades are important and technical, many organisations employ a CiviCRM expert service provider to carry them out.

docs.title: Configure mapping and geocoding
docs.text:
Set up the providers CiviCRM uses to display maps and find the latitude and longitude of contact addresses.

Before you enable these services, check that the server running CiviCRM can reach them over the public internet. If the server has no public internet access, or a firewall blocks communication, you may see one or more fatal errors when adding or editing contact records. To resolve this, disable Mapping and Geocoding or restore connectivity.

Some providers limit use of their Mapping and Geocoding APIs. If you exceed a limit, you may receive an overlimit error when saving an address.

  1. Go to Administer > System Settings > Mapping and Geocoding.
  2. Under Mapping Provider, select the service used to build and display maps in the CiviCRM UI.
  3. Under Mapping Provider Key, enter the API Key or Application ID for that provider. For Google Maps, refer to developers.google.com for the latest information. For OpenStreetMaps, you need an API key from CARTO: its map images come from CARTO, and without a valid key, maps may repeatedly show an “API KEY REQUIRED” watermark. See CARTO's documentation for information on API keys.
  4. Under Geocoding Provider, select the service used to look up the latitude and longitude of contact addresses so they can be shown on maps.
  5. Under Geo Provider Key, enter an API key if your geocoding provider requires one.
  6. Click Save. If the changes are saved, you will see “Your changes have been saved.” To leave without saving, click Cancel instead.

After enabling the mapping provider, configure the job.geocode scheduled job. It geocodes addresses without a latitude and longitude according to the configured options.

If you need an alternative geocoding provider, you may wish to evaluate the Geocoder extension, which includes many improvements.

docs.title: CMS permissions and roles
docs.text:
Use this page to find where your CMS exposes CiviCRM permissions and which permissions affect common public and logged-in activities.

All the CMSes described here have the same set of CiviCRM permissions, although the settings appear in different places and look slightly different.

docs.title: Where to find permissions and assign roles
Drupal
docs.text:
In the Drupal menu, choose People, then open the Permissions tab in the top-right corner of the pop-up window. The page lists CiviCRM and Drupal operations, with a column for each existing role. Checking an option grants that role permission to perform the action.

You can create roles and edit existing ones. From the Permissions tab, select Roles near the top right of the page.

You can assign a role to a user in either place:

  • In the user's CiviCRM contact record, select Actions > User Record. On the next screen, open the Edit tab and scroll to Roles.
  • As an administrator, choose People in the Drupal menu. Select the user from the list of active users, open the Edit tab in their Drupal user profile and scroll to Roles.

docs.title: Joomla!
docs.text:
To reach Joomla! permissions, log into the Joomla! administrative portal. Choose Components > CiviCRM, then Administer > User and Permissions > Permissions (Access Control) in CiviCRM. Select Joomla Access Control at the top of the list.

Joomla! arranges user groups as parents and children. Child groups inherit permissions from groups above them. Each permission for a user group can be set to:

Setting Meaning Inherited The group can perform the action if the group above it has the permission. Allowed Users in the group can perform the action. Denied Users in the group cannot perform the action.

Joomla! has two additional permissions that Drupal and WordPress do not use:

  • Configure Joomla! ACL: the user can configure Joomla! ACLs and is assigned all CiviCRM permissions.
  • Show CiviCRM Component: the user can see CiviCRM in the Components list.

An administrator can assign or change a user's group in either place:

  • In the user's CiviCRM contact record, select Action > User Record, then use Assigned User Groups.
  • In the Joomla! administrative portal, choose User > User Manager. Select a user to open their account settings, including their user group.

docs.title: WordPress
docs.text:
In CiviCRM, choose Administer > User and Permissions > Permissions (Access Control), then select WordPress Access Control. You can adjust CiviCRM settings for each predefined WordPress User Role there.

You can assign a role to a user in either place:

  • In the user's CiviCRM contact record, select Actions > User Record. On the Edit User screen, change their Role.
  • In the WordPress Site Admin area, choose Users. Select a user to open the Edit User screen and change their Role.

docs.title: Anonymous and authenticated roles
docs.text:
The anonymous role, called public in Joomla!, applies to visitors who have not logged in. It has the lowest level of permissions. The table shows the default CiviCRM permissions described for this role. Actual settings may vary by CMS and by how CiviCRM was installed, so check them on your site.

Permission Description CiviCRM: access all custom data View all custom fields—for example, see or enter information in custom data fields in forms. CiviCRM: access uploaded files View or download files, including images and photos. CiviCRM: profile create Add data in a profile form. CiviCRM: profile edit Edit data in a profile form. CiviCRM: profile view View data in a profile. CiviEvent: register for events Register for events on your website. CiviEvent: view event info View event information pages. CiviEvent: view event participants View participants who have signed up to an event. CiviContribute: make online contributions Make payments or donations through your website. CiviMail: access CiviMail subscribe/unsubscribe pages Subscribe or unsubscribe from mailing lists. CiviMail: view public CiviMail content View mailings on your website. CiviCampaign: sign CiviCRM Petition Sign petitions, if CiviCampaign is enabled.

The authenticated role, called registered in Joomla! and subscriber in WordPress, applies to visitors who have logged in. It is the default role for new user accounts and cannot be deleted. By default, its CiviCRM permissions are the same as those of the anonymous role.

docs.title: Contributions and events
docs.text:
• Taking online contributions: If only logged-in users should contribute, remove make online contributions from the anonymous or public role.
  • Viewing and registering for events: If view event info and register for events are enabled for anonymous and authenticated roles, all site visitors can register for any event. To give specific users access to only some events, use a CiviCRM ACL: grant a role “view” access to events if its users should only see event information, or “edit” permission if they can register. The CMS register for events permission must be disabled for these ACL settings to work, because it overrides them.

For example, a charity might hold public fundraising events and private dinners for some corporate donors. CiviCRM ACLs, rather than the CMS register for events permission, can specify which events each group of users can access.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profiles contain default and custom fields. They can collect information through online forms or provide searchable directories; see Profiles.

  • Editing a standalone profile: If an online form uses a standalone profile to search for and edit CiviCRM data, rather than as part of an event registration page, only authenticated users can edit it. An anonymous visitor cannot edit the data merely because the role has profile edit; they also need a checksum, a unique URL to a page where they can edit their own data. Anonymous users must have profile edit for checksum tokens to work. See Everyday tasks in the email section for more information.
  • Collecting data from anonymous visitors: For profiles on event registration pages, contribution pages or standalone forms, give the anonymous role profile create. A profile containing custom fields also needs a custom-data permission, depending on the circumstances; see “Custom data” below.
  • Public searchable directories: To let a role or user group use search pages published on the website, grant profile listings. A directory might, for example, find organisations in the database by location.
  • Viewing an embedded profile: Visitors need profile view to see a profile embedded in an online page, such as one displaying an organisation's name, description and contact details.

Caution

Profile listings and forms is equivalent to granting profile_view, profile_create, profile_edit and profile_listing. Assign it only to trusted roles, and grant the separate permissions instead where possible.

Profile listings and forms allows a role to add data through profiles in online forms, edit data displayed in standalone profiles on public pages if that option is available, and use public searchable directories. It is not enabled for the anonymous or authenticated roles by default. If anonymous users receive it, a visitor still needs to be logged in or use a checksum token to edit data; see Everyday tasks in the email section.

docs.title: Custom data
docs.text:
A user cannot interact with custom fields in an online form or profile without permission to view and/or edit custom data. There are two ways to provide access:

  • access all custom data gives a role view and edit access to all custom fields in online forms. For example, granting it to anonymous visitors would let them view and edit custom fields in a profile on an event registration page.
  • CiviCRM ACLs can give roles access to specific sets of custom fields. For example, an Amsterdam team might access only custom volunteer fields, while a head office in Scotland accesses both volunteer and donor fields. These ACLs will not function if the role has access all custom data.

docs.title: Uploaded files and contact dashboards
docs.text:
• Give access uploaded files to roles that need to view images, photos and files attached to CiviCRM records and pages. Give it to the anonymous role if visitors should see photos on contact records, personal campaign pages or documents intended for public consumption.
  • Give access contact dashboard to authenticated users' roles if they should review their mailing-group subscriptions, contributions, memberships and event registrations, where applicable. Do not enable it for the anonymous role.

docs.title: Other CMS roles
docs.text:
Each CMS has other predefined roles with varying levels of CiviCRM access. You can change their permissions or add roles for more graduated access. Always retain a role—Administrator, Super Users or Admin—that can administer CiviCRM, including access control.

More information about CiviCRM permissions, including permissions for certain back-office functions, is available at Default Permissions and Roles.

docs.title: Set permissions by financial type
docs.text:
Use this procedure when different users need access to contributions based on financial type—for example, when some users should manage event payments without seeing donation data.

By default, access CiviContribute, edit contributions and delete in CiviContribute control access to contribution data across all financial types. Access control by financial type is available when CiviCRM is installed within Drupal, Backdrop or WordPress. It is not yet available for Joomla.

Tip

Visitors can access your contribution pages only if you grant the anonymous user role the add and view permissions for each financial type.

  1. In CiviCRM, go to Administer > CiviContribute > CiviContribute Component Settings.
  2. Check Enable Access Control by Financial Type. CiviCRM then adds a 'view', 'edit' and 'delete' CMS permission for every financial type.
  3. Edit your CMS permissions to assign the new permissions as needed.

docs.title: Set up a CiviCRM ACL
docs.text:
Use a CiviCRM ACL when a CMS permission is too broad and you need a role to access a particular group of contacts, profile, set of custom fields or event. The setup has three parts: create an ACL role, assign a contact group to it, then define what the role can do with the data.

Go to Administer > User and Permissions > Permissions (Access Control). This screen links to the CMS access control list and the three steps for managing CiviCRM ACLs.

docs.title: Create an ACL role
docs.text:
In Manage Roles, CiviCRM has “administrator” and “authenticated” roles by default. Only the administrator role can be edited; “authenticated” is reserved and core to the system.

  1. Select Manage Roles.
  2. Select Add Acl Role.
  3. Complete the role settings:
Setting What to enter Label A name for the role, visible to users. Description A description of the role; you can format it. Weight A number that sets its place in the list. Lower numbers appear first: for example, “1” places a role near the top, while “20” may place it near the bottom. Enabled? Whether the role is active. Disabling it may cause functionality to stop working for some users.

docs.title: Assign users to the role
docs.text:
CiviCRM assigns users to an ACL role through an access control contact group. There are several ways to create a group; see Groups and tags.

  1. Create an access control group containing the users who should have the same level of access.
  2. On the access control menu screen, select Assign Users to CiviCRM ACL Roles.
  3. Select Add Role Assignment.
  4. Complete the assignment settings:
Setting What to choose ACL Role An available ACL role. Assigned To The contact group to assign to the role. Enabled? Whether this assignment is active.

docs.title: Create the ACL
docs.text:
An ACL defines which role can perform which operation on which data.

  1. Return to Administer > User and Permissions > Permissions (Access Control).
  2. Select manage ACLs. The list shows existing controls and may include one allowing administrators to edit all contacts.
  3. Select Add ACL.
  4. Complete the ACL settings:
Setting What to enter or choose Description A clear description of what the ACL does. Role The role this ACL applies to. Operation The allowed action, such as view, edit, create or delete. Type of Data A group of contacts, a profile, a set of custom data fields or events. Group/Profile/Custom Data/Event The specific group, profile, custom data or event. This field's label changes with Type of Data. Enabled? Whether the ACL is active.

docs.title: Choosing between CMS permissions and CiviCRM ACLs
docs.text:
You will understand how the two kinds of access control differ and when to use each one.

Permissions and access control lists (ACLs) are rules about who can see and do what in CiviCRM. You give roles permissions, then assign those roles to people. The rules can control access to CiviCRM areas, such as CiviContribute, CiviCase and CiviMail, and to records, such as contacts and contributions. They can also control actions such as viewing, editing and deleting records.

Caution

Check what a permission allows before granting it. Incorrectly configured permissions may expose your contacts' data.

docs.title: CMS permissions
docs.text:
Permissions in your content management system (CMS) grant roles access to CiviCRM sections and control whether users can view, edit, add or delete records. They generally apply to all records of a kind or to none of them. For example, a CMS permission cannot give someone access to contacts in one group while withholding access to contacts in another.

For many organisations, CMS permissions are enough. Start with them, then consider CiviCRM ACLs if you need more specific access rules.

docs.title: CiviCRM ACLs
docs.text:
CiviCRM ACLs can limit access to particular groups of contacts, profiles, sets of custom fields or events. They can control operations such as viewing, editing, creating, deleting and searching. A profile is a collection of existing and/or custom fields; see Profiles.

These examples need CiviCRM ACLs rather than CMS permissions:

  • An organisation has a head office and three regional offices. Its event director needs to view events across every office, while each regional event coordinator should view and edit only their own events. CMS permissions could allow access to all events or none, but could not distinguish the offices' events.
  • A team in Paris manages volunteers using one set of custom fields, while a team in London uses another set for donor information. Each team should access only its own fields. A CMS permission could grant access to all custom information or none; in this case, the CMS rule controlling access to custom fields should be disabled and a CiviCRM ACL used instead.
  • A charity in Chicago has three regional offices. Fundraising staff need to create and edit prospective donors' contact records, but each office should access only its local contacts. The CMS add contacts permission can allow authenticated users to create contacts. Granting view all contacts and edit all contacts in the CMS, however, would not distinguish the three offices' contacts; that requires a CiviCRM ACL.

docs.title: Configure and check scheduled jobs
docs.text: Use the Scheduled Jobs page to set a job’s frequency and parameters, execute it once when needed, and check whether it ran. Cron must be set up separately by your system administrator for jobs to run automatically; see Cron setup.

docs.title: Open scheduled jobs
docs.text: Go to Administer > System Settings > Scheduled Jobs.

docs.title: Start with a default job
docs.text:
A fresh CiviCRM installation includes more than a dozen partially configured scheduled jobs. You can use these as a starting point, rename them, or delete them. The Specific scheduled jobs reference gives the details needed to recreate a default job or add another listed job.

Parameters needed

Some default scheduled jobs need command parameters before they can run properly.

docs.title: Set the run frequency
docs.text:
When you add or edit a job, choose a Run frequency:

  • Yearly
  • Quarterly
  • Monthly
  • Weekly
  • Daily
  • Hourly
  • Every time cron job is run

Choose a frequency that suits the task. For example, the email send task should typically run every 5 or 10 minutes, while updating memberships can run once a day.

Note

Scheduled jobs cannot run more frequently than cron. Running cron every 5 minutes is common, but you cannot determine its schedule from the CiviCRM user interface. If cron runs weekly, a job set to Daily will run only weekly.

docs.title: Check the timing you need
docs.text: A monthly job runs one month after its first run and continues on that basis. The scheduled jobs system cannot specify a particular day of each month, such as the 15th. If you need more control over timing, a system administrator can create separate cron jobs to execute specific CiviCRM API calls.

docs.title: Enter command parameters
docs.text:
When editing a job, use the Command Parameters field for inputs that affect how it runs. Each job has its own parameters; some accept none. Check the parameters for that job in the Specific scheduled jobs reference.

For example, Job.mail_report requires an instanceId. Its optional format parameter can be pdf (the default), csv, or print. You could enter:

instanceId=7
format=csv

In the Command Parameters field:

  • Put one parameter on each line.
  • Separate each parameter from its value with =.
  • Do not use spaces or quotes.

Job.mail_report also accepts the optional sendmail parameter. Set it to 1 to send email, or 0 not to email the report. You can use sendmail=0 with print or csv to write the report to stdout so that you can save it to a disk file.

docs.title: Run a job once
docs.text: To run a scheduled job on a one-off basis, select More > Execute Now for that job on the Scheduled Jobs page. This is useful for jobs designed to run less frequently, including the geo-coding job and the greetings and addressees job.

docs.title: Check the job log
docs.text:
On the Scheduled Jobs page, select View Log (all jobs) or View Job Log for a specific job. Use the log to check that jobs are running and to examine errors.

The log has separate entries for when a job begins and finishes. The time between them shows how long the job took. Error messages appear only in the completion entry.

docs.title: Specific scheduled jobs
docs.text: Use this reference to find what each listed job does, its default scheduled-job name, its recommended frequency, and its parameters. These details can also help you recreate a default job that was renamed or deleted.

docs.title: Job.cleanup
docs.text:
Removes temporary data and files, and clears old data from cache tables. Running it every hour is recommended to help prevent database and file system bloat.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Clean-up Temporary Data and Files
  • Recommended frequency: Hourly
  • Parameters:
    • session (optional): 1 (default) cleans up the session cache; 0 skips it.
    • tempTables (optional): 1 (default) cleans up the tempTables cache; 0 skips it.
    • jobLog (optional): 1 (default) cleans up the jobLog cache; 0 skips it.
    • prevNext (optional): 1 (default) cleans up the prevNext cache; 0 skips it.
    • dbCache (optional): 1 cleans up the dbCache cache; 0 (default) skips it.
    • memCache (optional): 1 cleans up the memCache cache; 0 (default) skips it.
    • tplCache (optional): 1 cleans up the tplCache cache; 0 (default) skips it.
    • wordRplc (optional): 1 cleans up the wordRplc cache; 0 (default) skips it.

docs.title: Job.disable_expired_relationships
docs.text:
Disables relationships whose end date is in the past.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Disable expired relationships
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Job.fetch_activities
docs.text:
Retrieves inbound emails from a mail directory and inserts an activity for a contact or case.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Process Inbound Emails
  • Recommended frequency: Hourly
  • Parameters: None

For CiviMail in a multisite, configure this job to run for each site (CiviCRM domain ID).

docs.title: Job.fetch_bounces
docs.text:
Fetches bounces from mailings and writes them to mailing statistics.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Fetch Bounces
  • Recommended frequency: Hourly
  • Parameters:
    • is_create_activities (optional): 1 creates activities for bounces; 0 is the default.

docs.title: Job.geocode
docs.text:
Retrieves geocodes (latitude and longitude) and/or parses street addresses, populating details such as street number and street name.

Note

A geocoding provider must be configured at Administer > System Settings > Mapping and Geocoding. Street Address Parsing must be enabled at Administer > Localization > Address Settings.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Geocode and Parse Addresses
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters:
    • geocoding (required): 1 performs geocoding; 0 does not.
    • parse (required): 1 performs parsing; 0 does not.
    • start (optional): Contact ID (integer) at which to begin processing.
    • end (optional): Contact ID (integer) at which to end processing.
    • throttle (optional): 1 pauses for 5 seconds after processing a contact; 0 does not pause.

docs.title: Job.group_cache_flush
docs.text:
Purges aged smart group cache data based on the timeout value. Sites can choose this job, the group cache rebuild job, or both. Performance is generally better when old caches are cleared before an attempt to rebuild them, whether on demand or otherwise.

  • Default scheduled-job name: None
  • Recommended frequency: Always
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Job.group_rebuild
docs.text:
Builds the smart group cache for smart groups whose cache is empty. Without this job, those groups are built on demand. Building on demand is more efficient except when viewing the count for all groups on the manage groups page or expanding the smart groups tab on an individual contact record. If those operations matter to you, you can enable the job, but expect performance impacts unless you have only a few small smart groups.

Note

You can disable the ability to expand the smart group tab on a contact record. This is recommended for medium-sized sites (for example, 50,000 contacts) and larger.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Rebuild Smart Group Cache
  • Recommended frequency: Never
  • Parameters:
    • limit (optional): Number of smart groups to rebuild.

docs.title: Job.mail_report
docs.text:
Generates and sends a copy of a report instance to the email addresses in that instance’s Report Settings. Each report instance needs a separate job.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Mail Reports
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters:
    • instanceId (required): ID of the report instance to send.
    • format (optional): pdf (default); csv outputs a CSV file instead of a PDF; print outputs printer-friendly HTML.
    • sendmail (optional): 1 sends email; 0 does not email the report. Use 0 with print or csv to write the report to stdout so you can save it to a disk file.

docs.title: Job.process_batch_merge
docs.text:
• Default scheduled-job name: None
  • Recommended frequency: Not specified
  • Parameters:
    • rule_group_id: Dedupe rule group ID; defaults to the Contact Unsupervised rule.
    • gid: Group ID.
    • mode (optional): Determines how to behave when there are conflicts. safe (default) skips the merge if there are unresolved conflicts; aggressive forces a merge.
    • auto_flip (optional): 1 may let the API decide which contact to retain and which to delete; the source does not confirm this behaviour.

docs.title: Job.process_mailing
docs.text:
• Default scheduled-job name: Send Scheduled Mailings
  • Recommended frequency: Every time cron job is run
  • Parameters: None

For CiviMail in a multisite, configure this job to run for each site (CiviCRM domain ID).

docs.title: Job.process_membership
docs.text:
Updates membership statuses.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Update Membership Statuses
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Job.process_participant
docs.text:
Updates pending event participant statuses based on time. As space becomes available, it moves participants from On waitlist to Pending from waitlist. If an expiration period is set for an event, it moves any type of pending registration to Expired when that period passes. It sends participants notifications of status changes.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Update Participant Statuses
  • Recommended frequency: Every time cron job is run
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Job.process_pledge
docs.text:
Updates pledge payment and pledge statuses and can send payment reminders.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Process Pledges
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters:
    • send_reminders (optional): 0 (default); 1 sends pledge payment reminder emails.

docs.title: Job.process_respondent
docs.text:
Releases reserved survey respondents after they have been reserved for longer than the Release Frequency days specified for that survey.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Process Survey Respondents
  • Recommended frequency: Every time cron job is run
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Job.process_sms
docs.text:
Sends scheduled SMS.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Send Scheduled SMS
  • Recommended frequency: Every time cron job is run
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Job.run_payment_cron
docs.text:
Runs the handlePaymentCron method in the specified payment processor.

  • Default scheduled-job name: None
  • Recommended frequency: Not specified
  • Parameters: processor_id, processor_name

docs.title: Job.send_reminder
docs.text:
Sends scheduled reminders by email.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Send Scheduled Reminders
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Job.update_greeting
docs.text:
Updates contacts’ email greetings, postal greetings and/or postal addressees.

Note

To configure the format of generated values, go to Administer > Communications > Email Greeting Formats and Administer > Communications > Postal Greeting Formats.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Update Greetings and Addressees
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters:
    • ct (required): Individual, Organization, or Household.
    • gt (required): email_greeting, postal_greeting, or addressee.
    • id (optional): ID of a format option value, used to set a greeting or addressee format other than the default for a given contact type.
    • force (optional): 0 (default) updates only contacts with null values; 1 updates all contacts.
    • limit (optional): Number of contacts to update.

docs.title: Job.version_check
docs.text:
Checks for CiviCRM version updates, which is important for keeping the database secure. It also sends anonymous usage statistics to civicrm.org to assist in prioritising ongoing development.

  • Default scheduled-job name: CiviCRM Update Check
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters: None

docs.title: Mailing.update_email_resetdate
docs.text:
Updates reset_date on an email address to indicate that a valid delivery was made to that address.

  • Default scheduled-job name: Validate Email Address from Mailing
  • Recommended frequency: Daily
  • Parameters: minDays (optional), maxDays (optional)

docs.title: Multisite and multi-domain installations
docs.text:
For a multisite or multi-domain installation, most jobs need to run on only one site, usually the primary domain site (CiviCRM domain ID 1). Most jobs are not domain-aware and do not use the CiviCRM domain ID. The primary domain site has all the standard jobs by default and is a sensible place for additional jobs that are not domain-specific. Whether a job is domain-aware depends on the job, and its documentation may not say explicitly.

For CiviMail in a multisite, these two domain-specific jobs must run for each domain:

  • Job.process_mailing (Send Scheduled Mailings)
  • Job.fetch_activities (Process Inbound Emails)

When creating these jobs for each site—or creating any other jobs with duplicate API calls—give each job a unique name. For example, append the site name: Send Scheduled Mailings - Site A. Otherwise, CiviCRM will complain about the duplicate name.

docs.title: How scheduled jobs run
docs.text: Scheduled jobs keep CiviCRM data up to date and perform other regular tasks, such as sending scheduled reminders and checking for CiviCRM software updates. This page explains what starts them and how their schedules work.

docs.title: What starts a scheduled job
docs.text: Scheduled jobs run automatically, but CiviCRM cannot initiate an action by itself: like most web-based applications, it responds to an action initiated elsewhere. When a person submits a form, for example, CiviCRM responds by creating a contact record. For scheduled jobs, external software called cron initiates the action instead.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Cron is software, separate from CiviCRM, that is typically installed on a server to start tasks automatically. A system administrator must set up cron to initiate CiviCRM’s scheduled jobs before those jobs can run automatically. This is a system-level task that you cannot do in the CiviCRM user interface. See Cron setup in the System Administrator Guide.

A system administrator typically configures cron to run every 5 to 60 minutes. Each time it runs, cron tells CiviCRM to execute the scheduled jobs that CiviCRM deems necessary at that time. An administrator can instead configure separate cron jobs to run specific CiviCRM scheduled jobs, although that setup is less common. You cannot see how cron is configured from the CiviCRM user interface.

Cron’s frequency limits how often a CiviCRM scheduled job can run. For example, if cron runs only once a day, a scheduled job cannot run every hour. Your system administrator therefore needs to set a cron frequency that meets your organisation’s needs.

docs.title: Scheduled jobs and API calls
docs.text:
CiviCRM’s API lets developers and integrators instruct CiviCRM to perform tasks. You do not usually need to understand the API to use CiviCRM, but its relationship to scheduled jobs is useful to know. The API documentation is in the Developer Guide.

An API call has an entity and an action. For example, ContributionPage.create uses the entity ContributionPage and the action create to create a contribution page. The person constructing the call can add parameters to specify characteristics such as the page’s title and financial type.

A scheduled job combines an API call with a schedule, such as “hourly”. You can specify any API call when adding a scheduled job. In principle, you could create a new contribution page every day, although that would not be very useful. Jobs are useful because the API also provides actions that site maintainers commonly need to run regularly: Job.send_reminder, for example, sends scheduled reminders.

docs.title: Synchronize CMS users to CiviCRM contacts
docs.text:
Use Synchronize Users to Contacts to check existing Drupal or Joomla users and create CiviCRM contacts where no corresponding contact record exists.

This is most often useful when your organisation adds CiviCRM to an existing Drupal or Joomla site. User records belong to the CMS; CiviCRM contact records may also have been created through imports or data entry.

  1. Go to Administer CiviCRM.
  2. In Users and Permissions, choose Synchronize Users to Contacts. The confirmation message appears:

  1. Click OK to proceed. When synchronization finishes, you will see a message like this:

Synchronize Users to Contacts completed. Checked 5 user records. Found 3 matching contact records. Created 2 new contact records.

To view or edit the new contacts, go to Advanced Search, open the >>Change Log section and enter dates that include the date of synchronization.

docs.title: How CMS users are linked to CiviCRM contacts
docs.text:
Learn how a CMS user account relates to a CiviCRM contact, and when CiviCRM links the two.

CiviCRM runs within a CMS (Backdrop, Drupal, Joomla or WordPress). The CMS handles logging in and controls access to CiviCRM features through permissions. Contacts are individuals, organizations and households in CiviCRM; users are people with a username and password for logging in through the CMS. You probably will not have a user account for every contact.

docs.title: Drupal
docs.text:
When a new user registers, CiviCRM checks for an existing contact with the same email address:

  • If it finds a match, it links the user to that contact.
  • If it finds no match, it creates a contact with the new user’s primary email address.

When an existing user logs in without a linked contact, CiviCRM makes the same check. This can happen when CiviCRM is installed or enabled on an existing Drupal site. In that situation, the source recommends running Synchronize Users to Contacts rather than relying on users to log in.

docs.title: Joomla
docs.text:
CiviCRM does not natively use Joomla’s hooks and APIs to make this check on the com_user registration or login pages. Registering a Joomla user or logging in alone therefore does not trigger a check for a corresponding CiviCRM contact. CiviCRM makes the check when a logged-in Joomla user engages in a CiviCRM transaction, such as editing a Profile form, making a Contribution or registering a Membership.

For example, someone might make a Contribution without logging in. Their email address and any custom Profile fields on the Contribution form are recorded in a CiviCRM contact. If they later register as a Joomla user with the same email address, the accounts are not linked merely by registration. After logging in, they could select an Edit my details menu item visible only to registered users and linked to a CiviCRM Profile. Selecting it triggers the match, takes them to the Profile edit page and links the Joomla user account to the CiviCRM contact.

You can replace the Joomla registration form with a form that uses a CiviCRM profile with registration enabled. You can also create a user plugin that responds to one or more of these events:

Joomla 1.5 Joomla 1.6 onBeforeStoreUser onUserAfterDelete onAfterStoreUser onUserAfterSave onBeforeDeleteUser onUserBeforeDelete onAfterDeleteUse onUserBeforeSave onLoginUser onUserLogin onLogouUser onUserLogout

docs.title: WordPress
docs.text: CiviCRM uses add_action to listen for the WordPress functions user_register and profile_update. In both cases, it synchronizes the WordPress user account with the CiviCRM contact. This synchronization currently covers only the WordPress email field.

docs.title: Existing CMS users
docs.text:
Synchronize Users to Contacts is most often used when an organisation adds CiviCRM to an existing Drupal or Joomla site. It checks existing users and generates CiviCRM contacts for those without a corresponding contact. The source also describes automatic contact creation when user records are created after CiviCRM is turned on in Drupal or Joomla; for Joomla, the registration and login limitation described above is important when considering how a particular account becomes linked.

A CMS user record represents someone with a login. A CiviCRM contact record can also be created through an import or data entry, and CiviCRM often has many contacts without user accounts (read more).

docs.title: Understanding extensions
docs.text:
Extensions let your organisation tailor CiviCRM to its needs. This page explains the kinds of extensions available, where to find them and what happens when you change their status.

An extension packages features or functionality for a particular use case. Different sets of extensions can make two CiviCRM installations look and feel quite different.

docs.title: Core Extensions
docs.text:
Some CiviCRM functionality, such as taking donations and managing memberships, is provided by Core Extensions. These are bundled with the CiviCRM core code but can be enabled or disabled as needed.

The principal user-facing Core Extensions are:

  • CiviContribute — online fundraising and donor management.
  • CiviMail — send bulk emails to your contacts.
  • CiviMember — manage memberships for your contacts.
  • CiviEvent — set up an event calendar and manage registrations.
  • CiviCampaign — set up Campaigns to track events, mailings, activities and contributions against particular projects or goals; organise Surveys and Petitions.
  • CiviCase — manage structured sequences of activities for contacts.
  • CiviGrant — take and process grant applications.

These extensions are documented in later chapters of this guide.

docs.title: Other extensions
docs.text:
The Extensions Directory lists extensions written by members of the CiviCRM community and made freely available for other organisations to download. They typically provide more specific functionality, such as integration with a particular payment processor or an alternative to the core email template editor. By default, the directory lists extensions in order of popularity, calculated from the number of sites that report using each module.

Extensions fall into two broad categories:

  • Native extensions work with any CMS.
  • CMS-specific extensions add integration between CiviCRM and a particular CMS. You may know Drupal-specific extensions as Drupal Modules and WordPress-specific extensions as WordPress Plugins.

Extensions can also be written for one organisation or site. Someone might write a custom extension for their own CiviCRM installation, or an agency might package specific modifications for a client.

docs.title: Availability in CiviCRM
docs.text:
Extensions approved for automated distribution can be installed directly from a CiviCRM installation when extension management is configured correctly. At Administer > System Settings > Extensions, you should see extensions compatible with your version of CiviCRM. You may not see every extension listed in the Extensions Directory because some may not be compatible.

If no list of extensions appears there, your system may not be properly configured to manage extensions. Consult your system administrator.

docs.title: Enabled, Disabled and Uninstalled extensions
docs.text:
An extension is Enabled when you first install it. If you no longer need it, you can Disable it; this should deactivate its associated functionality or options. You can Enable a Disabled extension again to restore its functionality and data.

Uninstalling should remove data associated with an extension. You can Uninstall an extension after disabling it, but an Uninstalled extension must be re-installed before you can use it again. No data will be restored: it will be as if you installed the extension for the first time.

docs.title: Writing extensions
docs.text:
Anyone can write an extension to enhance their CiviCRM installation, or commission someone to do so. Writing one is a developer task, so the details are outside the scope of this guide.

If you write an extension for your own use case, you may want to consider whether other organisations could benefit from it. Publishing it and making it more generic can bring feedback, bug reports and code contributions that help improve it.

docs.title: Components and Extensions
docs.text: At the time of writing, the major Core Extensions are technically also called Components. The distinction between Components and Extensions is partly technical and partly historical, but is generally unimportant. Going forward, Extension is generally the preferred term.

docs.title: Decide whether CiviCRM is right for your organisation
docs.text: You can compare CiviCRM with your organisation’s needs, try it, and learn from people who use it. CiviCRM could help your organisation reach its goals, but it will not be the right choice for every organisation.

docs.title: Identify your needs and try CiviCRM
docs.text:
Start by identifying what your organisation needs. Then choose the ways of exploring CiviCRM that will help you assess whether it fits:

  • Read case studies about how similar organisations use CiviCRM.
  • Try a free CiviCRM demonstration site.
  • Try CiviCRM Spark to get your own CiviCRM installation running in minutes on SaaS hosting, starting from $15 a month. You can cancel at any time. Spark is an option for testing CiviCRM or for ongoing use by smaller organisations and activities with up to 10,000 contacts.
  • Download and install a free test CiviCRM database.

docs.title: Ask people who use CiviCRM
docs.text:
If you know another organisation that uses CiviCRM, ask about its experience. An organisation similar to yours may offer the most useful comparison. If you do not know anyone using CiviCRM, you can contact a CiviCRM Expert, read case studies on CiviCRM.org, or try your local non-profit technology mailing list.

You can also ask questions on CiviCRM StackExchange. Before posting, write your question concisely and use CiviCRM’s names and terms where possible, rather than terms specific to your organisation. Volunteers answer the questions, so a question they can understand easily may receive an answer sooner. You must register a Stack Exchange account to ask questions or join discussions.

docs.title: Talk to a consultant
docs.text: Consider meeting a professional to discuss how CiviCRM could help your organisation. The CiviCRM website lists contributors, partners and sponsors who can walk you through CiviCRM. You may also find a local website company with CiviCRM experience.

docs.title: How organisations have used CiviCRM
docs.text:
These examples show how organisations of different sizes have used CiviCRM to manage contacts and support their work. Some have no paid employees; others have several hundred. Their needs range from simple to complex.

You will see names such as CiviEmail, CiviMember, CiviPledge and CiviCRM Profiles. These are CiviCRM components, but you do not need to understand them in detail to follow the examples. For more examples, see the case studies on CiviCRM.org. The CiviCRM Statistics site provides an overview of usage.

docs.title: American Friends Service Committee: bringing constituent data together
docs.text:
The American Friends Service Committee (AFSC) is a large, Quaker-based peace and social justice organisation with over 400 employees. Its programmes provide immediate aid and long-term development to relieve and prevent suffering, serving people on all sides of violent strife.

AFSC is headquartered in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It has nine regional headquarters and about 50 area offices in the United States, as well as field offices in Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, the Caribbean and the Middle East. Each office maintains lists of constituents. Although their needs vary, offices generally need to search for constituents, send emails, newsletters, postal mail and announcements, and collect contact information from people signing online petitions or registering for events.

An AFSC Information Technology Department survey found that staff used many systems to track constituents. Data was scattered and contact information was duplicated, making contacts hard to manage and support difficult for the IT Department to provide. Staff also reported limited searching, no way to send high-volume newsletters or announcements, and no way to collect information online. After investigating several database systems, the department decided that CiviCRM might be the best fit.

docs.title: How AFSC used CiviCRM
docs.text:
AFSC first established externally managed CiviCRM sites with CiviMail for its Los Angeles, Rhode Island, San Francisco and Seattle offices. Los Angeles also used CiviEvent to track event registrations and CiviMember to track committee members’ contact information.

A Los Angeles staff member then found that CiviMember’s export component lacked functionality needed to compile a membership directory. AFSC contracted the CiviCRM Core development team to add it. The addition became part of CiviCRM, benefiting the wider community and removing AFSC’s concern about its compatibility with future upgrades.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
The external hosting arrangement caused problems when the vendor became unresponsive to issues and did not provide promised services, including timely CiviCRM updates. Once the hosting issue was resolved, staff could use the capabilities they had previously lacked.

The Los Angeles office used CiviCRM as its main repository for constituents, board and committee members, and volunteers. Constituents could sign up for events and petitions online, while staff could send high-volume newsletters and announcements. The Colorado office joined later, replacing its old system and meeting its main goal: identifying newsletter subscribers and sending them a monthly newsletter through CiviCRM.

At the time described, AFSC had nine CiviCRM sites, and its IT Department recommended CiviCRM as the “database of choice” for all offices. Staff could access data wherever they had internet access, run complex searches, manage online event registrations, and send online newsletters and postal mailings. AFSC also reported excellent support from the CiviCRM community and continuing improvements to CiviCRM.

docs.title: Schoolhouse Supplies: coordinating operations
docs.text: Schoolhouse Supplies (SHS) is a non-profit organisation in Portland, Oregon, USA, that gathers and distributes school supplies to students and teachers. Before CiviCRM, it used Exceed, EROI, Constant Contact, Salesforce, Auction Pay for online contributions, and hundreds of spreadsheets. A custom web application managed online store inventory and processed in-kind donations.

docs.title: How SHS used CiviCRM
docs.text: SHS migrated data from each source into CiviCRM Standalone, an installation not integrated with either Drupal or Joomla! CMS. CiviContact and CiviContribute replaced Exceed and Auction Pay; CiviMail replaced EROI and Constant Contact. SHS moved its Salesforce data into CiviCRM, integrated the custom e-commerce application it supported, integrated the inventory and in-kind management system, and imported its spreadsheets.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text: Bringing constituent data together let each business process use the full database and made activities easier to coordinate. At the time described, SHS was also moving manual processes, such as volunteer coordination, into CiviCRM. It could plan and run campaigns that would previously have been impossible or prohibitively expensive.

docs.title: New York State Nursery Landscape Association: managing members and certification
docs.text:
The New York State Nursery Landscape Association (NYSNLA) provides resources and advocacy for nursery and landscape professionals throughout New York State. It promotes sound business practices, expands state and local markets, and supports the development of sustainable communities.

NYSNLA had managed members first in spreadsheets and then in a Microsoft Access database. It moved to CiviCRM to consolidate data, give members real-time access to their contact details, and offer website visitors a searchable directory of nursery and landscape professionals.

docs.title: How NYSNLA used CiviCRM
docs.text:
With a CiviCRM consultant, NYSNLA analysed its existing database and mapped its functions to CiviCRM. It chose CiviMember, CiviEvent, CiviContribute and CiviMail for its core needs. It also considered future use of CiviPledge to solicit contributions for its associated non-profit, the Nurserymen’s Foundation.

Its Certified Nursery Landscape Professional programme (CNLP) needed particular attention. Designed by industry members with help from Cornell University, this ongoing educational programme develops garden and landscape employees’ skills. Applicants must pass a test, and certification lasts two years before recertification is required.

NYSNLA used CiviCRM’s membership functionality to track CNLP status. A rolling-period membership let it see when certification was nearing expiration. It tracked initial applications through CiviEvent because applying involved registering for one of the twice-yearly test events.

NYSNLA also customised the interface to make contact records more useful. Staff wanted to see whether employees of a particular nursery or landscape company were CNLPs or Lifetime CNLPs, and which employees were authorised to manage the company’s records.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text: To help the public find qualified professionals, NYSNLA added a searchable member directory to its website. Visitors could search by the association’s eight statewide regions and by services represented with CiviCRM tags. Because the directory connected directly to contact data, visitors saw current information. Members could also access their own contact details and maintain their services and other information.

docs.title: Green Party of New Zealand: supporting campaigns
docs.text:
The Green Party was New Zealand’s third-largest political party for most of the decade described, with roots in the Values Party of the early 1970s, the world’s first national Green party. It gained parliamentary representation in

  1. After the 2008 election, it had nine Members of Parliament, 5,000 financial members and about 50,000 contacts. It had more than 50 branches and contested elections across all 67 electorates in the election described.

Before CiviCRM, the Party and its parliamentary units used a range of systems for members, donations, contacts, campaigning, media and advocacy. Its policy stated that:

  • Development of IT must be socially responsible and sustainable.
  • The use of free and open source software should be encouraged.

docs.title: How the Party used CiviCRM
docs.text:
The Party adopted CiviCRM version 1.7 in 2007 alongside a move to Drupal. Work by the Canadian Greens on a Drupal voter-canvassing module partly inspired the decision. The Party established a CiviCRM database and introduced online donations, memberships and event registrations.

For media releases, the Party represented more than 100 issues in a check-box custom data field. It built a Smart Group for each issue to use when sending releases through CiviMail.

Complex access requirements led the Party to develop an alternative to ACLs (Access Control Lists) that was more granular and easier to manage. This approach was incorporated into CiviCRM’s core code as a hook, which developers can use to extend CiviCRM.

For the 2008 election campaign, the Party developed a look-up function. When a new contact was added, it checked the address against an Electoral Roll table, linked matches and recorded “soft” matches.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
During the 2008 campaign, the Party made extensive use of online fundraising and greatly exceeded its previous online income. Membership renewal became more streamlined, with more renewals taking place online.

As of May 2009, the Party was still using CiviCRM v2.0 on Drupal 5 and had not benefited from features introduced in versions 2.1 and 2.2. An upgrade was in progress. Training and developing more in-house super-users remained challenges. New CiviCRM features prompted the Party to reconsider some uses of custom data fields, particularly for CiviMail media releases; nested groups and Drupal Organic Groups suggested a potentially more time-effective approach.

docs.title: QuestBridge: managing student applications
docs.text: QuestBridge helps motivated, low-income high school students get accepted to college and pay for it. It recruits juniors across the USA to complete its online application. Its partner colleges and universities accept that application in place of their own admissions applications, with the aim of increasing the socio-economic diversity of their student bodies.

docs.title: How QuestBridge used CiviCRM
docs.text: QuestBridge built most of its business processes around CiviCRM. It wrote its online admissions application using CiviCRM and extended it with the PHP scripting language. CiviCRM stored students’ biographical and application information and their communication histories.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text: In the 2008–9 school year, QuestBridge helped more than 1,200 students get accepted to and pay for college at its 25 partner schools. Its effective CiviCRM implementation contributed to working efficiently. At the time described, QuestBridge planned to upgrade to the latest CiviCRM version to use new email features. If starting again, it would invest more in CiviCRM training at the outset.

docs.title: The San Francisco School: connecting families and staff
docs.text:
The San Francisco School (SFS) is a coeducational school from preschool through eighth grade, with a diverse student body of about

  1. Keeping families’ phone numbers, email addresses and information such as allergies current is important to meeting students’ needs. The head of school supported the project from the beginning, helping staff and parents commit to it.

docs.title: How SFS used CiviCRM
docs.text:
SFS used CiviCRM to create a Parent Portal that:

  • Required parents to log in to view their contact information and their child’s school information.
  • Automated scheduling for parent–teacher conferences.
  • Recorded sign-in and sign-out for after-school classes on a computer.
  • Managed registration for after-school classes, such as music, cooking and sports, and let parents view their child’s after-school fees.

SFS introduced these features gradually rather than showing the school community everything at once.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text: Parents and guardians could see the contact information held by the school and notify staff of changes. They could also see after-school fees and the classes their child had joined. Online sign-ups let families schedule conferences and classes at a convenient time. The shared portal helped families and staff keep contact information current, schedule conferences promptly and make information more widely accessible.

docs.title: What is CiviCRM?
docs.text: CiviCRM is a web-based constituent relationship management (CRM) system built by and for nonprofit organisations and NGOs. It helps your organisation keep information about the people and organisations it works with in one place.

docs.title: More than an address book
docs.text:
An address book holds contact details. A CRM can also help you keep a history of interactions and use that history to plan what happens next. For example, you might want to look up your conversations with Ji Lao or find out how many people helped your organisation this month.

Imagine organising a dinner party for people you met during the past year. An enhanced address book could help you email invitations, track RSVPs and dietary preferences, and see how many guests to expect two nights before the event. For an organisation, keeping this kind of information over time makes it easier to reach groups interested in particular topics, observe their responses and adjust future communications.

CiviCRM brings together information about contacts, donations, events, memberships, activities, cases, campaigns and mailings. It supports communications, community engagement, activism, outreach and donor management.

docs.title: What you can manage
docs.text:
CiviCRM is modular. In a simple set-up, you can:

  • Record names, home or postal addresses, email addresses and phone numbers.
  • Define relationships between contacts.
  • Send emails.
  • Keep a record of interactions with contacts.

Components and extensions add other possibilities, such as signing up members, taking event registrations, receiving donations and distributing grants. See the Components and Extensions chapters for more information.

docs.title: How CiviCRM works with a website
docs.text:
A content management system (CMS) is a tool for creating and managing a website. CiviCRM integrates with Backdrop, Drupal, Joomla and WordPress.
