The Contributions tab shows a contact’s financial contributions and a summary of their total amount, number and average amount over time.

Record Contribution records an offline contribution. Submit Credit Card Contribution records a credit card transaction on the contact’s behalf, such as a contribution made by phone. Both forms let you select the Financial Type alongside the usual information collected on public contribution pages.

See the Contributions chapter for more information.

docs.title: Memberships tab
docs.text:
The Memberships tab shows a contact’s memberships. You can add memberships, submit credit card payments for memberships with a fee, and use the more link on an existing membership to renew or delete it.

See the Membership chapter for more information.

docs.title: Events tab
docs.text:
The Events tab shows events the contact has registered for, attended or volunteered at. You can register the contact for an event or use Submit Credit Card Event Registration if payment is required. The related payment then appears in the first row of the contact’s Contributions tab.

You can use Edit to change the contact’s event information, such as changing their status from “registered” to “attended”.

See the Events chapter for more information.

docs.title: Groups tab
docs.text:
The Groups tab shows groups the contact belongs to. Groups can be used for mailing lists and permissions (ACLs). You can add or remove the contact and see a history of groups they have unsubscribed from or been removed from.

The Status column shows who added the contact to a group. Whether users can add themselves is configured when the group is created. If a group’s visibility is set to Public Listings, users can join through Profile forms. A later section discusses using Profiles for mailing-list sign-ups.

See Groups and Tags for more information.

docs.title: Notes tab
docs.text:
The Notes tab holds ad-hoc information about a contact. A note’s subject and content are both free-text fields. For information you plan to collect consistently, custom fields are generally more suitable. Because notes are unstructured, use this tab with care unless people working with your CiviCRM installation will remember to look there.

A note can have Author Only privacy. Only its author or someone with view all notes permission through your CMS can view or edit it.

docs.title: Tags tab
docs.text:
Tags categorise contacts; Custom Data and Groups are other ways to do this. Your organisation can configure its tags. You can search by tag and create Smart Groups based on tags.

Tags beside Keywords belong to the Keywords Tagset. A Tagset is a non-hierarchical grouping of tags. You can create a tag in a tagset by typing it into the field, or select an existing matching tag from the list that appears.

See Groups and Tags for more information.

docs.title: Change Log tab
docs.text:
The Change Log tab shows when a contact record changed and who made the change, but not what changed.

Administrators can use the Contact Logging Report for detailed information about who changed a contact record, what changed and when.

docs.title: Contact subtypes
docs.text: Contact subtypes extend the three core contact types. They let your organisation collect and display different custom data for different kinds of contacts. See custom fields for information about adding fields to specific subtypes.

docs.title: Custom field settings
docs.text: Use this reference to check what each custom field set and field option controls. Custom fields belong to custom field sets; set-level options apply to the set, while field options apply to individual fields.

docs.title: Set Name
docs.text: For a set displayed inline, Set Name appears as the field set’s legend. For a set displayed as a tab, it appears as the navigation tab label.

docs.title: Used For
docs.text:
Used For determines which records can have the set’s fields. The following are some of its options; custom fields can be added to more than 20 different entities.

Option Where the fields apply Activity All activities or a specific activity type, such as Meeting or Phone Call. Addresses An address block, allowing an administrator to create additional address-related fields. Contacts All contacts. Contributions All contributions or a specific Financial Type, such as Donations or Event Fees. Events All events or a specific event type, such as Conference or Fundraiser. These fields apply to the event, not its participant registration records. Grants Grants. Groups Group settings. These fields are not searchable. Household Household contacts. Individual Individual contacts. Memberships All membership records or a specific membership type. Organization Organization contacts. Participants Participant registration records. You can apply fields to all registration records, a specific participant role or a specific event. Pledges Pledges. Relationships All relationship records or a specific relationship type, such as “Spouse of” or “Employee of”.

It is also possible to add custom fields to entities not listed under Used For, including your own custom entities. For an entity that does not support custom fields, those fields might not appear in its forms, but they will be available in SearchKit.

Used For can be changed only while no data has been recorded with the set. Until then, use More > Settings for the set under Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Fields. Once data exists, you cannot change the set’s scope.

docs.title: Order
docs.text: Order controls how multiple custom field sets are presented. Lower numbers, such as 1 and 2, appear above higher numbers, such as 8 and 9.

docs.title: Multiple record fieldsets
docs.text:
By default, a custom field set has a one-to-one relationship with the record it is attached to. For example, a set holding a person’s height and eye colour can have one record for each Individual contact. A set holding educational history might instead need several records for one person, each with a subject, institution and grade.

Does this Custom Field Set allow multiple records? allows multiple records for a set, subject to these limits:

  • The setting applies to the whole set, not individual fields.
  • Multiple-record field sets can be added only to Contacts, not to Activities, Contributions or other entities.
  • Multiple-record data cannot currently be exported.

Before using a multiple-record set, consider whether the information should instead be an activity with custom data. An educational degree is one possible example.

docs.title: Display options
docs.text:
The display style tab is visible only for custom data fields attached to contacts. Contact field sets can appear inline on the summary screen or in their own tab. You can change the display style later. How often you need the data and the size of the set may help you choose.

You can also have a set start collapsed. Initially, only its title appears and its fields are hidden, reducing the space used by an infrequently accessed set. A similar collapsed setting is available for custom data in Advanced Search.

There are two tab styles:

  • Tab with table gives a concise overview of the set’s data. New records can be added and existing ones edited in pop-up windows. Under more, “copy a record” lets you copy a record and change just one or two fields before saving it as a new record.

  • Tab displays data in a format similar to the inline style.

docs.title: Is this Custom Field Set active?
docs.text:
When a set is active, its fields can be viewed and changed. When it is inactive, they remain in CiviCRM but are hidden from the user interface. Individual fields can also be made inactive in their own settings when the set is active.

For example, you could import historical membership records from an MS Access database with a unique Access ID. A custom field could retain that ID even if it has no direct use in CiviCRM. You could then leave the Activate option unchecked to hide the field while keeping its value for a later investigation or comparison with a printed record.

docs.title: Is this Custom Field Set public?
docs.text:
When a set is marked public, its fields appear on public-facing pages. For example, fields intended for an event information page should be in a public set; fields holding administrative information about the event should be in a set that is not public.

This setting applies to every field in the set. Individual fields cannot be marked public or not public.

docs.title: Pre-form Help and Post-form Help
docs.text: Use these settings for instructions about the entire set. Pre-form Help appears above the form field, and Post-form Help appears below it.

docs.title: Field label
docs.text: Field label is the text shown next to the field and used as its label in data exports. In a profile, you can override it with a different Field Label. This lets you use an administrator-facing label in the field settings and a more user-friendly one in the profile.

docs.title: Type
docs.text:
Type combines the format of data to store, selected from the left menu, with the way users interact with it, selected from the right menu. CiviCRM offers a dropdown list of data types when you create a field.

Data type Available input types or behaviour Alphanumeric Text, Select, Radio, Yes and No, Check-box, Multi-select, Advanced Multi-select or Autocomplete select. Note A longer, multiple-line text box: plain text or rich text with a WYSIWYG editor that allows HTML. Integer A whole number entered through a text box, select box or radio list. Number A number that can include decimals, such as 3.175, entered through a text box, select box or radio list. Money A number treated according to the local currency configured in CiviCRM’s administrative pages; entered through a text box, select box or radio list. Date A date, and optionally a time, entered with a calendar widget. You can set a selectable range of years before and after the current date. State/Province Locations configured in CiviCRM’s Localization settings at Administer > Configure > Global Settings > Localization; offered as a select box or multi-select box. Country A list of geographical locations, offered as a select box or multi-select box. File A browser control for selecting and uploading a file. Link An active internet hyperlink. Contact Reference An autocomplete widget for an existing CiviCRM contact.

The Alphanumeric input types behave as follows:

  • Text provides a simple area for entering text.
  • Select is a dropdown allowing one selection.
  • Radio shows all choices at once and allows one selection.
  • Yes and No is a radio list with two contrasting options.
  • Check-box allows multiple selections.
  • Multi-select shows choices in one box and allows multiple selections using control+click.
  • Advanced Multi-select shows two lists side by side; items can be moved between them.
  • Autocomplete select fills in a selection when the text entered uniquely identifies it.

The input type affects searching. For example, Check-box fields support both OR and AND searches in Advanced Search, while Multi-select fields do not.

docs.title: Display in Table?
docs.text:
Display in Table? appears only for a field in a multiple-record set displayed as Tab with table. It is checked by default. Uncheck it to omit a less important field from the table, for example when a large data set makes the table too wide for the screen.

A field omitted from the table is still available when you add a record or view, edit or copy a row.

docs.title: Database Field Length
docs.text: Database Field Length sets the number of characters a field can contain. Normally, leave it at the maximum. Shortening it might improve performance or reduce storage for an extremely large field set, but will make no difference for most users.

docs.title: Order
docs.text: Order controls where a field appears within its set. Set it in the field edit form or use the up/down icons in the main field listing. New fields appear at the bottom by default.

docs.title: Default Value
docs.text: Where applicable, Default Value is automatically shown or selected when someone opens a form containing the field.

docs.title: Pre-form Help and Post-form Help
docs.text:
Use help text when the label does not make clear what to enter or when you need to explain how to use the field. Pre-form Help appears above the field; Post-form Help appears below it.

This help appears wherever the field is used on administration pages. It also becomes the default help text when the field is assigned to a profile. The person creating the profile can change or remove that text without changing the original custom field definition.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
When Required is selected, the form cannot be submitted without a value for the field. An error message directs the person to complete it.

If a field should be required only in a particular profile, leave this setting unchecked and set Required in that profile instead.

docs.title: Optimize for Search
docs.text:
Optimize for Search creates a database index for the field. This can speed up searches substantially, but takes more storage and may slow the system when the data is updated frequently.

An index is recommended for fields often used in searches or as smart group criteria, such as identifiers or values selected from a list. It is likely to be inefficient for frequently updated text, such as notes or comments, that is rarely searched for an exact value.

This option changed in CiviCRM 5.75. Before that version, it was called “is searchable?” and also determined whether a field appeared in Advanced Search and Reports. From 5.75, all fields are available in Advanced Search and Reports.

docs.title: Active
docs.text: Active determines whether an individual field is enabled or disabled when CiviCRM displays it to users. The field set has its own active setting.

docs.title: View Only
docs.text: View Only makes a field visible but not editable. It can hold imported data that users should be able to consult but not change, or data entered by a method set up by your developer rather than through the user interface.

docs.title: Multiple choice options
docs.text:
For Select, Radio, Check-box, Multi-select and Advanced Multi-select fields, you can reuse an option set created for another custom field or create a new set. Options can be entered when you create the field or later. Each option’s label appears on the form; its value is stored in the contact record.

If you reuse an option set, CiviCRM notifies you when a change will affect several fields. For a new set, you can initially enter up to ten choices in a table. After saving the field, Edit Multiple Choice Options lets you add an unlimited number of further choices. At Administer > Customize > Custom Data > View and Edit Custom Fields > Edit Multiple Choice Options, you can later add choices or change their labels, order and active status.

You can mark one choice as the default. Inactive choices are hidden when the field is presented.

docs.title: Managing fields in a set
docs.text:
At Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Data, View and Edit Custom Fields shows the fields in a set. Available actions include editing settings, editing multiple choice options where applicable, previewing, disabling, deleting and Move.

You can move fields between sets used for all contacts or for contact sub-types. Otherwise, you can move fields only between sets of the same type.

docs.title: Plan how to organise custom data
docs.text: Choosing where to store information affects which records show it and how easily your organisation can use it. Custom fields extend the information CiviCRM provides by default, but a group or tag may better serve some contact-related needs.

docs.title: Fields and field sets
docs.text:
A field holds one unit of information, such as a person’s primary spoken language or high school graduation date. CiviCRM stores custom fields in field sets: groups of related fields associated with a type of record. A set might relate to an activity type, event participation or contributions.

A set can have a broad or narrow scope. For example, a “nationality” set might apply to all contact types, an “immigration status” set to a specific contact type such as Individuals, and another set to a component such as CiviMember or CiviEvent, or to Relationships or Groups. You might also add checkboxes to organisations to track the clients they serve, or add a subjects-studied field for contacts of a Student type.

Choose a set’s scope carefully: once data has been recorded with it, you cannot change what it is used for. Consider how its fields will be used, which contacts or records need them, and whether they apply broadly or only to a specific Contact Type, Event or Financial Type.

The record should match what the data describes. A dinner entrée choice belongs to the Participant record, not the Individual Contact record: the same person might make a different choice at another dinner. Similarly, eye colour is relevant to Individual contacts rather than all Contacts, which would also include Organization and Household contacts. Custom data for one event registration page can be associated with an Event type Participant for that specific Event. Appropriate scope keeps screens free of irrelevant fields.

Related fields can also be divided into topical sets. If an Individual contact has 20 custom fields and 12 relate to an online membership directory, you might put those 12 in a directory set and the others in a general Individual details set.

docs.title: Fields, groups and tags
docs.text:
Avoid creating a custom field for every contact attribute. Using fields where groups or tags are more appropriate can slow the system and make records harder for administrative staff to maintain.

  • Custom data fields suit information with a wide range of values, such as an address or biography. Related fields can appear together on their own tab in a contact record. A field set can apply to a specific record type, such as Household contacts.
  • Groups bring contacts together, such as board members, staff or volunteers. If you use Drupal, permissions can be based on group membership. A Smart Group automatically adds and removes contacts according to a characteristic. Contacts must belong to a Group to receive a particular CiviMail mass mailing; for example, a press release could go to a designated group or Smart Group.
  • Tags can be added and removed without reloading the page in edit mode. They offer more powerful search options than fields or groups: visitors can search across multiple tags using both AND and OR. Data fields support lists of words, effectively an AND search, except Check-box fields, which support OR. Once defined, tags are assigned to all contact types rather than to a specific record type.

Groups and tags can both have hierarchies. For example, “Regions” could contain a subgroup or subtag for each geographic region your organisation covers.

docs.title: Limits of large field sets
docs.text: Many custom field sets, or sets containing many fields, may cause problems with searches, exports or reports. There is no single useful limit: it depends on the types of data and the server hosting your installation. If you are unsure, discuss your plans with your system administrator or CiviCRM service provider.

docs.title: Create a custom field set and fields
docs.text: Create a field set first, then add the fields that will hold your organisation’s data. You can use custom fields to record information such as a contact’s primary spoken language or a high school graduation date.

docs.title: Create the field set
docs.text:
Before you choose Used For: decide which records need these fields. You can change Used For through More > Settings only until data has been recorded in the set; after that, you cannot change its scope.

  1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Data.
  2. Create a custom field set.
  3. Enter a title for the set.
  4. Choose the type of records under Used For.
  5. Select the display characteristics you need.
  6. Enter help text if the whole set needs instructions.

The field set configuration screen is shown here:

docs.title: Add fields
docs.text:
Before you choose a field’s data and input types: these are the exceptions to the field options you can change after creating it.

  1. Click View and Edit Custom Fields for the field set.
  2. Click New Custom Field. The field configuration screen opens.
  3. Enter a Field label.
  4. Choose the data type and input type under Type.
  5. Set any other field options you need.
  6. Click Save to return to the field listing, or Save and New to save the field and start another.

You can preview individual fields and the whole set while defining them. This is particularly useful for checking the layout of Radio and Check-box fields with many choices.

docs.title: Add headings to multiple choice options
docs.text:
If you use a Select or Multi-Select field, you can display headings within its list of options:

  1. Choose Select or Multi-Select as the input type.

  2. When configuring the options, set each heading’s Label to the text users should see and its Value to text prefixed with crm_optgroup_.

docs.title: Groups and group membership
docs.text:
Use this page to check how groups work, what their settings mean and where to manage their contacts.

Groups are collections of contacts with something in common. Well-defined groups help you segment your contact database and play a role in CiviMail and Profiles. On Drupal, they can also be used to set up advanced access rights.

docs.title: Regular and Smart Groups
docs.text:
• Groups, also called regular groups, have contacts that you add and remove manually. For example, you could put your organisation's board members in a Board of Directors group, then email the group without selecting each board member individually.

  • Smart Groups are populated automatically from configured characteristics or activities. CiviCRM checks contacts as they are added or edited and adds those that meet the criteria. A “2010 Contributors from California” Smart Group, for example, could include contacts with an address in California who contributed in

  • A Smart Group of donors who have not yet been sent a thank-you letter can also provide a working list: donors leave it as they receive letters.

docs.title: Group settings
docs.text:
Give each group a clear name and a description that explains its purpose to other database users, including people working in CiviMail. This becomes particularly useful as the number of groups grows. If you create a group for a particular person in your organisation, naming its owner in the description can help others decide later whether the group is still needed.

Setting Behaviour Mailing List group type Use this if you plan to use the group as a mailing list in CiviMail. It is available for regular and Smart Groups. Access Control group type On Drupal, use this to assign CiviCRM access permissions to a set of contacts. It is available only for regular Groups. User and User Admin Only visibility Membership is controlled only by authorised CiviCRM users. Public Pages visibility Contacts can join and remove themselves through Registration and Account Profile forms.

You can create additional group types to meet your organisation's needs. Group type is a filter on the Manage Groups screen, which can be useful if you have hundreds of groups. To create a type, go to Administer > System Settings > Option Groups and select Group Type.

docs.title: Parent and child groups
docs.text:
You can organise groups in a hierarchy by assigning child groups to a parent group. A mailing to the parent group, or a search within it, automatically includes contacts in its child groups.

For example, an organisation with a national office and five regional offices could put each region's constituents in a regional group and make a National group their parent. A mailing to National would then include contacts in all five regional groups.

docs.title: Group IDs
docs.text: CiviCRM assigns each group a unique numeric ID. A group ID can, for example, be used to define a URL for group sign-ups.

docs.title: Manage and find groups
docs.text:
Go to Navigation Menu > Contacts > Manage Groups to view and manage groups.

The Find Groups form searches by name, type, visibility and enabled or disabled status. You can also scroll or browse the list, which includes regular and Smart Groups. Each row shows how many contacts are currently in the group and provides these actions:

  • Contacts: open the group's contacts and add contacts.
  • Settings: edit the group.
  • The more pop-up menu: disable or delete the group.

A group's Contacts page lets you search within that group by name, email address, contact type, group status (Added, Removed or Pending) and tags.

docs.title: Ways to add contacts
docs.text:
You can add an individual contact through the Tags and Groups section of the Contact Details edit screen or the contact's Groups tab. Both places also let you remove an individual contact. Filling out a Profile can add a contact to a group.

To add multiple contacts at once, the source describes these routes:

  • Conduct a search, then use the Add Contacts to Group/Tag contacts batch action. It also describes selecting Add Contacts to a Group from the More Actions menu.
  • Go to Navigation Menu > Contacts > Manage Groups and open the group's Contacts link. The source also describes selecting Members for the group, then Add Members to this Group at the top of the screen.

docs.title: Remove or delete a membership record
docs.text:
Remove keeps a historical record of the contact's group membership, including when the contact was removed and by whom. This can help you identify former volunteer group members or answer a subscriber who asks when they opted out of a newsletter. If a contact was removed in error, Rejoin Group adds them again.

Delete eliminates any record of the contact being in the group. Use it only when that loss of history is appropriate.

To find contacts by membership status, go to Contacts > Manage Groups, select Contacts for the group and expand the search criteria to search by status. For example, you could find former Advisory Board members.

docs.title: Groups and access control
docs.text:
Access Control Lists (ACL) provide finer-grained permissions than Drupal's Permissions and Roles. Before you can use Groups, Custom Data Groups, Profiles and Roles in ACL, you must set up those required parts. Setting up ACLs requires an understanding of the concept; see the CiviCRM access control documentation.

Note

ACL support for Joomla was introduced in Joomla version 1.6.

docs.title: Organise records with tags and tag sets
docs.text: Use tags to categorise contacts, activities and cases, and tag sets when you want a named collection of tags that you can extend while editing records.

docs.title: Manage tags
docs.text:
Go to Contacts > Manage Tags (Categories) in the navigation menu to view tags. To create one, click Add Tag on that screen or go to Contacts > New Tag. Use the respective links in a tag's row to edit or delete it.

Give each tag a clear, unique name and a description that explains its purpose. You can make it a subtag by selecting a Parent tag from the dropdown list. You can designate tags for contacts, activities and/or cases; a contact tag is available for all contact types and subtypes, not just one type.

You can create as many tags as needed, but avoid duplicates and tags that are not necessary. A standard process for creating and using tags can help your organisation do this. Users can create more tags when needed; important tags can be locked against modification or deletion by users without the administer reserved tags permission. That permission is available in Drupal only.

Assign a tag while creating or editing a record, from the Contact Summary Tags tab, or through the Tag Contacts batch action after a search. You can remove a tag using the first two methods.

docs.title: Create a tag set
docs.text:
A tag set is a free-form “bucket” for related tags. For example, an Issues People Care About tag set might contain affordable housing, racial justice and water quality. Unlike regular tags, tag sets let you create tags without opening Manage Tags and add a search field to the Basic Criteria section of Advanced Search.

  1. Go to Contacts > Manage Tags (Categories) in the navigation menu.
  2. Click Add Tag Set.
  3. Give the tag set a name and description.
  4. Indicate whether it applies to contacts, activities or cases.

Selecting the Reserved checkbox prevents someone without Administrator permission from deleting the tag set. For more on permissions, see the Permissions and Access Control chapter in Initial Set Up.

The new tag set appears as a field on the relevant edit pages for activities or cases, or on the Tags tab for contacts. For example, a tag set called Issues Folks Care About associated with Contacts appears the next time you open a contact's Tags tab.

docs.title: Use tags in a tag set
docs.text:
The tag-set field uses autocomplete. As you type, CiviCRM shows matching tags from that set below the field. Select a match, or type a new tag in full and press Enter to create it. The tag then appears in a box within the field; clicking its X untags the contact, case or activity you are editing.

A tag created within a tag set also appears in Contacts > Manage Tags (Categories), where you can view and edit it. It is available only within the tag set in which it was created.

docs.title: Search tags and tag sets
docs.text:
Each tag set you create adds a field to the Basic Criteria section of Advanced Search. You can search that field only for tags that already exist in the set.

The All Tags field finds records with regular tags or tag-set tags containing a complete or partial word or phrase. For example, entering Donor can find contacts assigned any of several tags containing that word. For more on Advanced Search, see the Searching section.

docs.title: Choose between groups and tags
docs.text: You will learn what groups and tags are suited to, and which limitations matter when you use them to organise data.

docs.title: A way to think about the difference
docs.text:
Tags describe contacts, activities and cases. Groups bring contacts together as a unit that your organisation can work with, such as a mailing list. This is a guideline, not a rule: the right choice depends on how you intend to segment your contacts.

For example, volunteer, ally organisation, vegetarian and musician could be tags. Volunteer Committee, Allied Organisations Coalition, Vegetarian Newsletter and This Awesome Band With A Bad Name could be groups.

You can use groups and tags together in more refined searches using AND and OR. If journalists, volunteers and members are groups, and development, art and history are tags, you could find journalists interested in art or development, or volunteers or members interested in history.

docs.title: What tags offer
docs.text:
• Tags are easy to set up and use. You can search by tag in Basic or Advanced Search and combine tags with other properties, such as residence state/province, to create Smart Groups.
  • Tags can apply to contacts, activities and cases; groups consist only of contacts.
  • A tag for contacts cannot be restricted to one contact type, such as Individuals.
  • Tags allow multiple selections, so they may not suit mutually exclusive characteristics such as Democrat, Republican and Green Party.
  • You cannot selectively hide tags or control permissions for individual tags on built-in or Profile create and edit forms: all tags appear on edit forms.
  • When you export tags, all tags assigned to a record appear as a list in one cell, such as Teacher, Volunteer.

docs.title: What groups offer
docs.text:
• Groups can segment contacts for recurring work, such as sending an enewsletter or printing mailing labels. They are integrated with other CiviCRM functions, notably CiviMail, and can be associated with Drupal Organic Groups.
  • Smart Groups can add contacts automatically based on their characteristics. You can also create Smart Groups that combine members of Group A and Group B.
  • Groups can restrict access to particular sets of contacts. They support administrative and end-user subscribe and unsubscribe actions, and keep a history of those actions.
  • Visibility settings let you decide which groups appear to end-users on Profile forms, so some groups can be private.
  • Every existing group appears under Manage Groups and in search forms. Too many groups can make these lists difficult to use; groups created for short-term projects should be purged when they are no longer needed.
  • When you export contact records, all groups a contact belongs to appear as one comma-separated list, such as Administrators,Newsletter Subscribers.

docs.title: Mapping your data to CiviCRM
docs.text:
Learn how the information your organisation already holds can fit into CiviCRM. Mapping data before you import it helps you avoid duplicate fields and records that are difficult to manage or report on later.

Your data may come from spreadsheets, paper records or what colleagues remember. The same information may also have different names in different systems: Donation, Opportunity and Contribution, for example, can all describe money given to your organisation. Mapping means deciding where each piece of information belongs in CiviCRM rather than copying the structure of an old system.

Do not add custom fields before checking what CiviCRM already provides. For example, rather than entering membership expiration dates in a new field, consider the membership module, which manages membership duration, expiration and renewal reminders. Multiple fields for the same information can cause confusion.

docs.title: Contacts and contact types
docs.text:
CiviCRM provides fields for names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, notes and other contact information. Its three Contact Types describe who or what a constituent is:

  • Individuals: People your organisation wants to keep a record of.
  • Organizations: Other non-profits, companies, chapters of your organisation or committees. You will generally want at least one Organization contact to represent your own organisation, particularly when configuring memberships.
  • Households: Families or groups of people who share a physical location.

Each contact type has fields suited to it. For example, the gender field is available for Individual contacts and subtypes, not Organizations or Households. See Contacts for more about built-in contact fields.

docs.title: Information specific to your organisation
docs.text:
Your organisation may need to record information that the standard contact fields do not cover, such as an individual's allergies or an organization's service area. First decide whether each item belongs to an Individual, Organization or Household. A service area, for example, makes sense for an Organization.

If you need a field that CiviCRM does not provide, see Creating Custom Fields.

docs.title: Relationships between contacts
docs.text:
A flat spreadsheet may not show how constituents connect. Relationships link two contact records and can capture information that colleagues otherwise keep in memory, such as family connections, employment or connections with other constituents.

CiviCRM includes relationship Types such as employer--employee, parent--child and employee--employer. You can define types specific to your organisation, such as vicar--church. A Relationship can have a start date and, where relevant, an end date. Ended relationships remain accessible, so you can still see where someone used to work.

A Household groups people who share an address, which can help you send one letter rather than several. The relationship Types household member of--head of the household help identify whom to address—for example, a parent rather than a child. See the Relationships section in Organising Your Data for configuration and use.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activities record exchanges such as phone calls, emails and meetings between staff and constituents. They help your organisation retain a record of how people engage with it. For example, someone who gives monthly, volunteers frequently and renews a membership each year may respond to opportunities that strengthen their relationship with your organisation.

Activities are linked to other CiviCRM modules. When you record contributions, event attendance, membership subscriptions and emails, CiviCRM automatically creates a related activity in the Contact record. Consider whether you also need activity types such as training, review, exam or support. See the Activites section in Organising Your Data for configuration and use.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
CiviEvents manages occasions that bring people together at a particular time and place, including online webinars, performances and meetings. Events have start and end dates and times, meeting places and a purpose. They may be ticketed, RSVP only or require no reservation. CiviCRM can promote events and record registrations; records of participation in past events can be transferred into CiviEvents.

The Event Types field distinguishes the kinds of events you host. It can help you evaluate participation across a series or see whether someone prefers one kind of event. See the Events chapter later in this book.

docs.title: Memberships
docs.text:
A membership is a structured arrangement in which a constituent receives benefits for a defined period. Memberships may have different dues levels and associated benefits, or they may be free—for example, a life-time membership awarded to a long-time volunteer. Benefits can include access to member directories, extra content or discounts. Individuals, families or households, and organizations can all sign up for memberships.

Unlike a one-time donation, a membership changes someone's relationship with your organisation for a period and is often expected to renew. An organisation may need to acknowledge a donation, but it has not promised the donor the advertised benefits of a membership in return for that donation or Contribution.

Review your membership structure before importing records. Consider removing unused levels and simplifying promised benefits. The information you need to transfer for each member is the start date, duration, membership dues paid and membership type. More than 10–15 membership types may be hard to manage. If existing types hold other information about constituents, check whether CiviCRM already has membership-related fields for it before extending membership records.

Some information previously stored as a fixed value can instead be calculated. For example, CiviCRM can calculate years of membership from the Membership since date and display the result in reports or other fields. See the Memberships chapter later in this book.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
A Contribution records money, goods or services coming into your organisation. CiviCRM can record money from event tickets, memberships and other paid activities as Contributions, using different Types to retain where it came from. You can record the date, the status—including pending before money is deposited in your bank account—and the form of payment, such as check or cash.

You may leave transactions in an external donations system if you plan to keep using it. Past event or webinar registrations may still be worth transferring because they show a constituent's history of involvement. Decide how far back to import Contributions: large contributions should be preserved, while a $5 donation from 10 years ago may no longer be relevant. See the Contributions chapter later in this book.

docs.title: Campaigns
docs.text:
Campaigns bring together activities that support a goal, usually for a limited time. For example, a fundraising gala, email appeal and Contributions might all support a goal of raising $50,000 for a kids camp. A Campaign gives you a high-level view of how people responded to those initiatives.

Campaigns may suit fundraising with a distinct theme, such as a year-end pledge drive or project-specific fundraiser. One Campaign might include several appeals for the same project, including a final notice and one or more countdown appeals.

docs.title: Groups and tags
docs.text:
Groups identify two or more contacts with something in common; Relationships describe a connection between two contacts. Groups can also act as mailing lists. A group of newsletter subscribers, for example, can help you manage communications.

Groups and tags can hold information that staff use when deciding whom to invite to an event, exclude from an appeal or approach about volunteering. An Individual tagged member and volunteer can receive communications relevant to both. Groups can also hold issue- or program-specific communication preferences. For example, you can exclude a group of people who have requested no fundraising appeals when creating an email appeal mailing.

Avoid creating a group for information CiviCRM already stores elsewhere:

  • Contacts who have opted out of bulk mailings have that option on their Contact records. CiviCRM automatically excludes them from bulk mailings.
  • You can find donors through an advanced search for Contact records with an associated Contribution, including within a chosen date range. Most functions available to groups are also available from search results.

A Smart Group, created from an advanced search, adds new records that meet its criteria automatically. For example, a Smart Group could contain members who donated more than $100 in the past year. When another member makes a qualifying donation after the group is created, their record is added.

Tags work more like keywords associated with a record. You can add and remove them easily, but there is no easy way to see their history of changes. Use Relationships when you need to see the history of a connection.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Profiles bring together sets of fields for different purposes and can reduce staff administration. They determine how data is edited or displayed to staff or other users—not how the data is stored.

The chapters named above cover specific CiviCRM functionality in more detail, including functionality from major extensions.

docs.title: Plan your data move to CiviCRM
docs.text: You will understand what to consider before mapping your organisation’s data to the building blocks CiviCRM uses to store it.

docs.title: Understand what you have
docs.text:
Your organisation’s data may be in spreadsheets, another database or CRM such as Constant Contact, Convio or The Raiser’s Edge, paper files, or someone’s memory. Talk with co-workers who have been around the longest and those who have just joined. Their different experiences can help you understand how your organisation interacts with its contacts.

Think about who your contacts are, how different groups of people differ, and how each group interacts with your organisation. Feedback from contacts, whether anecdotal or systematic, may help you build a fuller picture.

Use these questions to examine your current data and ways of working:

  • Do you have an existing CRM?
  • Do you have spreadsheets with information about contacts, donations or other valuable data?
  • Do post-it notes or file cabinets hold information about your community?
  • Does anyone in your organisation know a lot about community members?
  • How does money come into your organisation?
  • What day-to-day tasks do staff and volunteers carry out?
  • How do you communicate with donors, members, volunteers and other community members? How would you like to communicate with them?
  • How do you track activities and communications, such as emails, meetings, webinars and other events?
  • Do you have a list of donors’ interests and preferences?
  • How do you handle new contacts?
  • What classifications or labels do you use for contacts, such as alumni, students, parents, major donors or volunteers?
  • What reports would you like to create, and what information would they contain?

docs.title: Decide what to keep
docs.text:
A move to CiviCRM is an opportunity to consider whether existing data still has a purpose. An old organisational division you no longer use, or office locations in a facility you no longer occupy, may no longer be useful.

Age alone does not make data worthless. One organisation in a financial pinch used an old list of founding donors who had not given for many years. Those donors still had strong emotional ties to the organisation they had founded and came to its financial rescue.

docs.title: Prepare for a different structure
docs.text:
CiviCRM is designed to be flexible and adaptable, based on feedback from many non-profits, but it may not match your organisation’s current ways of working exactly. Mapping data into CiviCRM takes planning. You may need to adapt a workflow or reconsider a current practice; CiviCRM may also offer ways to interact with contacts that you have not used before.

Allow time to review and clean the data you decide to move. Standardise how contact details are recorded—for example, whether a state appears as NY or New York—and remove obvious duplicates, accidental entries, outdated information and corrupted records. The Mapping your data section of this chapter discusses this further. The following chapters explain what data CiviCRM can store and how to map your existing records into its structure.

docs.title: Profile settings and field options
docs.text: Use this reference when deciding which fields to include in a Profile and how its settings affect forms, directories and search views. Many settings apply only to particular uses.

docs.title: Field combinations
docs.text:
Plan the Profile’s purpose and fields before creating it. Some uses restrict the available fields, and unsupported combinations produce an error when you save a field. Finding a suitable configuration may take trial and error.

  • A Profile used for Search Views can contain only fields from Contact records and Contact types, such as Individual.
  • Contact fields are available in all Profiles, but you cannot mix fields from different Contact types, such as Individual and Organization.
  • For a field that applies to more than one Contact type, such as Street Address or Email, choose it from Contacts rather than a specific type. The Organization field menu, for example, contains only fields that do not also apply to other Contact types.
  • Except in Search Results Profiles, you can combine Contact fields with fields from one other record type: Activity, Participants, Contributions or Membership.

Create any custom fields you intend to use before adding them to a Profile.

docs.title: Profile settings
docs.text:
The settings are available when you create a Profile and, later, through Settings at Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles.

  • Profile Name: A meaningful name for the Profile.
  • Used For: Offers Standalone Form or Directory; Search Views; Drupal User Registration; and View/Edit Drupal User Account. You can select more than one use. Selecting Search Views limits field choices to Contact and Contact type records.
  • Order: Controls the display order when a page contains more than one Profile. Lower numbers appear first. CiviCRM fills this in automatically when the Profile is created, and you can change it.
  • Pre-form Help and Post-form Help: Text shown before or after the Profile to help people complete a form.
  • Is this CiviCRM Profile Active?: Checked automatically. An active Profile is available for insertion into forms and for use by the Batch Update function. Uncheck it if you later want to take the Profile out of use.

docs.title: Advanced settings
docs.text: Open the grey advanced settings bar to see these fields. You can leave settings that do not apply to your Profile’s use unchanged.

docs.title: Public listings and directories
docs.text:
Limit listings to a specific group restricts which records visitors can view or search through a public Profile. If you do not choose a Group, a search can expose every record in your database. Choose a Group when you do not intend to make your whole database searchable.

For an active-member directory, for example, you could create and select a Smart Group of members with a status of New, Current or Grace. Smart Groups are dynamic: when a new membership meets the group’s criteria, the corresponding contact is included in the directory.

  • Proximity search: For a searchable directory, adds fields for a start address and search radius. Choose None to omit it, Optional to offer it, or Required to require both values.
  • Enable mapping for this profile?: Adds a map to searchable-directory results.
  • Include profile edit links in search results?: Adds an edit link to directory listings. Only users with permission to edit a result contact see its link.
  • Include Drupal user account information links in search results?: Adds links to result contacts’ Drupal user account information, such as their My Account pages. A link appears only for a contact who has a user account on the website.

docs.title: Sign-up forms
docs.text:
Add new contacts to a group adds new contacts who complete the Profile to the selected Group. For example, a volunteer sign-up form could add new contacts to a Volunteers Group. To offer a choice of more than one group, consider the Groups Profile field instead.

By default, contacts receive no confirmation that they have been added to the group and are not asked to validate their email address. To send an email, go to Administer >> CiviMail >> CiviMail Component Settings and check "Enable Double Opt-in for Profiles which use the "Add to Group" setting". Contacts must respond to opt in before they are added to the group.

Notify when profile form is submitted applies to sign-up forms. Enter an email address to receive a notification whenever someone submits the form. Separate multiple addresses with commas.

docs.title: Standalone forms and anonymous visitors
docs.text:
• Redirect URL: For a standalone form, sends people to a specified page after submission. It does not apply when the Profile is embedded in an event sign-up or contribution form. If left blank, people see a page displaying the information they entered.
  • Cancel redirect URL: Works like Redirect URL, but applies when someone cancels a form submission.
  • Include reCAPTCHA?: Applies when anonymous users complete a Profile. CAPTCHA asks visitors to enter text shown in a graphic to prevent automated submissions; the source recommends including it. To use this feature, set up a free reCAPTCHA account and enter its configuration in Administer > Customize Data and Screens > reCAPTCHA Settings. That page includes sign-up instructions.

docs.title: User account registration
docs.text:
• Drupal user account registration option: For Profiles used on public pages, determines whether people can or must register for a website account as well as submit the form. This can be used during membership sign-up or event registration.
  • WordPress user account registration option: WordPress also allows Profiles to create accounts. In WordPress Settings > General, "Membership [ ] Anyone can register" must be clicked.

docs.title: Duplicate matches on public pages
docs.text:
What to do upon duplicate match controls what happens when submitted contact data matches an existing record. You must choose an option; "Issue warning and do not save" is the default. Profile matching uses the Unsupervised deduplication rule. If several contacts match, the first matching record is used. The Deduping and Merging chapter in Working with Your Data discusses deduplication rules.

  • "Issue warning and do not save": Outside an online contribution, membership sign-up or event registration form, the person sees a message that a record already exists and cannot submit the form. When a Profile is embedded in one of those forms, this option is ignored and the transaction is linked to the matching contact.
  • "Update the matching contact": Adds submitted information to the matching record and overwrites existing values in fields included on the form. For example, a submitted address replaces the address already in the database.
  • "Allow duplicate contact to be created": Saves every submission as a new contact, without overwriting existing data. It can create many records that need deduplication later; see Deduping and Merging in Working with Your Data.

docs.title: Field settings
docs.text:
Choose a field’s record type from - select - under Field Name, then choose a field from the secondary menu. The following options apply to each field you add.

  • Field Label: The text displayed wherever the Profile is used. It starts with the field’s default label. You could, for example, change Postal Code to Zip Code if that is more familiar to your audience.
  • Required?: Requires the field whenever the Profile is used. It can help ensure a form submission includes First Name, Last Name or Email. It does not apply to Search Views, known as Search Results in 4.1 and previous versions.
  • View Only?: Allows people to view but not edit the field. A View Only field is omitted if the Profile exposes search results. This setting is not relevant to a Profile used only to collect information.
  • Field Pre Help and Field Post Help: Provide guidance in the interface. Pre help appears inline; post help creates a small speech bubble that, when clicked, displays help in yellow.
  • Order: Sets the field’s display order in the Profile; lower numbers appear first.
  • Active?: Must remain checked for the field to appear when the Profile is used.

docs.title: Visibility and search options
docs.text:
Visibility determines where a field can appear:

  • For fields on sign-up forms, use User and User Admin only so other visitors to the form cannot view database data.
  • For searchable-directory fields, use Public Pages or Public Pages and Listings. Use one of these options for any field you want on the directory search form.
  • For Search Views, use Public Pages or Public Pages and Listings.

Either Public Pages option reveals two further settings:

  • Searchable?: For searchable directories, includes the field on the search form.
  • Results Column?: For Search Views, includes the field in the view. Search Views were called Search Results in 4.1 and previous versions.

docs.title: Create and manage a Profile
docs.text:
Create a Profile when you need a particular set of fields for a form, directory or other supported use. Decide what it will be used for before you choose its settings and fields: some uses restrict which fields you can include.

Create any custom fields you plan to use in the Profile first. You may need to try different field combinations if CiviCRM reports an unsupported combination when you save a field.

docs.title: Create the Profile
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles.
  2. Click Add Profile.
  3. Enter a meaningful Profile Name.
  4. Select the intended Used For option or options.
  5. Set any other Profile settings that apply to your intended use.
  6. Save the Profile settings.

The Profile is now ready for fields. Is this CiviCRM Profile Active? is checked automatically; leave it checked if you want the Profile available for forms and Batch Update.

docs.title: Add fields
docs.text:
1. Click Add Field.
  2. Under Field Name, choose the record type from - select -.
  3. Choose the field from the secondary dropdown menu.
  4. Review its Field Label, Required?, View Only?, Visibility, help text, Order and Active? settings.
  5. Click Save and New if you have another field to add, or Save when you are finished.

A field with Active? checked appears when the Profile is used. Its Order value controls its position relative to other fields.

docs.title: Find and manage Profiles
docs.text: Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles to view your Profiles. Use Fields to add fields or edit their settings, Settings to change Profile settings, and more to preview a Profile, get its links or embed code, or copy it as the basis for another Profile. You can uncheck Is this CiviCRM Profile Active? in Settings when you want to take a Profile out of use.

docs.title: Publish a standalone Profile form
docs.text: Use an existing Profile as a standalone form to collect information. In Drupal and Joomla!, you can share the page CiviCRM creates or place the form’s HTML in a website page. WordPress also offers a shortcode option.

docs.title: Share the CiviCRM page
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles.
  2. Click more beside the Profile.
  3. Choose Use Profile-Create Mode.
  4. Publish the resulting link where people should find it, such as in an email or on a blog.

docs.title: Place the HTML form on a page
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles.
  2. Click more beside the Profile.
  3. Choose HTML Form Snippet.
  4. Copy the code shown on the next screen.
  5. Paste the code into the website page where you want the form.

docs.title: Insert a Profile in a WordPress post
docs.text:
1. While creating or editing a post, click the CiviCRM button to insert a CiviCRM shortcode.
  1. In the popup form, select Profile as the frontend element.
  1. Use the second select widget to choose the Profile.
  2. Select the form’s purpose: create, edit or view.
  3. Click Insert Form.

docs.title: Make a searchable directory with a Profile
docs.text:
Use a Profile to let website visitors search selected contact information. You can choose which fields they search, which appear in results and which appear when they view a record.

Before making the directory public, limit its listings to an appropriate Group. If no Group is selected, a search can expose every record in your database.

docs.title: Configure the Profile
docs.text:
1. Create a Profile for the directory.
  2. In its advanced settings, select the Group whose records visitors may view or search.

For example, a Smart Group of members with a status of New, Current or Grace can provide a dynamic directory of active members.

Other advanced settings may be useful:

  • Enable mapping: Lets visitors map directory contacts using Google or Yahoo! maps and obtain directions to a record’s address. Mapping must already be enabled at Administer > System Settings > Mapping and Geocoding.
  • Include profile edit links: Adds an edit link to listings for users with permission to edit the contact. This is not commonly needed for a membership directory.
  • Include Drupal user information: On Drupal, adds a link to a contact’s user account information, such as their My Account page, if that contact has a website user account.

docs.title: Choose the directory fields
docs.text:
1. Add the fields you want in the directory.
  2. Set every directory field’s Visibility to Public Pages or Public Pages and Listings.
  3. Check Searchable for each field visitors should be able to search.
  4. Check Results Column for each field you want displayed in the results list.

A field set to Public Pages and Listings is hot-linked in the detail view. Clicking its value starts a search for other records with that value. For example, clicking a City value searches as though the visitor had selected that city on the Profile search screen.

A field with Results Column checked appears both in the results list and in the record’s detail view. Without that check, it can still appear in the detail view. Setting more fields as Searchable gives visitors more ways to find information.

The following images show a membership-directory search form, a results list containing fields marked Results Column, and the detail view reached through a view link. The detail view shows all Profile fields.

docs.title: Link to the directory
docs.text:
• Drupal: Link to http://www.myorganization.org/civicrm/profile?reset=1&gid=N, where N is the Profile directory’s ID. Add &force=1 to show a result set directly. Add &force=1&search=0 to show the result set and hide the search criteria.
  • Joomla!: In Menu Manager, create a front-end menu item. Select CiviCRM, choose the profile search option, then choose the Profile in the parameters pane.
  • WordPress: Linking to the directory this way is not yet implemented in the source material.

You can also prepopulate search criteria in the URL. The options are described at Linking Profiles.

docs.title: Update multiple records with a Profile
docs.text:
Use Update multiple ... to edit fields for several records on one screen. The Profile must contain fields for the type of records in your search results: only contact, contribution, activity, participant or membership fields, respectively.

You can update up to 100 records at a time. You cannot update different Contact types, such as individuals and organisations, in the same batch. To update participant fields, start from Find Participants results and use a Profile containing only participant fields. If a batch of 100 takes a long time, four batches of 25 may be quicker.

Before saving, check every changed value. The update saves the changes across the displayed records.

docs.title: Update the search results
docs.text:
1. Find the records you need to change.
  2. Choose the appropriate Update multiple ... action from Actions.
  3. Select a Profile containing only fields for that result type.
  4. Click Continue.
  5. Change the values needed in the grid.
  6. Click the Copy icon beside a column title if you want the first row’s value copied to every displayed record in that column.
  7. Click the relevant update button to save, or Cancel to cancel the changes.

Actions provides multiple-record updates for most search results, including Search, Advanced Search, Find Contributions, Find Memberships, Find Participants and Find Activities. It is also available from event participant lists generated through Manage Events. For memberships, use Update multiple memberships from Find memberships results or from Advanced Search with Display results as set to Memberships.

For example, suppose you have a custom contact field named “Diving Skill Level” and want to set it to “Intermediate” for everyone who attended an Intermediate Diving course. On Advanced Search, set the appropriate filters in the Event accordion. Leave Display Results As set to Contacts, because the field belongs to contacts, and click Search. Choose Update multiple contacts and the Profile you want to use.

The next screen shows a grid with each contact’s name and the fields in your Profile. To give every displayed contact the same Diving Skill Level, enter Intermediate in the first row and click the Copy icon—the image of two documents beside the column title. Click Update Contacts to save or Cancel to cancel.

docs.title: Use Profiles with website accounts
docs.text: Use a Profile to collect information when someone registers for a website account or to let a logged-in Drupal user review and update information on their My Account page.

docs.title: Include fields during registration
docs.text:
1. Create a Profile with User Registration selected under Used For.
  1. Add the fields people should complete when registering.
  2. Set those fields’ visibility to Public User Pages.

docs.title: Add a Profile to Drupal’s My Account page
docs.text:
The Profile must contain only fields related to the Individual contact type.

  1. Create a Profile, or open Settings for an existing one.
  2. Select View/Edit User Account under Used For.
  3. Click Save.
  4. Add the fields people should be able to edit on their Drupal My Account page.

You can embed one or more CiviCRM Profiles on that page so logged-in users can review and update their information.

docs.title: Offer account creation with a Profile form
docs.text:
Include a Primary Email Address field in the Profile; this feature needs it to function properly.

  1. Under Customize Data and Screens > Profiles, click Settings beside the Profile.
  2. Set User account registration option to invite or require anonymous visitors to create a Drupal or Joomla! account when they complete the form.

Anonymous visitors are then invited or required to create an account; logged-in users see only the Profile fields.

This feature also works when the Profile is embedded in an online contribution page or event registration page. For example, you can invite or require an anonymous visitor to sign up for an account while registering for an event.

docs.title: Profiles in CiviCRM component forms
docs.text:
You can include Profile fields in event registration, contribution and membership sign-up pages. The component determines which related record fields may be relevant.

An event registration Profile can include fields specific to participant records, while a contribution-page Profile can include fields specific to contributions. For instructions on including Profiles in these forms, see the Set-up chapters of Events, Contributions and Memberships, respectively.

docs.title: What Profiles are for
docs.text:
A Profile brings together database fields for a particular purpose, such as collecting information on a form or displaying it in a directory.

You can add core fields and custom fields, including multi-value custom fields, to a Profile. Two special fields are Groups, which shows a checkbox for each public group, and tags, which includes public tags. Choosing only the fields needed for a purpose can make a form or display easier to use.

docs.title: Collect information
docs.text:
A Profile can appear on a standalone page or be embedded in a contribution, membership sign-up or event registration page. A page can contain more than one Profile. You can choose required fields and provide text to help people complete the form.

For example, a volunteer sign-up form could include first name, last name, mailing address and a custom field for volunteer interests. A Profile with custom food-preference fields could be added to registration pages for events where food is served. The Profile below collects address information on a donation page.

Profiles can also present public groups as checkboxes so visitors can choose which of your organisation’s email lists to join. The Set-up chapter of Email discusses this use.

docs.title: Display information
docs.text:
A Profile can display database information on a public page. For example, a membership directory can be searchable and reflect new members as they join. An organisation can also display donors’ names after contributions are made, without entering the information separately on its website.

Native Americans in Philanthropy (NAP) replaced an expensive annual printed membership directory with a searchable Profile on its website. The printed directory took time to produce and could already be out of date when members received it. The website directory saved resources and gave members a way to search for and connect with one another.

docs.title: Simplify work for staff
docs.text:
A Profile can provide a data-entry form containing only the fields that volunteers or interns need. It can also control selected fields shown in advanced search results. For example, a Profile containing phone number and a custom volunteer-interests field could give a volunteer coordinator an on-screen call list. The Customizing the User Interface chapter in Initial Set-up discusses this use.

Profiles are also used with Update multiple ... actions to edit fields across search results on one screen. For example, an organisation might update event attendance to Attended or No-show, or update the Thank-You Sent field for a week’s donations.

docs.title: Show repeating information
docs.text: Multi-value custom field sets hold more than one set of custom data per contact, such as work experience. A Profile can expose those fields for adding, editing and deleting multiple instances. This example collects a name and work experience.

docs.title: Other approaches
docs.text:
Profiles are not the only way to build these forms and displays. The alternatives depend on your content management system (CMS) and the skills available to your organisation.

  • Drupal Views can make sophisticated displays of CiviCRM data, such as a public list of members.
  • Drupal Webform-Integration can work with multiple contacts, events, memberships and relationships. It also offers pagination, draft-saving, advanced spam-control, conditional fields and more flexibility in form display than Profiles. See the Drupal Integration chapter or the Webform CiviCRM Integration page.
  • Fields added directly to Drupal user accounts are not available in CiviCRM, but are more available in Drupal. Whether that is suitable depends on why you collect the information.
  • The API offers a flexible way to display data on a website if you have basic coding skills. See the Developer Documentation wiki for an introduction.

Other discussions of Profiles appear in Customizing the user interface in Intitial Set-up, and in the Set-up chapters of Email, Contributions, Events and Memberships.

docs.title: Connect an individual to an employer
docs.text:
Use Current Employer on an individual's record to connect them to an organisation. CiviCRM stores employees as individuals and employers as organisations.

  1. Open the individual's record.
  2. Click Edit.
  3. Begin typing the organisation's name in Current Employer. Matching organisation contacts appear in a dropdown list. If the organisation is there, select it by pressing the down arrow key or clicking it. If it is not, enter its full name.
  4. Once the full name is in the field, press Enter or click Save.

If you selected an existing organisation, CiviCRM creates an Employee/Employer relationship with it. If the organisation did not exist, CiviCRM creates an organisation contact and the relationship. You can open the Relationships tab to see the new Employee of relationship and any existing relationships. From the organisation's side, the relationship is Employer of.

docs.title: Current Employer on forms
docs.text:
Current Employer can also connect employees and employers when it appears on CiviCRM Profiles or CiviCRM Contribution Pages. People enter their employer's name rather than choosing from a list, to preserve privacy.

When the form is processed, CiviCRM tries to use an existing Organisation contact before creating one, reducing potential duplicates:

  1. It checks for a match using the Deduplication Rule, Organisation Unsupervised. If it finds one, it uses that contact.
  2. It checks whether the Individual contact already has a Current Employer with the same name entered on the form. If so, it uses that contact.
  3. If neither check finds a match, it creates an Organisation contact and an Employee Of Relationship linking the Individual to it.

docs.title: Add contacts to an organisation
docs.text:
Use the search results Actions menu to connect selected contacts to an organisation.

  1. Select the contacts you want from your search results.
  2. Select Add relationship - to organization from the dropdown from the Actions menu.
  3. On the Add Contacts to Organization screen, select the Relationship Type.
  4. Enter part of the organisation's name in Find Target Organization, then click Search.
  5. Find the organisation in Mark Target Contact(s) for this Relationship, below the Search and Cancel buttons. If it is missing, try another search. If you still cannot find it, click Cancel, add a new organisation, and try again.
  6. Click the radio button next to the organisation.
  7. Click Add to Organization. A message states how many selected participants were added to the organisation.
  8. Click Done to return to your search results.

docs.title: Add contacts to a household
docs.text:
Use the search results Actions menu to connect selected contacts to a household.

Choose the relationship type carefully. CiviCRM does not prevent you from adding multiple contacts as Head of Household for one household. This can cause problems if you later expect that label to identify only one person. Household Member of may be the better choice in most situations.

  1. Select the contacts you want from your search results.
  2. Select Add relationship - to household from the Actions menu.
  3. Select the Relationship Type.
  4. Enter part of the household's name, such as a last name shared by its members, in Find Target Household, then click Search.
  5. Find the household in Mark Target Contact(s) for this Relationship, below the Search and Cancel buttons. If it is missing, try another search. If you still cannot find it, click Cancel, add a new household, and try again.
  6. Click the radio button next to the household.
  7. Click Add to Household. A message states how many selected participants were added to the household.
  8. Click Done to return to your search results.

A Household relationship can apply the household address to a member's record. If the Household already exists, CiviCRM creates a relationship with it; if none exists, it creates a new household.

docs.title: Create a relationship type
docs.text:
CiviCRM provides common relationship types. If none describes a connection your organisation needs to track, you can create one.

  1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > Relationship Types.
  2. Review the existing relationship types so you do not create a duplicate.
  3. If the type you need is not listed, click New Relationship Type.
  4. Enter a descriptive label in Relationship Label-A to B for the connection from Contact A to Contact B. If the connection needs a different label in the other direction, enter it in Relationship Label-B to A.
  5. Set Contact Type A and Contact Type B to the contact types this relationship connects. Check that they make sense with the labels you entered.
  6. Optionally enter a Description, especially if the type's purpose may not be obvious to other users.
  7. Leave Enabled checked unless you want to create the type now but prevent people from using it until later.
  8. Click Save. A message confirms that the relationship type was saved, and the new type appears in the list.

For a relationship with the same label in both directions, enter the label only in Relationship Label-A to B and leave Relationship Label-B to A blank. For example, Sylvia is Partner of Audre, and Audre is Partner of Sylvia.

For a relationship with different labels, fill in both fields. For example, Kiyoshi is Grandparent of Yuki, while Yuki is Grandchild of Kiyoshi. The source also gives Grandparent is as a possible label for the B-to-A direction.

docs.title: When a custom field is more useful
docs.text: You can store additional information on all relationships or on selected relationship types without creating more types. For example, a custom field can record an employee's department instead of requiring a separate relationship type for each department. See creating custom fields for instructions.

docs.title: Disable or delete a relationship type
docs.text:
If a relationship type is no longer useful to your organisation, you can disable or delete it. Either choice removes it as an option for new relationships.

Consider disabling before deleting. Disabling keeps existing relationships of that type visible and lets you enable the type again later. Deleting removes the type from the list and from contact relationships data.

  1. Go to Administer > Option Lists > Relationship Types.
  2. Click More in the row of the type you want to disable or delete.
  3. Select Disable or Delete from the pop-up menu.
  4. Review the confirmation. Disable displays a confirmation bubble; Delete opens another screen with a more serious warning. The source identifies Delete as the button to confirm and Cancel as the button to stop.
  5. If you chose Disable, the type appears in red in the Relationship Types list, and existing relationships of that type remain visible on contacts. If you chose Delete, the type no longer appears in the list or in contact relationships data.

To make a disabled type available again, return to Administer > Option Lists > Relationship Types, click More in its row, and select Enable from the more pop-up menu.

docs.title: Create a relationship between contacts
docs.text:
Use a relationship to show how two contacts are connected. For example, if a mother and son are both in your database, you can make that connection visible from either record. Relationships can also connect organisations, or individuals and organisations.

  1. Open one of the contact records you want to connect.
  2. Click Add Relationship from the Actions button on the contact summary or from the Relationships tab.
  3. Select the Relationship Type. For example, choose Sibling of to connect siblings.
  4. Begin typing the last name of the related person or people. If a contact you need is not yet in the database, you can create a new contact from this screen.
  5. Add any further information you need:
  6. Start Date and End Date if the relationship is time limited.
  7. Description for short text shown on the relationship summary screen.
  8. Notes for longer text shown when viewing the relationship.
  9. Permissions to allow another user of the database to view or update the related contact.
  10. Enabled to show that the relationship is active.
  11. Click Save Relationship.

docs.title: Relationship permissions
docs.text:
If a relationship connects User 1 and User 2, setting Permissions to give User 1 View access to User 2 lets User 1 view User 2's details through a Profile in View mode when logged in. View and Update also lets User 1 update those details through a profile in Edit mode.

The Related Permissions extension can extend this functionality.

docs.title: Create a smart group
docs.text:
Use a search to define a group whose contacts are selected by criteria you choose. Smart groups can be created from the results of many CiviCRM search forms.

For example, a smart group of donors who have not yet been sent a thank-you letter can help you manage that work. As you send letters, the donors who receive them automatically leave the group, keeping the list of people to thank up to date.

docs.title: Create a group with Advanced Search
docs.text:
If your CiviCRM installation has no contributions, you can try this example on the CiviCRM demo site.

  1. Go to Search > Find Contacts > Advanced Search.
  2. Scroll down to Contributions.
  3. Check Thank-you date not set and choose Donation from the financial type drop-down menu.
  4. Click Search at the bottom of the page.
  5. Select all records.
  6. From Actions, select Group - create smart group.
  7. Give the group a name and description. You can also designate it as a mailing list and give it a parent group.
  8. Click Save Smart Group.

The smart group appears in the usual places where you see groups. To see how the criteria work, edit a contact in the group so that they no longer match: they will leave the group. If they are not removed immediately, smart group caching may be on.

docs.title: Create a group with SearchKit
docs.text: From any SearchKit search that returns contacts, click +Add on the left-hand side and select Smart Group.

docs.title: Change smart group criteria
docs.text:
