docs.title: Other resources
docs.text:
• Transifex keeps files in a version control system. Some users, mostly programmers, find working with the GitHub site easier than downloading each file separately from Transifex.
  • The localisation community-building tips explain how to set up a localisation community.

docs.title: Organise a translation sprint
docs.text: A translation sprint brings people together in one room to translate as many documents as they can. Use these preparations and activities to help your team make progress.

docs.title: Before the sprint
docs.text:
• Choose a location with enough computers for everyone, or desks for laptops, and a decent Internet connection.
  • If people will work offline, provide instructions in advance for installing a tool such as PoEdit. Arrange for someone to help others install and use it.
  • Create a glossary in advance. Share it with everyone, print enough copies, and plan to discuss terms that do not yet have team consensus.
  • Set goals: decide which component to translate and what percentage the team aims to achieve.
  • Form sub-teams with clear objectives for a component, a file or part of a file.
  • If translators are unfamiliar with CiviCRM, prepare a demo of the features they will translate.
  • Designate someone whom translators can interrupt with questions.
  • Have enough coffee, tea, chocolate or other refreshments to keep everyone going through the night.

docs.title: At the end of the sprint
docs.text:
• Present the translation results in a demo CiviCRM installation.
  • Discuss whether the team reached its goal and how to improve further.

docs.title: How CiviCRM localisation works
docs.text:
Localisation adapts CiviCRM to an organisation’s language and regional conventions. It covers more than the text you see on screen.

CiviCRM is written with English-language code and display strings, but organisations worldwide need to adapt it to local circumstances without modifying the software technically. Localisation can affect:

  • Currency: USD or $ in the United States, and GBP or £ in Great Britain.
  • Dates and times: November 16th, 2009 might be written as 11/16/2009 in the United States or 16.11.2009 in Russia.
  • Numbers: The same number might appear as 1 234 567,89 in Slovakia or Hungary and 1,234,567**.**89 in Japan or the United States.

An administrator can select the locale for an organisation’s language and country at Administer > Configure > Global Settings > Localization.

CiviCRM provides functionality for language- and region-specific needs, and the development team continues to develop tools in this area.

docs.title: Translations and coverage
docs.text:
CiviCRM supports different languages, but its developers rely on the community to translate display text. Coverage varies: some languages have more than 90% of the text translated, others have only 5%, and some have not been translated at all. Check Transifex for the language that interests you. Download and install a translation on your CiviCRM installation to find out how well it suits your needs.

Even when a translation is correct, your organisation might prefer different terms. You are encouraged to take part in translating your language.

docs.title: Components and files
docs.text:
CiviCRM has many strings—phrases that need translation. They are divided into components, such as CiviCRM core, CiviMail and CiviContribute, so translators can focus on the parts they know best. A separate component should be available for each CiviCRM version starting with 3.2, or 3.1 for language teams that have chosen to do so.

Each component contains files of translatable strings. The main CiviCRM component, or core, has close to 20 files, including files for countries, provinces and menu.

For more background, see the CiviCRM localisation FAQ.

docs.title: Ways to contribute to the CiviCRM community
docs.text:
Look up ways to take part, whether you have a question, a useful example from your organisation or something you have built.

Participation helps sustain CiviCRM as open source software for nonprofits. Asking a question can help someone else with the same problem; answering questions and sharing ideas or feedback also builds the community’s knowledge.

Contribution Where to start Help with questions and discussions Ask or answer questions on CiviCRM Stack Exchange, or take part in CiviCRM Chat. Improve documentation Follow the instructions in contributing to this manual. This book was written by community members. Share your organisation’s experience Share use cases or case studies about how your organisation uses CiviCRM and the solutions and processes you have developed. See existing case studies. Post to the CiviCRM blog Share successes, experiences at Civi-related events, interesting customisations or other ideas on the CiviCRM blog. You can add content by registering with CiviCRM or emailing info@civicrm.org with your idea and a request to post. Share training materials Post your training resources and materials on the CiviCRM blog or your own site. Register your organisation’s site Register your organisation to add its site to a publicly searchable directory and map of CiviCRM installations. This supports CiviCRM’s marketing efforts. Contribute code Share code you have written to extend CiviCRM; someone else may need the same functionality. See the Developer Guide for recommended steps for developing and contributing to the core codebase. If you have developed a Drupal module, see Drupal.org for information on contributing modules. Joomla! extensions can be posted here. Sponsor development If your organisation needs functionality that does not yet exist and cannot develop it in-house, it can sponsor outside developers, alone or with other organisations that need the same functionality. See CiviCRM’s website or email info@civicrm.org for more information. Report bugs See Bug Reporting for information on reporting bugs you find.

docs.title: CiviCRM community spaces and events
docs.text:
Find places to ask questions, follow community news and meet other people who use, implement or develop CiviCRM.

CiviCRM is shaped by a community of users, developers and implementers. Much of its activity takes place online, so you can participate wherever you live or work if you have internet access. English is the predominant language for discussion and contributions.

docs.title: Online spaces
docs.text: Resource What you can find there CiviCRM website Information about getting and using CiviCRM, community blog posts and event announcements. Its Get Involved section links to community resources. CiviCRM Stack Exchange The primary place to find or ask questions about installing, upgrading, configuring, using and customising CiviCRM. You can search the millions of questions already asked or ask a new one. CiviCRM Chat Live discussion in chat channels and direct messages. Powered by Mattermost, it is a place for technical questions, community news and resources shared by members. CiviCRM blog Posts by the CiviCRM core team and community members about news, events, case studies, use cases, ways to get things done, features and development. Comments can lead to discussions that inform future development.

docs.title: In-person events
docs.text:
Meeting people in person can help you connect with others in your area who develop, implement or use CiviCRM.

  • Local events: Cities and regions hold meetups to learn about CiviCRM, share ideas, developments and use cases, and meet other community members. CiviCRM also conducts user and developer training around the world. Check local events for meetups, training and sprints.
  • CiviCon: Conferences bring together prospective and current end-users, administrators and developers for discussions, lectures and networking. The first CiviCon was held in San Francisco in April 2010, and the number hosted around the world each year is growing.
  • CiviCamps: One-day meetups where you can learn, connect with other users, ask questions and share tips.
  • Other conferences: CiviCRM core developers and community members also attend DrupalCon, the NonProfit Technology Conference, Joomla! events and Aspiration Tech events.

docs.title: Add dashlets to your dashboard
docs.text:
Choose which reports appear on your CiviCRM Home dashboard so you can see information relevant to your work.

When you log in, CiviCRM Home is the first page you see. It displays reports called dashlets. CiviCRM includes many dashlets by default, and you or your administrator can create others for your organisation.

For example, available dashlets may include:

  • Donor Report: a bar graph of total contributions.
  • Activities: recent activities recorded by CiviCRM, such as emails sent to constituents, donations made or meetings scheduled.
  • Membership Report: a monthly table of members by type, total payments and numbers of contributions, among other information.

docs.title: Choose your dashlets
docs.text:
1. On CiviCRM Home, click Configure Your Dashboard. A list of dashlets appears.
  2. Drag each dashlet you want into the right or left column.
  3. Click Done to save your dashboard.

Your chosen dashlets appear on your dashboard when you log in. To check for more recent changes, click Refresh Dashboard Data; this reloads each dashlet and pulls in new information. Dashlets are cached for performance, so their data may not otherwise update immediately.

docs.title: Create a dashlet from a CiviReport
docs.text: Create a report dashlet to display the information you need on CiviCRM Home. Any CiviReport can be made available as a dashlet.

docs.title: Create the report
docs.text:
1. Go to Reports > My Reports and click New Report.
  2. Select the report template you want to use.
  3. Configure the report using the Columns, Sorting and Filters tabs. For example, the Date Received filter can show data for “This Quarter” or “This Year”.
  4. Click View results.
  5. Choose Tabular, Bar Chart or Pie Chart from the dropdown to the right of Actions.
  6. At the bottom of the Access tab, select Available for Dashboard?. Users with permission to see the information can then add the dashlet. See permissions for more information.
  7. Click Actions > Create Report.

docs.title: Add the dashlet to your dashboard
docs.text:
1. In the menu, click the CiviCRM logo, then click CiviCRM Home.
  2. Click Configure Dashboard.
  3. Drag the dashlet from Available Dashlets to the column where you want it.
  4. Click Done.

The dashlet now appears on your dashboard. See Reporting for more details on working with reports.

docs.title: Change how often a dashlet refreshes
docs.text:
Dashlets are cached for performance. You can change how often a dashlet refreshes by editing its report. For example, to change the Contribution Summary report:

  1. Go to Reports > Contribution Reports and click Contribution Summary.
  2. Open the Access tab.
  3. If Cache dashlet for is unavailable, select Available for Dashboard? first.
  4. Set Cache dashlet for.
  5. Click Actions > Save.

Note

You can also use SearchKit with FormBuilder to add dashlets. See FormBuilder for details.

docs.title: Navigation menu
docs.text:
Use the navigation menu to reach CiviCRM’s main areas or find a page by name.

The menu appears at the top of every CiviCRM “back office” page. It includes these areas:

Menu item What it is for Quick Search Look up a name, email address or custom field. Menu Search and Logout Search the CiviCRM menu or log out. Search Search your CRM data. Contacts Find, add and manage contacts. Contributions Search contributions and manage contribution pages. Events Create and manage event registrations. Mailings Send bulk emails and view mailing history. Reports Generate and access reports. Administer Configure system settings and custom data.

The Quick Search field is at the far left of the menu. See Searching for more details.

docs.title: Find a menu item
docs.text: Hover over the CiviCRM logo next to the quick search bar. A panel opens with a search field and a list of available menu items. Type part of a name, such as “display preferences” or “groups”, to filter the list, then select the item you want.

docs.title: Change the menu
docs.text:
Go to Administer > Customize > Navigation Menu to add, disable or rearrange menu items.

Note

Menu changes are visible to everyone who has the appropriate permissions to see the menu. Check the effect on other users before making changes.

docs.title: Link to a form with a message token
docs.text:
Create a token for your form, then use it in a message template to give recipients a link to the form.

You do not need to accept Id from URL for this setup. If you do not need that setting, leaving it off is more secure.

  1. Create a token for the form in the Expose field. This lets CiviMail authors link to the form.

  1. On the Individual tab, set Autofill to Current User.

  1. In a message template, select the Afform Token named after your form. Two tokens are created: URL and Hyperlink.

When a recipient clicks the link, they access the form with their contact data populated.

docs.title: Restore deleted contacts
docs.text:
You can find deleted contacts in the trash and restore them if you are an administrator or have the access deleted contacts permission. By default, deleted contacts are sent to the trash and can be recovered later.

  1. Go to Advanced Search.
  2. Enter the contact’s details.
  3. Check Search in Trash at the bottom of Basic Criteria.
  4. Restore contacts from the results using one of these options:
  5. To restore a contact individually, select Restore at the end of its row.
  6. To restore contacts using the action drop-down menu, choose Restore contacts.

Only delete a contact permanently if you are sure you no longer need them.

You can disable the trash function in Administer > System Settings > Misc (Undelete, PDFs, Limits, Logging, etc.).

docs.title: Create a custom data entry form
docs.text: Use CiviCRM’s FormBuilder to create a form for manual data entry, such as adding contacts or logging activities. You can collect information from members, supporters or staff without technical knowledge.

docs.title: Start a form
docs.text:
1. In FormBuilder, find New Submission Form at the top of the interface.
  2. Click the downward-pointing arrow beside the button to see the available item types, such as Activities, Contacts and Cases.
  3. Select the type of item your form will create. The form design workspace opens.

The workspace has a configuration pane on the left and a layout view on the right.

docs.title: Choose who can use the form
docs.text:
In Form Settings, use the Permission dropdown to choose the option that fits your purpose:

  • Access CiviCRM backend and API is the default. Users with access to CiviCRM can access the form.
  • Generic: Allow any authenticated contact limits access to supporters who are logged into your website or use a verified email link.
  • Generic: Anyone with secret link is for forms shared through direct, private email invitations.
  • Generic: Allow all users (including anonymous) makes the form open to anyone, such as for a public sign-up page.

docs.title: Set entity options
docs.text:
Each entity tab in the left-hand pane has additional settings. For a form that captures information for an Individual, these include:

  • Individual 1: Security: Choose whether autofill works based on the form permissions or the user’s permissions.
  • Individual 1: Autofill: Choose from options such as Current User or the Contact being Viewed.
  • Individual 1: Allowed Actions: Choose create, update or both.
  • Individual 1: Accept ID from URL: If Update is an allowed action, the ID can be taken from the URL to autofill fields.

docs.title: Publish the form as a website page
docs.text:
If people need to visit the form as a standalone page, set its placement in the left-hand pane:

  1. Find the Placement options.
  2. Enter a path beginning with civicrm/ in Page Route, such as civicrm/volunteer-signup.
  3. Select Accessible on front-end of web site so regular visitors can view the page.

If staff need to find the form in CiviCRM, select the option to add it to the CiviCRM navigation menu.

docs.title: Add fields and layout elements
docs.text:
The second tab in the left-hand pane lists standard and custom fields for the entity you selected, for example, 'Inidividual 1'.

  1. Find a field in the left-hand pane.
  2. Drag it into the layout view on the right.
  3. Drag the field up or down if you need to change its order.
  4. Click the field’s Settings icon in the layout to change its label or make it required.

To add instructions or section breaks, drag structural blocks, text containers or HTML areas from Elements into the layout.

docs.title: Save and review the form
docs.text:
1. Click Save in the upper-right area of the screen.
  2. Click View, which appears after you save, to preview how the live form will look to users and copy its website link for distribution.

docs.title: Create a donation form with FormBuilder
docs.text:
You will create a public donation form with a flexible layout, rather than the fixed layout of a core Contribution form.

This example assumes the Stripe Payment Processor is already installed. See the Stripe Extension documentation. Other payment processors are available as FormBuilder Checkout Options.

docs.title: Create the form
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. On the Submission Forms tab, click New Submission Form.

The form starts with Individual and some fields, including first name and last name. If you also want someone to register for an event, click the + symbol at the top of the form and choose Participant.

docs.title: Configure the form
docs.text:
Use the configuration pane on the left to set the following:

  1. Set Title to Make a Donation.
  2. Change Permission to Allow all users (including anonymous).
  3. Set Page Route to a public URL, such as civicrm/support-us.
  4. Set Frontend or Backend to Frontend so members of the public can access the form.

Before choosing civicrm/donate as the Page Route: A packaged form called New Donation already uses that URL. To use it for your donation page, edit that form instead. See Contribution Forms.

Optionally, use Post-Submit to redirect people after submission: enter a full web link, such as https://example.com. Alternatively, add a confirmation message to display after submission. If you add a confirmation message, save it.

docs.title: Add contribution fields
docs.text:
1. Click the + symbol at the top of the form and choose Contribution. A Contribution 1 tab appears.
  2. Under Values in the left configuration pane, change Contact from ‘Select Current User’ to Individual 1.
  3. In the Add Value select list, choose Checkout Option.
  4. For the new Checkout Option value, choose Stripe Embedded Checkout option from the drop-down.
  5. In the Add column, drag Checkout Details onto the Contribution 1 section of the form Layout.
  6. On the Contribution 1 section in the right panel, click the settings wheel for Contribution Source and choose Remove field.

docs.title: Add contact details
docs.text:
1. Click the Individual 1 tab in the left panel.
  2. In the Add column, drag Contact Email(s) onto the Individual 1 section of the form Layout.
  3. Toggle Multiple to Single in the Email block.
  4. Select is Primary.
  5. Select a Location type.
  6. On the Individual 1 tab, scroll to Duplicate Matching and choose the appropriate rule. The default is ‘Email (reserved)’.
  7. In the right pane, click the settings wheel for each field in the form Layout and tick Required.

You can use the settings wheels to rename a Fieldset or Field, change background colors, and adjust other layout options. You can also drag other individual fields, such as address or phone number, from the Individual 1 tab onto that section of the form Layout.

docs.title: Save and test the form
docs.text:
1. Click Save at the top right of the form screen.
  2. Click the View Page link that appears next to Save to access and test the form.

You can adjust the form as needed. Share the View Page link with members of the public; if you added Participant, they can use the form to register for the event.

docs.title: Create an event booking form with online payment
docs.text:
In this example, you will create a form for the Christmas Fundraiser event. People will be able to book and pay online using a layout that is more flexible than the core Event booking forms.

This example assumes that the Stripe Payment Processor is installed on your CiviCRM system. See the Stripe Extension documentation. Other payment processors are available as FormBuilder Checkout Options.

docs.title: Create the event
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Events > New Event.
  2. Enter Christmas Fundraiser as the Title.
  3. Set the Start date and time, Event type, and a default role of attendee.
  4. On the Fees tab, add the required Fee options with their labels and amounts.
  5. Select Save.

The event is now available to select when you build the form.

docs.title: Start the form
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. On the Submission Forms tab, select New Submission Form.

The form automatically includes Individual and some fields, including first name and last name.

  1. At the top of the form, select the + symbol, then choose Participant. This enables the individual to register for an event.

docs.title: Set up public access
docs.text:
Use the configuration pane on the left to set the following options:

  • Title: Enter Register For Our Christmas Fundraiser.
  • Permission: Select Allow all users (including anonymous).
  • Page Route: Enter a public URL, such as civicrm/christmasfundraiser.
  • Frontend or Backend: Select Frontend so members of the public can access the form.
  • Post-Submit (Optional): To redirect people after submission, enter a full web link, such as https://example.com, in the Post-Submit text box. Alternatively, add a confirmation message to display when they submit the form. If you add a confirmation message, save the message.

docs.title: Add the booking and payment fields
docs.text:
1. At the top of the form, select the + symbol, then choose Contribution. A Contribution 1 tab appears for adding contribution fields.
  2. Select the Participant 1 tab.
  3. Under Values in the left configuration pane, change Contact from ‘Select Current User’ to Individual 1.
  4. Set Event to Christmas Fundraiser, the event you created.
  5. Set Status to Pending (incomplete transaction).
  6. In the Add column, drag Contribution Amount:Christmas Fundraiser onto the Participant 1 section of the form Layout. The event’s Fee options appear on the form.
  7. Select the Contribution 1 tab.
  8. Under Values, change Contact from ‘Select Current User’ to Individual 1.
  9. From the Add Value select list, choose Checkout Option.
  10. For the new Checkout Option value, choose Stripe Embedded Checkout option from the drop-down.
  11. In the Add column, drag Checkout Details onto the Contribution 1 section of the form Layout.
  12. In the Contribution 1 section of the right panel, use the settings wheel beside Contribution Amount to choose Remove field.
  13. Use the settings wheel beside Contribution Source to choose Remove field.

docs.title: Add contact details
docs.text:
1. Select the Individual 1 tab in the left panel.
  2. In the Add column, drag Contact Email(s) onto the Individual 1 section of the form Layout.
  3. In the Email block, toggle Multiple to Single.
  4. Select is Primary.
  5. Select a Location type.
  6. On the Individual 1 tab, scroll to Duplicate Matching and choose the appropriate rule. The default is ‘Email (reserved)’.
  7. In the right pane, use the settings wheel on each field in the form Layout to tick Required.

You can also use the settings wheels to rename a Fieldset or Field, change background colors, and adjust other layout options. To include more individual fields, such as address or phone number, drag them from the Individual 1 tab onto the Individual 1 section of the form Layout.

docs.title: Save and access the form
docs.text:
1. Select Save at the top right of the form screen.
  2. Use the View Page link that appears beside Save to open the form. Share this link with members of the public so they can register for the event.

You can now test the form and adjust it as needed.

docs.title: Create a membership signup form with online payment
docs.text:
Create a public FormBuilder form for membership signup and online payment. FormBuilder lets you use a layout that is more flexible than the strict layout of core Contribution Pages.

This example assumes the Stripe Payment Processor is installed on your CiviCRM system. See the Stripe Extension documentation. Other payment processors are available as FormBuilder Checkout Options.

docs.title: Check the membership type
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Membership > Membership Types.
  2. Check that you have a suitable membership type. For more information, see Membership Types.

docs.title: Create and configure the form
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. On the Submission Forms tab, select New Submission Form.
  3. In the configuration pane on the left, set Title to Join As A New Member.
  4. Set Permission to Allow all users (including anonymous).
  5. Set Page Route to a public URL, such as civicrm/christmasfundraiser.
  6. Under Frontend or Backend, choose Frontend so members of the public can access the form.

Optionally, configure what people see after submitting the form:

  • To redirect them to a page, enter its full web link, such as https://example.com, in Post-Submit.
  • Alternatively, add a confirmation message to display after submission. If you add one, save the message.

docs.title: Add membership and payment details
docs.text:
1. At the top of the form, click the + symbol and choose Membership. A Membership 1 tab appears.
  2. On Membership 1, click the down symbol under Values and choose Individual 1.
  3. From Add Value, choose Membership Type.
  4. Set Membership Type to the correct type for this form.
  5. From Add Value, choose Status.
  6. Set Status to Pending.
  7. From Add Value, choose Contribution Amount: Membership Amount.
  8. Choose the Membership Amount required for the form.
  9. At the top of the form, click the + symbol and choose Contribution. A Contribution 1 tab appears for contribution fields.
  10. On Contribution 1, under Values, change Contact from Select Current User to Individual 1.
  11. From Add Value, choose Checkout Option.
  12. Set Checkout Option to Stripe Embedded Checkout.
  13. From the Add column, drag Checkout Details onto the Contribution 1 section of the form layout.
  14. Use the settings wheel beside Contribution Amount to choose Remove field.
  15. Use the settings wheel beside Contribution Source to choose Remove field.

docs.title: Add contact fields
docs.text:
1. Return to the Individual 1 tab in the left panel.
  2. From the Add column, drag Contact Email(s) onto the Individual 1 section of the form layout.
  3. In the email block, toggle Multiple to Single.
  4. Select is Primary.
  5. Select a Location type.
  6. On Individual 1, scroll to Duplicate Matching.
  7. Choose the appropriate Duplicate Matching rule. The default is Email (reserved).
  8. In the right pane, use the settings wheel on each field in the form layout to tick Required.

You can also use the settings wheels to rename a Fieldset or Field, change background colors, and adjust other layout options. On Individual 1, you can drag other individual fields, such as address or phone number, onto the Individual 1 section of the form layout.

docs.title: Save and access the form
docs.text:
1. Click Save at the top right of the form screen. A View Page link appears next to Save.
  2. Use View Page to open the form for testing and adjustment. This is the link you will share with members of the public so they can register for the event.

docs.title: Add a custom autocomplete list to a form
docs.text: Create a filtered list of existing records, then add it to a form so your team can identify and select the right person. For example, you can list contacts with the Volunteer subtype and show their street address and city alongside their names when assigning event activities.

docs.title: Create the search list
docs.text:
1. In the main CiviCRM menu, go to Search and click SearchKit.
  2. Click New Search.
  3. In Search for, choose Contact or another specific record type you need to display, such as volunteers.
  4. In Where, add any filters needed to limit the list. For example, you might filter by availability, age or group membership.

docs.title: Set up the autocomplete display
docs.text:
1. Click + Add on the left and choose Autocomplete.
  2. Put the main searchable field, usually the contact's name, first in the list layout.
  3. Add informative fields below it, such as Street Address and City. They will appear alongside the name in the dropdown, helping users distinguish people with similar names.
  4. Set the contact name field to sort in Ascending order to display names alphabetically.
  5. Give the autocomplete display a clear name and save your progress.

docs.title: Add the list to your form
docs.text:
1. Open your form layout in FormBuilder.
  2. Find Existing Contact in the available fields under Add in the left-hand panel.
  3. Drag Existing Contact onto the form canvas where users should see it.
  4. Click the field's settings wheel on the canvas to open its properties.
  5. If relevant, change Type to Autocomplete.
  6. Under Saved Search, select the custom search list and autocomplete display you created.
  7. Check Required if a record must be selected before the form can be submitted.
  8. Turn on Auto-open if you want the dropdown to expand when someone clicks inside the field.

Choose the permission type before saving. Form-based lets anyone filling out the form see the full list of options; User-based applies when your organisation uses Access Control Lists (ACLs) to limit which contacts staff members can view based on their user accounts.

  1. Choose Form-based for a standard administrative form, or User-based when those ACL restrictions should apply.
  2. Save your form changes.

docs.title: Send a form using secret links
docs.text: You can email contacts individual form links that identify them and pre-fill their existing records without requiring a standard user account login. This uses secret-link access, similar to standard CiviCRM checksum behavior, rather than general public access.

docs.title: Configure the form
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. Open your form.
  3. In the left-side Form Settings pane, click the Permission selection box.
  4. Select Generic: Anyone with secret link. This setting authorizes incoming traffic only when the link includes a unique security token.
  5. Under Placement, find Expose To.
  6. Select Message Tokens. The form will then be available as an interactive mail-merge choice when you design broadcast communications.

docs.title: Insert the link into a message
docs.text:
1. Open your mailings manager or template builder to write a message to your supporters.
  2. Open the Tokens list in the message composer editor.
  3. Find your form in the token list.
  4. Insert its token into the email text or use it as the destination address for an “Update Your Info” button.

When CiviCRM sends the email, it replaces the token with a uniquely generated, encrypted link for each recipient. When clicked, the link matches the recipient to their database profile and pre-populates their existing records without exposing your system to general public tampering.

docs.title: Pre-fill a form using URL parameters
docs.text:
You can make a submission form quicker to complete by adding known default values to its published link. The values can pre-fill specific text fields or choice selections.

  1. Find the field key name for each field in your FormBuilder setup that you want to pre-fill.
  2. Add a question mark, the field key and the desired default value to your form’s published page route. For example: https://yourorganisation.org/civicrm/volunteer-signup?status=interested

docs.title: Date values
docs.text:
For a date default, use a value without spaces or special symbols. The source provides these formats:

  • receive_date=2026-06-30
  • receive_date=20260630
  • receive_date=20260630105600 — specifies the hour, minute and second
  • receive_date=this.month — uses a relative date; see the list of relative date formats

docs.title: Types of forms in FormBuilder
docs.text: The main FormBuilder page has tabs for submission forms, search forms and field blocks. Use this page to identify what each tab contains.

docs.title: Submission Forms
docs.text:
Submission forms collect information from members, supporters or staff. You can use FormBuilder to create interactive forms for manual data entry, such as creating new contacts or logging specific activities, without technical knowledge.

See creating data entry forms for more details.

docs.title: Search Forms
docs.text:
Search forms connect existing SearchKit configurations to FormBuilder so users can filter CiviCRM records on a dedicated screen. Your organisation might use one for a directory, a volunteer portal or an internal search page tailored to specific criteria.

See searching and reporting for more details.

docs.title: Field Blocks
docs.text: Field blocks are reusable templates for submission forms. By default, CiviCRM provides field blocks for items that can have more than one entry, including addresses, emails and notes, as well as a block for each custom field set. You can edit these blocks to suit your site's needs.

docs.title: What is FormBuilder?
docs.text: FormBuilder is a workspace for designing custom forms that capture and store information from members, supporters or staff. You can also connect it to SearchKit to create a directory, volunteer portal or internal search page tailored to specific criteria.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text: If FormBuilder is not already installed, the extension can be enabled on the extensions page. Once enabled, a FormBuilder link appears under Administer > Customize Data and Screens.

docs.title: Access to forms
docs.text:
Two permissions control who can create and edit new forms:

  • FormBuilder: edit and delete forms
  • FormBuilder: edit and delete own forms

You can control who can see a form in that form’s settings. If the form displays a SearchKit display, you can also control which results appear depending on the user. See SearchKit permissions for more detail.

docs.title: How CiviCRM translations work
docs.text: CiviCRM’s code and display strings are written in English. Translations make the interface available in dozens of languages, and each local language can be installed for use in CiviCRM.

docs.title: Where translated text comes from
docs.text:
CiviCRM starts with an English string in a translation call. If the user’s current language differs from the default, English US, it looks for a translation in this order:

  1. The .mo files downloaded and installed for different languages.
  2. The translation repository, if the .mo files have no match.
  3. Older translation columns for custom fields and option values or groups, if no match is found in the repository.

CiviCRM supports different languages, but developers rely on the community to translate missing interface text and languages that are not integrated. Community members can contribute through Transifex. You can download and install a language locally to see how well its translations suit your needs.

docs.title: Translating your own text
docs.text:
There are currently several ways to translate your own labels and strings. The aim is to move these into one system eventually:

  • FormBuilder
  • Custom Fields and Profiles
  • Option Values and Groups

If untranslated text is in a custom extension, you can normally contact its author and propose a translation. For more about contributing translations, see localising CiviCRM.

docs.title: Configure CiviCRM localization
docs.text: After initial setup, you can select a locale for your organisation’s language and country. If the default French translation is not the one you need, you can also map it to Canadian French.

docs.title: Select a locale
docs.text:
1. Go to Administer > Configure > Global Settings > Localization.
  2. Select the locale for your organisation’s language and country.

The Localization screen lets an administrator make this selection:

docs.title: Map French to Canadian French
docs.text:
If you need fr_CA instead of the default fr_FR (French from France), add this code to your civicrm.settings.php file:

define('CIVICRM_LANGUAGE_MAPPING_FR', 'fr_CA');

See CRM-9558 for more information.

docs.title: Translate profile field labels
docs.text: Translate labels you have changed in a Profile so they appear as intended in another language. Profiles work much like Custom Fields: if you do not change the default Label, Description, Pre/Post help text, the Profile uses a translation already available in core or in a previously translated Custom field.

docs.title: Translate a changed label
docs.text:
For example, you might have changed First Name to Your Name.

  1. Go to Administrator > Customize Data and Screens > Profiles.
  2. Click Fields for the Profile you want to translate.
  3. Click Edit for the field whose label you changed.
  4. Click the corresponding translate button. A popup opens where you can translate the label or value.

  1. Click Save.
  2. Repeat for other fields whose default labels you have changed.

You can now view the Profile in another language and see your field translations.

docs.title: Translate custom fields and groups
docs.text:
Translate an existing Custom Group and its fields so people can see your labels and values in another language. By default, CiviCRM normally copies labels and values from the default language into additional languages; you can then replace those copies with translations.

This process assumes you have already set up a multilingual system.

docs.title: Translate a custom field
docs.text:
1. Go to Administrator > Customize Data and Screens > Custom Fields.
  2. Edit the Custom Group that contains the field.
  3. Click Edit Field for the field you want to translate.
  4. Click the corresponding translate button.
  1. In the popup, translate the label or value.
  1. Click Save.
  2. Repeat for other translation options and fields as needed.

You can now view the group in another language and see your field translations.

docs.title: Translate a custom group
docs.text: In the Custom Group, click its Settings link rather than an Edit Field link. Use the language buttons to translate any group settings that have one, following the same process as for a custom field.

docs.title: Translate a FormBuilder form
docs.text:
You can translate text in a FormBuilder form by saving your changes and adding translations for an installed language. FormBuilder supports this translation process as of CiviCRM 6.10.

Your organisation must already have a multilingual system. During an upgrade, strings should normally be populated in the new translation system.

docs.title: Save text for translation
docs.text:
For field labels, options and descriptions, only changed values are saved in the translation repository. Unchanged values use their default translations.

  1. Go to Administer > Customize Data and Screens > FormBuilder.
  2. Edit your form.
  3. Change the labels, options or descriptions you want to translate.
  4. Click Save.

The changed strings from the form are now saved in the translation repository.

docs.title: Add a translation
docs.text:
Each installed language has its own translation repository. These repositories are used by FormBuilder and Scheduled Reminders; the source also identifies Searchkit as coming soon.

  1. Go to Administer > Locations > Translations to yourlanguage, where yourlanguage is one of the installed languages.

  1. Click + to translate a string into another language.

docs.title: How FormBuilder finds translations
docs.text:
FormBuilder looks in the translation system first, then in internal or extension translation files (.po files). This lets translations set for individual fields on a form take precedence.

Most FormBuilder strings can be translated, including options, titles, custom text, pre/post text and labels. If you find a string that should be translatable but is not, open a ticket.

docs.title: Translate option values and groups
docs.text:
Use this guide to translate option labels, group titles and descriptions in a multilingual system. When you create new Pricesets or Option Values, you need to translate them too.

Before you begin, make sure you have set up a multilingual system.

docs.title: Translate option values
docs.text:
1. Go to Administrator > Customize Data and Screens > Dropdown Options.
  2. Find the option group you want to translate and click Edit Options.
  3. Click Edit for an option, then click the translation button in its Label field.

A popup opens for translating the label.

  1. Translate the label in the popup.
  2. Click Save.
  3. Repeat for the other options you want to translate.

You can then view the group in another language to see the translated labels.

docs.title: Translate an option group
docs.text:
1. Find the option group under Administrator > Customize Data and Screens > Dropdown Options.
  2. Click its Settings link.
  3. Translate its Group Title and Description.
